noun:September.tx: Inherited from Middle High German september.

adj:synonym.tx: From Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), and συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”).

noun:Samstag.tx: From Middle High German sameȥtac, samȥtac, from Old High German sambaȥtag (“Sabbath day”), from Gothic *𐍃𐌰𐌼𐌱𐌰𐍄𐍉 (*sambatō), an alteration (possibly dialectal) of earlier, Biblical 𐍃𐌰𐌱𐌱𐌰𐍄𐍉 (sabbatō). The altered Gothic form derives from Koine Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”). Compare French samedi, Old French sambedi, Romansh somda, Romanian sâmbătă, Hungarian szombat, Old Church Slavonic сѫбота (sǫbota).

adv:so.tx: From Middle High German sō, from Old High German sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, compare with Old Dutch so and Dutch zo.

conj:so.tx: From Middle High German sō, from Old High German sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, compare with Old Dutch so and Dutch zo.

pron:so.tx: From Middle High German sō, from Old High German sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, compare with Old Dutch so and Dutch zo.

intj:so.tx: From Middle High German sō, from Old High German sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, compare with Old Dutch so and Dutch zo.

adj:safe.tx: English safe, originally borrowed in the context of safe sex (safer Sex, 1980s), later generalized.

adv:safe.tx: English safe, originally borrowed in the context of safe sex (safer Sex, 1980s), later generalized.

intj:servus.tx: An ellipsis from the commoners’ greeting once said to feudal lords, "servus humillimus [, Domine spectabilis]", in Latin meaning "(I am your) most humble servant[, (O/my) noble lord]".

verb:sehen.tx: From Middle High German sëhen, from Old High German sëhan, from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan. Compare Low German sehn, Hunsrik sihn, Dutch zien, English see, Danish se, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐍈𐌰𐌽 (saiƕan), Yiddish זען (zen).

verb:stricken.tx: From Middle High German stricken (“to tie, to knit”), from Old High German stricken (“to tie”), derived from the noun stric, whence modern Strick (“short rope for binding”). Compare Dutch strikken. Displaced Middle High German bretten (“to knit”). The obsolete sense “to tie” still underlies in compounds (see below).

adj:still.tx: From Middle High German stille, from Old High German stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.

adv:still.tx: From Middle High German stille, from Old High German stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.

adj:sicher.tx: From Middle High German siher, from Old High German sihur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“secure, sure”), from Latin sēcūrus (“worryless; carefree; secure”).

adv:sicher.tx: From Middle High German siher, from Old High German sihur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“secure, sure”), from Latin sēcūrus (“worryless; carefree; secure”).

noun:Sonnabend.tx: From Middle High German sunābent, sunnenābent, from Old High German sunnūnāband (literally “Sunday eve”) (9th c.), calqued on Old English sunnanǣfen. In the Germanic reckoning, the day begins at sunset. Compare Low German Sünnavend, West Frisian snjoen, sneaun, sneon.

noun:Straße.tx: Inherited from Middle High German strāȥe, from Old High German strāȥa, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), from Latin (via) strata. Sense 6 (“strait”) is a calque of Middle Low German strâte, itself a phono-semantic matching of Middle English streit, from Old French estreit (“narrow”), from unrelated Latin strictus.

noun:Sohle.tx: From Middle High German sole, from Old High German sola, borrowed from Vulgar Latin sola, plural of solum (“bottom, base”). Cognate with Hunsrik Sohl, English sole.

adj:schnell.tx: From Middle High German snël, from Old High German snël (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.

adv:schnell.tx: From Middle High German snël, from Old High German snël (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.

pron:sonne.tx: The usage of this term for plurals stems from the similarity or identity of female singular and (gender-unspecific) plural declensions in German grammar.

noun:Schaf.tx: From Middle High German schâf, from Old High German scāf. Akin to Bavarian Schåf, Luxembourgish Schof, Hunsrik Schof, German Low German Schaap, Dutch schaap, Afrikaans skaap, English sheep, and West Frisian skiep. See sheep for more.

noun:Schicksal.tx: 17th century, from schicken + -sal, after now archaic Dutch schiksel (16th c.).

verb:sein.tx: Inherited from Middle High German sīn, from Old High German sīn (“to be”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, an analogical infinitive formed within the suppletive paradigm of “to be” from forms ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be, exist”). It replaced the older infinitive wesan, from *wesaną (“to be, remain”). The paradigm is additionally suppleted with forms from *beuną (“to …

det:sein.tx: From Middle High German sein, sīn, from Old High German sīn, from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, from Proto-Germanic *sīnaz (“his own, her own, its own, their own”) (a reflexive possessive), from genitive of Proto-Indo-European *swé with denominative suffix Proto-Indo-European *-nós, equivalent to the genitive form of *se-. Cognate with Low German sien (“his, its”), Dutch zijn (“his, its”), Danish sin …

noun:Sehnsucht.tx: From sehnen (“to long”) + Sucht (“anxiety; sickness; addiction”).

noun:Stadt.tx: From Middle High German stat, from Old High German stat, from Proto-West Germanic *stadi, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis. Cognate with English stead. Doublet of Statt and Stätte.

pron:sie.tx: From Middle High German siu, si, from Old High German siu, si, from Proto-West Germanic *si(j)u, *sī, from Proto-Germanic *sī (see Proto-Germanic *iz). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌹 (si) and Old English sēo f (“that one”).

adj:schön.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz.

adv:schön.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz.

noun:Schlucht.tx: There are two etymological paths whose accuracy and possible interrelation are not conclusively established. * Schlucht is most readily explained as a Middle Low German form of the archaic High German equivalent Schluft, with the Low German development of -ft- → -cht- (cf. Nichte). Schluft pertains to the verb schliefen (“to slip, to move through”). This etymology is favoured by most authorities, …

noun:Sabbat.tx: From Middle High German sabbat, sābāot, sābot, from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”).

noun:Seele.tx: From Middle High German sēle, from Old High German sēula, sēla, from Proto-West Germanic *saiwalu, from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō. Cognate with Low German Seel, Dutch ziel, English soul, Danish sjæl. The type of bread is probably related to Allerseelen (“All Souls' Day”).

noun:Schnee.tx: From Middle High German snê, from Old High German snēo, from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw.

noun:Schmerz.tx: From Middle High German smerze m or f, from Old High German smerza f, smerzo m, from Proto-West Germanic *smertan. Cognate with English smart, Dutch smart.

noun:Schelm.tx: From Middle High German schelme (“pest, plague; those who have fallen in battle”), Old High German scalmo (“plague”), from Proto-West Germanic *skalmjan, umlauted derivation from *skalman (“plague, epidemic, corpse”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, part, divide”) or *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”). Cognate with Middle Low German schelm (“carrion, …

adj:schade.tx: From predicative use of Schade, the obsolete nominative singular of Schaden (“damage”). The sense “too good” from a conditional construction es wäre zu schade … (“it would be a pity to …”), but now usually construed with an indicative verb.

noun:Schatz.tx: From Middle High German schaz, schatz, from Old High German skaz, scaz, from Proto-West Germanic *skatt (“cattle, treasure”). Cognates Cognate with Old Norse skattr (Danish skat, Norwegian Bokmål skatt, Norwegian Nynorsk skatt, Swedish skatt), Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍄𐍄𐍃 (skatts), Old English sċeatt, Dutch schat.

adj:super.tx: Borrowed from Latin super; modern usage influenced by English super.

noun:Schlüssel.tx: From Middle High German slüȥȥel, from Old High German sluȥȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *slutil, which is derived from *sleutan (“to close”), from which also modern German schließen. Cognate with Dutch sleutel and English slot.

adj:schwarz.tx: From Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare Dutch zwart, English swart and swarthy, West Frisian swart, Danish sort, Yiddish שוואַרץ (shvarts).

adj:schwul.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German swōl, swūl (“sultry, hot and humid”) (17th century), adopted into Standard German as schwül in the 18th century, ultimately from the root of schwelen (“to smoulder”). The older form without umlaut appears in Berlin dialect in the 19th century in the current sense, building on the slang term warm (as in warmer Bruder) for ‘homosexual’. The earliest attestation of …

noun:Sekunde.tx: Borrowed from Latin secunda. The units of time and angle are from pars minuta secunda (literally “second minute part”).

noun:Schmeißfliege.tx: From schmeißen (“to defecate”, literally “to throw”) + Fliege (“fly”).

noun:Sprache.tx: From Middle High German sprāche, from Old High German sprāhha, from Proto-West Germanic *sprāku. Cognate with Dutch spraak, English speech, Danish sprog, Swedish språk.

noun:Schweinefleisch.tx: From Schwein (“pig”) + Fleisch (“meat”). Compare Silesian East Central German Schweinefleesch, English swineflesh (“pig-meat, pork”).

noun:Schwert.tx: From Middle High German swërt, from Old High German swërt (attested since the 8th century); from Proto-West Germanic *swerd, from Proto-Germanic *swerdą. The further etymology outside the Germanic branch is currently unknown: * According to Pfeifer, *swerdą, swerða- seems to be a nominal derivative with dental suffix originating from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to fester, to cut”) and may, thus, …

adj:schmuck.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German smuk (“supple, bendsome, pleasing, beautiful, petite, cute”) (compare Middle Low German smuk (“ornament, jewellery”)), from Old Saxon *smuk, *smukk, from Proto-Germanic *smukkaz (“flexible, bendsome, easy”).

num:sechs.tx: From Middle High German sehs, segs, ses, from Old High German sehs, from Proto-West Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

adj:stet.tx: Middle High German stæte, Old High German stāti, ultimately from the root of stehen (“to stand”). Cognate with Bavarian stad.

adj:spitz.tx: From Middle High German spiz, spitze, from Old High German spizzi. Related to Spitze.

adj:stark.tx: From Middle High German starc, from Old High German stark, from Proto-West Germanic *stark.

adj:stringent.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin stringēns, stringentem.

noun:Satan.tx: Inherited from Middle High German satān, from Old High German satan, borrowed from Latin Satan.

noun:Spielkarte.tx: From spielen + Karte or Spiel + Karte.

verb:spielen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German spil(e)n, from Old High German spilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spilōn. Cognate with Bavarian spuin, Alemannic German spiele.

noun:Sommer.tx: From Middle High German sumer, from Old High German sumar, from Proto-West Germanic *sumar. The expected modern form is Summer, as indeed found in most southern dialects, such as Alemannic German Summer, Bavarian Summer and Luxembourgish Summer. The vocalism -o- is of Central and Low German origin (compare Middle Low German som[m]er). Further cognates are Dutch zomer, West Frisian simmer, English …

noun:Schwein.tx: From Middle High German swīn, from Old High German swīn (akin to Old Saxon swīn), from Proto-West Germanic *swīn. Compare Low German Swin, Swien, Schwien (Schweyn), Dutch zwijn, English swine, Danish svin (also comparable to Latin suīnus and to Polish świnia).

noun:Sau.tx: From Middle High German sū, from Old High German sū, from Proto-West Germanic *sū.

noun:Steven.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German steven (“stick, support”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *stamniz (“tree stalk”).

noun:Säule.tx: Plural of now dialectal Saul, from Old High German sūl, from Proto-West Germanic *sūli, from Proto-Germanic *sūliz. Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌿𐌻𐍃 (sauls), English sile. More at sile.

conj:seit.tx: From Middle High German sīt, from Old High German sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīþuz. Akin to Old Saxon sīd, Old English sīþ. Related to Dutch sedert and sinds.

prep:seit.tx: From Middle High German sīt, from Old High German sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīþuz. Akin to Old Saxon sīd, Old English sīþ. Related to Dutch sedert and sinds.

adj:spack.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German spak (“thin, dry, brittle”) from spake (“brushwood”). Or from rare Middle Low German spak (“tame, calm”) from an unknown source.

verb:schreien.tx: From Middle High German schrien, from Old High German scrian, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skrīan. Compare English scream.

verb:sprechen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German sprëchen, from Old High German sprëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *sprekan. Compare Dutch spreken, English speak.

adj:solvent.tx: Ultimately from Latin solvens. In German possibly a backformation from insolvent.

adj:schwer.tx: From Middle High German swær, from Old High German swār, from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy, grave, serious”).

noun:Schlange.tx: From Middle High German slange, from Old High German slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô. Cognate with German Low German Slang (“snake”), Dutch slang (“snake”), West Frisian slang (“snake”). Compare also Albanian shlligë (“adder”).

noun:Sarg.tx: From Middle High German sarc, from Old High German sark, sarh, from Proto-West Germanic *sark (“grave, coffin”), ultimately from Greek sarcophagus. Cognate with Hunsrik Saarich, Sarrich.

noun:Seil.tx: From Middle High German seil, from Old High German seil, from Proto-West Germanic *sail, from Proto-Germanic *sailą.

adj:straff.tx: From late Middle High German straf, cognate with Dutch straf, with further origin uncertain. However, a semantic connection Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter(h₁)- (“to be stiff; be rigid; exert”) (whence Proto-Germanic *staraz (“stiff”)) has been proposed (DWDS).

noun:Schiedsrichter.tx: The second part is akin to Richter; the first part is akin to Middle High German schideman and to Old High German scidōn (“to separate, distinguish, decide”).

verb:strafen.tx: From Middle High German strāfen, most likely from Proto-Germanic *strēpōną (see Strafe (“punishment”)). Cognate with Luxembourgish strofen, Dutch straffen.

verb:steuern.tx: From Middle High German stiuren, from Old High German stiuren, from Proto-West Germanic *stiurijan, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną.

noun:Saxophon.tx: 19th century, from French saxophone. Equivalent to the name Adolphe Sax + -o- + -fon, from Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice”).

noun:Schuh.tx: From Middle High German schuo, levelled variant of schuoch (inflected schuo(h)-), from Old High German scuoh (“shoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *skōh. More at shoe. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schong, Dutch schoen, Low German Schoh, West Frisian skoech, English shoe, Danish sko.

noun:Sekretariat.tx: From French secrétariat, from Medieval Latin secretariatus, derived from sēcrētārius (“secretary”).

noun:S.tx: For the origin of the letter, see s. Orthography and pronunciation Single s in prevocalic position is pronounced /z/, except when it follows an obstruent within the word stem (e.g. Achse, bugsieren, Lotse, schubsen). /s/ is usually retained in recent borrowings from English (e.g. Sex), to a lesser degree also in recent borrowings from other languages (e.g. Salsa). Words from the classical …

noun:Saal.tx: From Middle High German sal, from Old High German sal, sali, seli, from Proto-West Germanic *sali, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, *salą, from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”). Cognate with Dutch zaal, Swedish sal, Old English sele, Russian село́ (seló). Also cognate with French salle. Compare English salon.

noun:Sabotage.tx: Ca. 1900, unadapted borrowing from French sabotage. By surface analysis, sabotieren + -age.

noun:Sache.tx: From Middle High German sache, from Old High German sahha, from Proto-West Germanic *saku, from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Cognate with Bavarian Såch, Yiddish זאַך (zakh), German Low German Sake, Low German Sake, Dutch zaak, Afrikaans saak, English sake, Danish sag, Swedish sak.

noun:Sack.tx: From Middle High German sac, from Old High German sac, from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz, from Latin saccus. Cognate with Dutch zak, English sack. The sense “man” without doubt partly from “scrotum”, but Sack was also formerly used to refer to the belly or the human body as a whole.

noun:Safari.tx: Early 20th century, from English safari, from Swahili safari (“journey”), from Arabic سَفَر (safar).

noun:Sage.tx: From Middle High German sage, from Old High German saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagā, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ.

noun:Sal.tx: Coined by Eduard Suess in 1909, in Das Antlitz der Erde, as a blend of translingual Si (silicon) + Al (aluminum).

noun:Salamander.tx: From Middle High German salamander, from Latin salamandra. The name of the drinking ritual may stem from the fact that it was once executed with flaming schnapps.

noun:Same.tx: From Northern Sami Sámi, from one of the Sami languages, of uncertain origin/meaning, but possibly related to Proto-Balto-Slavic *źémijāˀ (“land”). More at Sápmi and Sami.

noun:Samen.tx: From Middle High German sām, sāme, from Old High German sāmo, from Proto-West Germanic *sāmō, from Proto-Germanic *sēmô, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.

noun:Sand.tx: From Middle High German sant, from Old High German sant, from Proto-West Germanic *sand, *samd, from Proto-Germanic *sandaz, *samdaz. The forms with -n- are due to early assimilation. The more original form with -m- is attested in Middle High German sambt, sampt, which survives in some Bavarian dialects and in Yiddish זאַמד (zamd). Further cognate with Dutch zand, Low German Sand, English sand, Danish sand.

noun:Sauerkraut.tx: sauer (“sour”) + Kraut (“cabbage”). The sense “cabbage” in the word Kraut is southern German. Sauerkraut is not a traditional term in northern and central Germany, but has now become predominant in these areas, too.

noun:Scanner.tx: Borrowed from English scanner (“electronic device”). Analysable as scannen + -er. In the sense “one who scans” an independent ad-hoc derivation.

noun:Schatten.tx: From Middle High German schate, schatwe, schatewe, schetewe, from Old High German scato, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu; akin to Old Saxon skado, Dutch schaduw, English shadow and shade. More at shadow.

noun:Schema.tx: Borrowed from Latin schema. Not related to Schemen.

noun:Schmuck.tx: Borrowed from German Low German smuk, related to schmücken (“to decorate”); see there for more. Somewhat displaced Zier (“ornament”).

noun:Schmutz.tx: From Middle High German smuz. Cognate with Middle English bismitten (“to stain, soil”), Dutch smet (“spot, dirt”), English smut. Likely related to schmuddeln (“to become dirty”); see there for more.

noun:Schnecke.tx: From Middle High German snëcke, from Old High German sneggo, snecco, from Proto-Germanic *sneggô.

noun:Schwa.tx: Learned borrowing from Hebrew שווא / שְׁוָא (š’wā, “nought”).

noun:Schwarz.tx: From the adjective schwarz, from Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare German schwarz, Dutch zwart, English swart.

noun:See.tx: From Middle High German sê, from Old High German sē, sēo m (“sea”), from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi m (“sea”), from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz m (“sea”). Compare Low German See (“sea, lake”), Dutch zee f (“sea”), English sea, Danish sø c (“sea, lake”).

noun:Seiche.tx: From Middle High German seiche f, seich m (“urine; urination”), from Old High German seih m (“urine”), from Old High German seihhen, seichen (“to melt, liquify, strain, urinate”), from Proto-West Germanic *saikijan, from Proto-Germanic *saikijaną (“to make drip”), causative of *sīhwaną (“to filter, strain”). Related to German seihen.

noun:Sensation.tx: Borrowed from Latin sēnsātiō, from sēnsātus, from sēnsus, from sentīre. Semantic evolution influenced by English sensation.

noun:Sense.tx: From Middle High German sē̆nse, contraction of seinse, from older segense, from Old High German segansa, itself by metathesis from segisna, from Proto-West Germanic *sagisnu. Cognate with Dutch zeis. The development ei < ege is found in Central German, but also in Bavarian (compare Getreide, verteidigen etc.). In the latter, contraction of the diphthong yields sanse (as in zwanzig < zweinzec). …

noun:Seraph.tx: Back formation from Latin seraphim, also seraphin, a plural, from Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (s'rafím), plural of שָׂרָף (saráf) of which the meaning is uncertain; perhaps related to the root Hebrew שרף (“to burn”).

pron:Sie.tx: From Proto-Indo-European language pronominal stem -i and initial s. In the early Germanic languages, the sie is formed according to the above pattern, compare Gothic 𐍃𐌹 (si). The si/se was originally used to strengthen demonstrative pronouns, which is still preserved today in dieser, diese, dieses. The sie probably found its way into German primarily via the Old Saxon se, which developed as a …

noun:Singer.tx: Middle High German singer, equivalent to singen + -er

noun:Single.tx: In all senses from English single. The pronunciation is without /ɡ/ because German allows the cluster /ŋɡ/ only before full vowels, not before /ə/. The feminine gender of the musical sense is probably after Schallplatte f.

noun:Sinn.tx: From Middle High German sin, from Old High German sin, from Proto-West Germanic *sinn.

noun:Sirup.tx: From Middle High German sirup, sirop (13th c.), from Medieval Latin siruppus, siropus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “drink”). See English syrup for more.

noun:Ski.tx: Early 19th century, from Norwegian ski. Doublet of Scheit.

noun:Slalom.tx: Early 20th century, from Norwegian Bokmål slalåm.

noun:Slip.tx: Formally from English slip (“kind of underskirt”), but with the sense of etymologically related German Schlüpfer, also Schlüpper (“briefs, panties”).

noun:Smaragd.tx: From Middle High German smaract, from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language. Also written schmaragd in Early Modern German, and still widely so pronounced until the diffusion of the Siebs standard.

noun:Smog.tx: Borrowed from English smog (“a portmanteau word formed from smoke and fog”).

noun:Soap.tx: Borrowed from English soap, shortened from soap opera.

noun:Sofa.tx: 17th century, from French sofa, from Italian sofà, from Ottoman Turkish صفه (sofa), from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa).

noun:Sol.tx: Borrowed from Latin sol(ve) in the hymn for St. John the Baptist where all note names were taken from.

noun:Sold.tx: From Middle High German solt, from Old French solt, from Latin solidus (“a Roman gold coin”).

noun:Sole.tx: From Middle High German sol, sul, borrowed from Middle Low German sōle, sāle (“saltwater, brine”). Cognate with German Low German Söle, Sööl (“brine, pickling”).

noun:Sonne.tx: From Middle High German sunne, from Old High German sunna, from Proto-West Germanic *sunnā, from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *sh̥₂uén-, oblique stem of *sóh₂wl̥. Akin to Low German Sünn, Zunne, Dutch zon, English sun, West Frisian sinne, Icelandic sunna. Further Indo-European cognates include Latin sōl, Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios), Sanskrit सूर्य (sū́rya), Russian солнце …

noun:Sorge.tx: From Middle High German sorge (“sorrow; worry; care”), from Old High German sorga, sworga (“sorrow; worry”), from Proto-West Germanic *sorgu, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”). Cognate with Hunsrik Sorrich, Dutch zorg, English sorrow, Danish sorg.

noun:Soul.tx: Borrowed from English soul, from Middle English, from Old English sāwol (“soul, life, spirit, being”), from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō (“soul”). Doublet of Seele.

noun:Spalte.tx: From Middle High German spalde, variant of spalt, from Old High German spalt.

noun:Span.tx: From Middle High German spān, from Old High German spān (“chip of wood, shaving”), from Proto-West Germanic *spānu (“chip, shaving”). Cognate with Old English spōn (“piece of wood, chip”). More at spoon.

noun:Speck.tx: From Middle High German spec, from Old High German spek, from Proto-West Germanic *spik, from Proto-Germanic *spiką. Cognate with Old English spic (whence English speck).

noun:Spiel.tx: From Middle High German spil, from Old High German spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“dance”).

noun:Spindel.tx: From Middle High German spinnel, spinele, from Old High German spinnila, spinnela, spinnala, spinula, from Proto-West Germanic *spinnilu.

noun:Spirit.tx: Late 20th century, borrowed from English spirit. Doublet of Esprit, Spiritus, and Sprit.

noun:Sprung.tx: From Middle High German sprung, from Old High German sprung, sprunc, ultimately from the root of the verb springen (“to leap”). Compare Dutch sprong and Icelandic sprunga (“crack”).

noun:Spur.tx: From Middle High German spur, spor (usually n, also rarely m and f), from Old High German spor, *spur, from Proto-Germanic *spurą n. Cognate to Dutch spoor, whence (through Afrikaans) English spoor.

noun:Staat.tx: From Middle Low German stāt, from Middle Dutch staet, probably via Old French estat from Latin status. The semantic development was influenced by cognate modern French état. Doublet of Status and Etat.

noun:Stab.tx: From Middle High German stap, stab, from Old High German stab, from Proto-West Germanic *stab. Cognate with English staff, Dutch staf, Swedish stav, Old Norse stafr. The meaning co-workers is secondary: in the German word Generalstab (“General Staff”) the meaning changed from the staff as a symbol of authority to the group of military officers and later to any group of co-workers.

noun:Stall.tx: From Middle High German stal, from Old High German stal, from Proto-West Germanic *stall, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz.

noun:Stand.tx: From Middle High German stant, from Old High German *stant (attested in Old High German firstant, urstant), from Proto-West Germanic *stand, a deverbal from *standan (“to stand”). Cognate with English stand.

noun:Star.tx: From Middle High German star, stare, from Old High German stara, staro, star, from Proto-West Germanic *star. Cognate with Middle Dutch sterre, Middle Low German stār(e), Old English stær, Old Norse stari, and further with Latin sturnus.

noun:Status.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin status. Doublet of Staat and Etat.

noun:Steak.tx: Borrowed from English steak, from Old Norse steik.

noun:Stein.tx: From Middle High German stein, from Old High German stein, from Proto-West Germanic *stain, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *steyh₂-. Cognate with Yiddish שטיין (shteyn), Dutch steen, Low German Steen, West Frisian stien, Saterland Frisian Steen, English stone, Danish sten, Swedish sten, Norwegian stein, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (stains).

noun:Stern.tx: From Middle High German stërne, from Old High German sterno, from Proto-West Germanic *sternō, from Proto-Germanic *sternǭ, *sternô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. See also Dutch ster (“star”), Old English steorra (“star”) (Modern English star), Danish stjerne (“star”), Swedish stjärna (“star”), Icelandic stjarna (“star”), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌽𐍉 (stairnō); also Latin stēlla (“star”), …

noun:Stock.tx: From Middle High German stoc, from Old High German stoc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk.

noun:Stollen.tx: From Middle High German stolle, from Old High German stollo (“prop, post”), from Proto-Germanic *stullô (“support, post”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).

noun:Strafe.tx: From Middle High German strāfe, from Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”). Compare Dutch straf, German Low German Straaf, Luxembourgish Strof.

noun:Strand.tx: From Middle High German strant, from Old High German *strand, from Proto-Germanic *strandō. Cognate with English strand (“shore; beach”). More at strand.

noun:Strom.tx: From Middle High German stroum, strūm, strām, from Old High German stroum, strōm, from Proto-West Germanic *straum.

noun:Student.tx: From Middle High German studente, from Medieval Latin studēns.

noun:Sumo.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 相(す)撲(もう) (sumō).

noun:Sure.tx: Borrowed from Arabic سُورَة (sūra, “chapter of the Qur'an”).

noun:Swastika.tx: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit स्वस्तिक m (svastika).

noun:Synonym.tx: From Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon).

noun:System.tx: Borrowed from Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).

adj:secondhand.tx: Borrowed from English secondhand. Compare Romanian second-hand and Russian сѐконд-хе́нд (sèkond-xénd).

noun:Süßwasser.tx: From süß (“sweet”) + Wasser (“water”). For examples of the typology (fresh water being “sweet”), see English sweet water.

adj:süß.tx: From Middle High German süezi, from Old High German suozi (akin to Old Saxon swōti), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus. Compare Bavarian siaß, Low German sööt, German Low German soit- (Paderbornisch), Hunsrik sies, Dutch zoet, English sweet, Danish sød.

noun:Süße.tx: From Middle High German süeze, from Old High German suozī. Analyzable as süß + -e.

noun:Scharte.tx: From Middle High German scharte f, also schart f or m, from the adjective Old High German *scart (“wounded, cut up”, attested in liduscart), from Proto-Germanic *skardaz. Related with German scheren (“to shear”). Cognate with Middle Dutch schaert m, Middle Low German schārt n, Old English sceard n, Old Norse skarð n. All possibly from Proto-Germanic *skardą, although the deviating genders in …

verb:scheren.tx: From Middle High German schërn, from Old High German skëran, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran, from Proto-Germanic *skeraną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Akin to Low German scheren, Dutch scheren, West Frisian skarre, English shear, Danish skære.

noun:Schaufenster.tx: From schauen (“to look, to watch”) + Fenster (“window”).

verb:sparen.tx: From Middle High German sparn, from Old High German sparēn, sparōn, from Proto-West Germanic *sparēn. Compare English spare.

noun:Schnittlauch.tx: Inherited from Middle High German snitlouch, from Old High German snitalouh. By surface analysis, Schnitt + Lauch.

verb:schneiden.tx: From Middle High German snīden, from Old High German snīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *snīþan (“to cut”). Cognate with Dutch snijden (“to cut, carve, intersect”), Low German snieden (“to cut”), dialectal English snithe (“to cut”) (related to snide), Swedish snida (“to carve, engrave”), Icelandic sníða (“to trim, tailor”).

noun:Schneider.tx: From Middle High German snīdære, equivalent to schneiden + -er. Compare Yiddish שנײַדער (shnayder), dated Dutch snijder and Afrikaans snyer. Compare Schröder and Schrödinger as other German counterparts of Tailor and Taylor; also compare Cutter.

noun:Seide.tx: From Middle High German sīde, from Old High German sīda, from Proto-West Germanic *sīdā (“silk”), from sēta (“silk”), from Latin saeta (“horsehair; bristle; silk”).

verb:stochern.tx: 16th century, from archaic stochen (“to stir, stoke”) + -ern (frequentative suffix). Said verb is derived from Proto-West Germanic *stokōn (whence English stoke), possibly through Middle Low German stōken. See stochen for more. Ultimately related with stoßen (“to thrust”) and Stock (“stick”).

verb:stoßen.tx: From Middle High German stōȥen, from Old High German stōȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *stautan, from Proto-Germanic *stautaną, from Proto-Indo-European *stówd-e-ti, an o-grade intensive formation from *(s)tewd- (“to hit, push”). Akin to Old Norse stauta and steyta (whence Danish støde), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (stautan). Non-Germanic cognates include Latin tundo. Compare Sanskrit तुदति (tudáti, “to …

noun:Stößel.tx: From Middle High German stœʒel, from Old High German stōʒil, from Proto-West Germanic *stautil (compare Middle Low German stȫtele), from Proto-Germanic *stautaną + *-ilaz. Equivalent to stoßen + -el.

noun:Säure.tx: From Middle High German siure, from Old High German sūrī. Analysable as sauer (“sour”) + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Sekt.tx: Borrowed in the 17th century, and provided with a paragogic -t, from French (vin) sec (literally “dry wine”), which is also the original sense in German. The sense “sparkling wine” is believed to originate from an anecdote in 19th-century Berlin. The actor Ludwig Devrient supposedly ordered a bottle of wine using the phrase “Bring [er] mir Sekt, Schurke!”, based on the German translation of the …

noun:Sonntag.tx: From Middle High German sunne(n)tac, sun(n)tac, from Old High German sunnūntag (9th c.), from late Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag (“day of the sun”), a calque of Latin diēs Sōlis (4th c.), equivalent to Sonne + Tag. Compare Low German Sünndag, Dutch zondag, West Frisian snein, English Sunday, Danish søndag.

noun:Sonntagskleidung.tx: Sonntag (“Sunday”) + Kleidung (“clothing”). From the habit of going to church on Sunday. Especially in the rural population, the work clothes were changed for special fine clothing only worn on that day.

noun:Schrift.tx: From Middle High German schrift, from Old High German scrift, from Proto-West Germanic *skrifti (“writing, scripture”), from Latin scriptum.

verb:schreiben.tx: From Middle High German schrīben, from Old High German scrīban, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīban (“to write”), from Latin scrībō.

noun:Stickstoff.tx: Introduced by the Swiss physician Christopher Girtanner in 1791. Roughly equivalent to (er)sticken + Stoff, so called for its ability to quench fire.

noun:Sauerstoff.tx: From sauer + Stoff, calque of French oxygène, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp; of taste: pungent, acid”) + γένος (génos, “birth”), due to a mistaken early belief that oxygen was a necessary ingredient in all acids.

noun:Schwefel.tx: From Middle High German swëvel, from Old High German swëval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz; cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌹𐌱𐌻𐍃 (swibls).

noun:Selen.tx: Borrowed from French sélénium, the name coined by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1818 from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).

noun:Silber.tx: From Middle High German silber, from Old High German silbar, from Proto-West Germanic *silubr. Cognate with Dutch zilver, English silver.

noun:Scheiße.tx: From Middle High German schīze, from Old High German *skizi, from Proto-West Germanic *skiti, from Proto-Germanic *skītaz, *skitiz, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd- (“to part”). Germanic cognates include English shit, Low German Schiet, Dutch schijt, West Frisian skyt, Swedish skit. Standard High German terms derived from Low German are Schiet and Schitte.

verb:scheißen.tx: From Middle High German schīȥen, from Old High German *skīȥan (attested in biskīȥan), from Proto-West Germanic *skītan, from Proto-Germanic *skītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd-, *sḱeyd- (“to part with, separate, cut off”). Compare Low German schieten, Dutch schijten, and English shit, Danish skide.

noun:Stuhl.tx: From Middle High German stuol, from Old High German stuol, from Proto-West Germanic *stōl. Cognate with Dutch stoel, English stool, Swedish stol; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- and thus related to stehen.

noun:Schiss.tx: Deverbal from scheißen. Compare German Low German Scheet (“shit, fart”), Saterland Frisian Schäät, Skäät (“shit, fart”), English shit.

noun:Suaheli.tx: Ultimately from Arabic سَوَاحِل (sawāḥil, “coasts”); compare German Sahel.

noun:Schimmel.tx: From Middle High German schimel, schimmel, from Old High German skimbal (“mould”), ultimately from the root of scheinen (“to shine”). The expected Middle High German form is seemingly unattested *schimbel, but all three forms (schimel, schimmel, *schimbel) would have yielded modern German Schimmel. Cognate with Dutch schimmel (“mould”).

pron:sich.tx: From Middle High German sich, from Old High German sih, from Proto-Germanic *sek. Compare Yiddish זיך (zikh), Dutch zich. Unrelated to sicher. This pronoun was originally restricted to the accusative case, while simple personal pronouns were used in the dative. Dative use of sich in Middle High German was restricted to northern dialects of Central German. In Early Modern German, a rare dative sir …

verb:schnorren.tx: Rotwelsch, from a musical instrument, formerly used by beggar musicians, the Schnurre or Schnurrpfeife.

verb:stellen.tx: From Middle High German stellen, from Old High German stellen, from Proto-West Germanic *stalljan (“to put, position”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand”).

adj:spinal.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna.

adv:schon.tx: From Middle High German schōne (“beautifully; appropriately; completely”), from Old High German scōno (“beautifully”), adverb of scōni, whence German schön (“beautiful”). For sense development from "beautiful" to "indeed, surely; already" compare English pretty.

verb:schmecken.tx: From Middle High German smecken, from Old High German smecchen, from Proto-West Germanic *smakkijan (“to taste”), from Proto-West Germanic *smakku (“a taste”). Compare English smack and smatch, as well as Lithuanian smagù (“cheerful, enjoyable, pleasant”).

verb:schicken.tx: From Middle High German schicken (“to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately”), from Old High German *skihhen, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan (“to order, send”). This represents the causative of Middle High German geschehen, geschēn (“to happen, rush”). Akin to Middle English skekken (“to send out”), Old English sċēon (“to happen”), Dutch schie- in schielijk (“hasty”). Related to English chic.

verb:scheinen.tx: From Middle High German schīnen, from Old High German skīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan. Cognates include German Low German schienen, Dutch schijnen, English shine, Danish skinne, Esperanto ŝajni.

verb:stehen.tx: From Middle High German stān, stēn, from Old High German stān, stēn, from Proto-West Germanic *stān, from Proto-Germanic *stāną. The -h- was introduced into the spelling by analogy with sehen, in which it had become mute but was retained in spelling. Past forms are inherited from Old High German stuond, stuonden, etc. These are themselves suppletive of Proto-West Germanic *standan's past forms in …

verb:sitzen.tx: From Middle High German sitzen, from Old High German sizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan. Cognate with Dutch zitten, Low German sitten, English sit, Danish sidde.

noun:Schanze.tx: Of uncertain origin. Attested since the 15th century. Several etymologies have been proposed. Pfeifer suggests the regional Franconian/Hessian term Schanze (“basket”) (itself of unknown origin) as the origin, arguing that entrenchments resemble baskets from the inside, being dug-out earth pits that have been reinforced from the inside with brushwood. He rejects a derivation from Italian scansi …

verb:schaden.tx: From Middle High German schaden, from Old High German scadōn, from the root of the noun Schaden (“damage, harm”).

noun:Schaden.tx: From Middle High German schade, from Old High German skado, from Proto-West Germanic *skaþō, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô. Compare Dutch schade, Low German Schaden, Schaad, English scathe, Danish skade, Swedish skada.

noun:Schande.tx: From Middle High German schande, from Old High German scanta, from Proto-West Germanic *skandu, from Proto-Germanic *skandō (“shame, disgrace”). Cognate with Yiddish שאַנדע (shande), English shand, Dutch schande.

adj:scharf.tx: From Middle High German scharpf, from Old High German scarf, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Low German scharp, Dutch scherp, English sharp, Danish skarp.

noun:Schiff.tx: From Middle High German schif, from Old High German skif (“ship, barrel, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship, hollow object”). The sense “nave” is a semantic loan from Latin nāvis. Cognate with Low German Schipp, West Frisian skip, Dutch schip, Yiddish שיף (shif), English ship, Danish skib, Swedish skepp. Related also to Lithuanian skiẽbti (“to rip up”), …

noun:Schnur.tx: From Middle High German snuor, from Old High German snuor, from Proto-Germanic *snōrō. Cognate with Dutch snoer. Also related to English snare.

adj:strack.tx: From Middle High German strac (“straight”), from Old High German *strac (attested in framstrac), from Proto-Germanic *strakkaz (“straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *streg-, *treg- (“stiff, rigid”). Cognate with Dutch strak. More at stretch.

verb:strecken.tx: From Middle High German strecken, from Old High German strecken, from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan.

noun:Stunde.tx: From Middle High German stunde, from Old High German stunta, from Proto-West Germanic *stundu, from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“point in time, hour”). Cognate with Catalan estona (“while”), Hunsrik Stunn (“while, hour”), Low German Stunn, Stünn (“hour”), dated Dutch stond (“time”), English stound (“hour, while, moment, time”), Danish stund (“while”), Norwegian stund (“while”), Northern Sami stund …

noun:Stange.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German stanga, from Proto-Germanic *stangō. Compare English stang.

noun:Salz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German salz, from Old High German salz (akin to Old Saxon salt, Old Dutch salt, Old English sealt, Old Norse salt), from Proto-West Germanic *salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Compare Dutch zout, English salt, Danish salt. The Internet slang sense is a semantic loan from English salt.

noun:Schleier.tx: From Middle High German sleier, sleiger, sloiger, slogier. Of uncertain ultimate origin, but most likely borrowed; perhaps related to Latin stragulus (“covering”). Compare Middle Low German sleyer, sloier, sloiger, Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”).

noun:Schmetterling.tx: Attested ca. 1500, standard since the 18th century. From an East Central German dialect word, equivalent to Schmetten (“cream”) + -ling, due to an old belief that butterflies eat milk products or, in a more ornamented form, that witches transform themselves into butterflies in order to steal such products. Compare English butterfly.

noun:Sahne.tx: From Middle High German sāne, from Old French sain, saime, from Latin sagīna (“nourishment”), of uncertain origin. Compare Middle Low German sān, sāne, saeum, from the same Old French source.

noun:Schale.tx: From Middle High German schale, from Old High German scala, from Proto-West Germanic *skalu, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Dutch schaal (“shell”) and English shale. Also related with Dutch schil, English shell.

verb:schälen.tx: From Middle High German scheln, schelen, from Old High German skelen, skellen, from the noun scala, from Proto-West Germanic *skalu, from Proto-Germanic *skalō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, divide”) or *(s)kel- (“to cover”). Cognate with Bavarian schäin, schöln, schön, and Yiddish שיילן (sheyln).

verb:sterben.tx: From Middle High German stërben, from Old High German stërban, from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną, itself either from Proto-Indo-European *(s)terp- (“to lose force; lose sensibility, become numb; be dead, be motionless”) or from Proto-Indo-European *sterbʰ- (“to be stiff, become stiff”). Cognate with Dutch sterven, Low German starven, stiärven, sterven, staarven, West Frisian stjerre, English starve.

adj:sozial.tx: From Latin sociālis, via 18th century French social.

noun:Schmarotzer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German smorotzer. By surface analysis, schmarotzen + -er.

noun:Smoking.tx: Borrowed from French smoking, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English smoking jacket.

noun:Stahl.tx: From Middle High German stahel, from Old High German stahal, from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, *stahliją. Cognate with Dutch staal, Danish stål, Icelandic stál, also English steel.

verb:stehlen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German stëln, from Old High German stëlan, from Proto-West Germanic *stelan, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną.

noun:Stiefel.tx: From Middle High German stivel, from Old High German stival, borrowed from Old French estivel, perhaps from Latin aestas (“summer”) or Latin stipes (“tree trunk, log”).

noun:Siebenmeilenstiefel.tx: From sieben (“seven”) + Meilen (“miles”) + Stiefel (“boots”). In the German-speaking countries a mile was about 7.5 km (thus roughly 5 international miles).

num:sieben.tx: From Middle High German siben, from Old High German sibun, from Proto-West Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier Proto-Germanic *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Compare Dutch zeven, English seven.

verb:sieben.tx: From Middle High German siben or sieben, likely from Old High German sib (“a sieve”). By surface analysis, Sieb + -en.

noun:Sucht.tx: From Middle High German suht, from Old High German suht, from Proto-West Germanic *suhti, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz. Akin to German Low German Sücht, Dutch zucht, Old Norse sótt.

adj:süchtig.tx: From Old High German suhtīg, equivalent to Sucht + -ig. Related to Sucht. Cognate to Dutch zuchtig.

adj:schmackhaft.tx: Inherited from Middle High German smachaft, equivalent to (Ge)schmack + -haft

adj:schwach.tx: From Middle High German swach, from Old High German *swah, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Cognate with Dutch zwak, Scots swack, also English dialectal swack.

noun:Stehaufmännchen.tx: steh auf (“get up!”) + Männchen (“little man”), from aufstehen.

noun:Säge.tx: From Middle High German sage, from Old High German saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagu, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Compare Dutch zaag, West Frisian seage, English saw, Danish sav, Swedish såg; as well as (from Latin secāre) Italian sega, French scie.

noun:Schwanz.tx: From Middle High German swanz, from swanzen (“to swing”), derived from swanken, whence modern German schwanken (“to wobble”). Compare also Middle Low German swansen, swensen (“to skip, dance, strut, twirl”). Cognate of Yiddish שוואַנץ (shvants).

noun:Schwalbe.tx: From Middle High German swalwe, from Old High German swalwa, from Proto-West Germanic *swalwā. Cognate with Middle Dutch swaluwe (modern Dutch zwaluw), Old Saxon swala, Old English swealwe (modern English swallow), Old Norse svala (Danish svale, Swedish svala). The football sense from a saying „Der fliegt wie ’ne Schwalbe!“ (“The man flies like a swallow!”), or the like, punning on fliegen in the …

verb:schwänzeln.tx: From Middle High German swenzeln. By surface analysis, Schwanz + -eln.

noun:Speise.tx: From Middle High German spīse, from Old High German spīsa, from Proto-West Germanic *spīsā, borrowed from Latin expēnsa (“expense”) (Late Latin form spēsa).

verb:schweben.tx: From Middle High German swëben, from Old High German swëbēn, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną (“to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksweybʰ- (“to twist, turn around”).

noun:Skorpion.tx: From Middle High German scorpiōn, schorpiōn, relatinised variants of older schorpe, from Old High German scorpio, from Latin scorpiō, from Ancient Greek σκορπίων (skorpíōn), variant of σκορπίος (skorpíos).

noun:Stube.tx: From Middle High German stube, from Old High German stuba, from Proto-West Germanic *stubu.

noun:Spiegel.tx: From Middle High German spiegel, from Old High German spiegal, spēgal, from Proto-West Germanic *spēgl (“mirror”). Cognate with Hunsrik Spieghel.

noun:Spinne.tx: From Middle High German spinne, from Old High German spinna. Ultimately an agent noun from the verb from which spinnen (“to spin”) is derived. Cognate with Dutch spin (“spider”), archaic English spinner (“spider”).

verb:springen.tx: From Old High German springan, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sprenǵʰ-. Compare Low German springen, Dutch springen, West Frisian springe, English spring, Danish springe.

verb:speien.tx: From Middle High German spīen, from older spīwen, from Old High German spīwan, from Proto-West Germanic *spīwan, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną. Compare Dutch spuwen, spugen, English spew, Danish spy.

verb:spucken.tx: 16th century, expressive intensivation of Late Middle High German spūgen (15th c.), an East Central German variant of spīwen (“to spit”), whence modern speien. Until the earlier 19th century, spucken was considered colloquial, but then established itself as the usual standard word. The above-mentioned form spūgen is a dissimilation of Middle High German spūwen, which comes via the regular Central …

verb:schleudern.tx: From Middle High German slūdern, perhaps ultimately from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Related to schludern and schlottern.

noun:Schleuder.tx: From Early New High German schleuder, slewder, also attested as schluder, sluder. By surface analysis, back-formation from schleudern.

verb:sieden.tx: From Middle High German sieden, from Old High German siodan, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.

noun:Stachelbeere.tx: Stachel + Beere (“berry”). The term has been attested since at least the late 16th century; the 1607 dictionary Dictionnaire François-Allemand & Allemand-François contains the variant forms "Stachelbeer" and "Stichelbeer".

noun:Stachel.tx: From Middle High German stachel, from Late Old High German stahhil, from Old High German stakulla, from an extension of stechen with nominalizing suffix -ila.

noun:Stachelschwein.tx: 16th century, from Stachel (“spine, spike”) + Schwein (“pig, swine”), a calque of Latin porcus spīnōsus, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros).

noun:Schal.tx: Borrowed from English shawl, from Persian شال (šâl).

adj:schal.tx: From (late and northern) Middle High German schal (“tasteless, turbid”), borrowed from Middle Low German schal, from Proto-Germanic *skal-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to dry out”). Compare Swedish skäll (“thin, weak, bleak”), Old English sċeald (“shallow, flat”), whence modern English shallow and shoal.

noun:Specht.tx: From Middle High German spëht, from Old High German spëht, from Proto-West Germanic *spiht, from Proto-Germanic *spihtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *spiktós.

noun:Süden.tx: From Middle Low German sūden and Middle Dutch sūden. The form is already attested in Middle High German sūden, which replaces native Middle High German sunden from Old High German sundan. However, the modern form with a preserved monophthong must be directly from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch. The latter's influence is seen in the umlaut (compare the Middle Dutch pronunciation of -ū- [yː]). …

noun:Sülze.tx: From Middle High German sülze, from Old High German sulza, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“salt water, brine”). Compare Dutch zult.

num:sechzehn.tx: From Middle High German seh(s)zehen, from Old High German seh(s)zehan, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun. Equivalent to sechs + zehn. Compare Dutch zestien, West Frisian sechstjin, English sixteen, Danish seksten.

num:siebzehn.tx: From Middle High German sibenzehen, from Old High German sibunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to sieben + zehn. Compare Dutch zeventien, West Frisian santjin, English seventeen, Danish sytten.

num:sechzig.tx: From Middle High German seh(s)zec, from Old High German sehszug, from Proto-Germanic *sehs tigiwiz. Equivalent to sechs + -zig.

num:siebzig.tx: From Middle High German sibenzec, from Old High German sibunzug, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą. Equivalent to sieben + -zig. Cognate with Hunsrik sibzich.

noun:Streifen.tx: From Middle High German strīfe, from Old High German *strīfo, from Proto-West Germanic *strīpō, from Proto-Germanic *strīpô.

noun:Schild.tx: From Middle High German schilt m (“shield”) (genitive schiltes or schildes), from Old High German skilt, from Proto-West Germanic *skeldu, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keyt- (“shield, cover”). Cognate with Dutch schild, English shield, Danish skjold. The -ld- is due to sporadic revoicing, reinforced by unshifted forms in Central and Low German (cf. dulden, …

o: (die/ein) schiltkräd (plural: schiltkräden; 2nd half of the 15th century)
noun:Schildkröte.tx: By surface analysis, compound of Schild (“shield”) + Kröte (“toad”). Inherited from Middle High German (die/ein) schiltkräd (plural: schiltkräden; 2nd half of the 15th century), (ain) schiltkroten (ca. 1350).

noun:Schildpatt.tx: Middle Low German schildepadde, compare Dutch schildpad (“tortoise”).

verb:schildern.tx: 17th century, from Dutch schilderen (“to paint, picture”), in part through Middle Low German schildern. Equivalent to Schild (“shield”) + -er (agent suffix) + -n. From the painting of coats of arms on shields and related objects.

noun:Spargel.tx: From 15th-century Middle High German sparge, spargen, sparges, from Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, in part through Italian sparago, sparagio. The form in -el (16th c.) probably after such plant names as Kerbel, Kümmel.

noun:Säugetier.tx: Compound of säugen (“suckle, give suck”) + Tier (“animal”). Säuge- (from säugen (“to suckle”) is part of the compound Säugetier ("suckling animal") because female mammals nurse their young with milk, which is secreted from special glands, the mammary glands.

verb:säugen.tx: From Middle High German söugen, from Old High German sougen, from Proto-West Germanic *saugijan, from Proto-Germanic *saugijaną (“to cause to suck, nourish”), causative of Proto-Germanic *sūganą (“to suck”). Cognate with Old Saxon sōgian (“to suckle”), modern German Low German sögen (“to suckle”). Related to German saugen (“to suck”).

verb:saugen.tx: From Middle High German sūgen, from Old High German sūgan (“to suck”), from Proto-West Germanic *sūgan, from Proto-Germanic *sūganą, from Proto-Indo-European *sewk-. The sense “be inferior or objectionable”, which was never common and always somewhat jocular or tongue-in-cheek, is a semantic loan from English suck in the same sense. Compare Low German sugen, Dutch zuigen, Danish suge.

noun:Segel.tx: From Middle High German sëgel, from Old High German sëgal, from Proto-West Germanic *segl. The word was originally masculine in Upper German, while Central German usage varied. The neuter was later reinforced by cognate Middle Low German sēgel, seil n.

noun:Schlitz.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German sliz, related to archaic schleißen (“to split, tear”); see the latter for more.

noun:Strahl.tx: From Middle High German strāle f (rarely m), from Old High German strāla f, from Proto-West Germanic *strālu (“arrow”). Compare Dutch straal, English streal.

noun:Schminke.tx: An originally Central and Low German word, from late Middle High German smicke, smyncke (“make-up”), Middle Low German sminke. Further origin uncertain, but probably related with schmeichen, Middle Low German smēken (“to spread, stroke”).

adj:superb.tx: Borrowed from French superbe, from Latin superbus.

verb:schnarchen.tx: From Middle High German snarchen, from Old High German snarhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *snarkōn.

noun:Schnabel.tx: From Middle High German snabel, from Old High German snabul, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz (“snout, muzzle”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksnew- (“to scratch, rub”). Cognate with Dutch snavel, Saterland Frisian Snoabel (“beak, bill”), Old English snofl (“mucus, snivel”).

noun:Schulter.tx: From Old High German scultera, scultra, originally *skuldera, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldru (“shoulder”). Compare Low German Schuller, Dutch schouder, English shoulder, Danish skulder, Swedish skuldra.

noun:Scheitel.tx: From Middle High German scheitele, from Old High German sceitila, skeitila (“crest, summit, hill”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaidlu, *skaidilu (“top, crown, summit”). Compare with Yiddish שייטל (sheytl).

noun:Schiefer.tx: From Middle High German schiver, from Old High German skivaro. Related with Scheibe and scheiden.

noun:Schnaps.tx: From German Low German Snapps, originally “a sip (of liquor)”. Related to schnappen.

noun:Scheibe.tx: From Middle High German schībe, from Old High German skība, from Proto-West Germanic *skībā, from Proto-Germanic *skībǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, part, divide, separate”). Cognate with Dutch schijf, English shive, sheave, skive, Old Norse skífa.

noun:Silberfischchen.tx: Mid-19th century, from Silber (“silver”) + Fischchen (literally “little fish”), which latter had already been used in this sense on its own. As in English silverfish, the name is based on the somewhat fish-like form as well as movement of the insect.

noun:Silberfisch.tx: From Silber (“silver”) + Fisch (“fish”). In the name of the insect a backformation from Silberfischchen, itself an extended form of older Fischchen.

noun:Senf.tx: From Middle High German sënf, sënif, sënef, from Old High German sënaf, from Proto-West Germanic *senap.

noun:Suppe.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German suppe, soppe, sope, which spread under the reinforcing influence of French soupe. Both from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppô, *suppǭ (“broth, sop”), which is related to German saufen (“to drink”).

noun:Salbe.tx: From Middle High German salbe, from Old High German salba, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu, from Proto-Germanic *salbō.

noun:Seeteufel.tx: From See (“sea”) + Teufel (“devil”). Compare Dutch zeeduivel.

noun:Schrecke.tx: Clipping of Heuschrecke, but so already in Middle High German schrecke.

noun:Schober.tx: From Middle High German schober, from Old High German scobar, itself from the Proto-Germanic stem *skup- (“barn, shed”), from which also Schopf, Schuppen and English shop.

conj:sondern.tx: From Middle High German sunder, from Old High German suntar, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“isolated, particular, alone”).

intj:sondern.tx: From Middle High German sunder, from Old High German suntar, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“isolated, particular, alone”).

verb:sondern.tx: From Middle High German sundern, from Old High German suntarōn (“separate, distinguish”), from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną (“to sunder, to separate”). Cognate with English sunder, Dutch zonderen.

noun:Schafott.tx: 16th century, at first in the more general sense of “stage, podium”, from Dutch schavot, from Middle Dutch scavot, scafaut, from Old French eschafaud, variant of chafaud, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, probably derived from Latin fala. Doublet of Katafalk.

noun:Sund.tx: From Middle High German sunt (ca. 1300), borrowed from Middle Low German sunt, from Proto-Germanic *sundą.

noun:Satz.tx: From Middle High German saz, satz, deverbal from setzen. Compare Yiddish זעץ (zets, “a punch”).

verb:singen.tx: From Middle High German singen, from Old High German singan, from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.

verb:schwimmen.tx: From Middle High German swimmen, from Old High German swimman, from Proto-West Germanic *swimman, from Proto-Germanic *swimmaną. Compare Low German swimmen, Dutch zwemmen, English swim, Danish svømme.

verb:schlagen.tx: The more original form is schlah(e)n, from Middle High German slahen, from Old High German slahan, from Proto-West Germanic *slahan, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną. The modern -g- in the infinitive and present is inserted by analogy with the past forms and the related noun Schlag (see Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with Low German and Dutch slaan and Old English slēan (“to strike, beat, smite”) …

adv:sehr.tx: From Middle High German sēr, from Old High German sēr (“sored, injured”), from Proto-West Germanic *sair. Compare Dutch zeer and English sorely for a similar semantic development.

adv:schlechterdings.tx: 17th century, from schlechter Dinge (adverbial genitive plural) + -s (adverbial suffix, here redundant). The adjective schlecht retains the older sense “plain, simple”, now otherwise restricted to the variant schlicht (see there).

noun:Schwuchtel.tx: Probably akin to or derived from regional schwuchteln (“to dance around; prance”).

verb:scheiden.tx: From Middle High German scheiden, from Old High German sceidan, from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþan. See also Dutch scheiden, West Frisian skiede, and English shed. Outside Germanic, see Latin scindō (“to split”), Irish scian (“knife”), Lithuanian ski̇́esti (“to separate”), Old Church Slavonic чѣдити (čěditi, “to filter, strain”), Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”), Old Armenian ցտեմ (cʻtem, …

adj:simpel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German simpel, from Old French simple.

verb:sagen.tx: From Middle High German sagen, from Old High German sagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ-. Cognate with Bavarian sogn, Alemannic German säge, Low German seggen, Dutch zeggen, English say, Danish sige, Swedish säga.

adj:schuldig.tx: From Middle High German schuldec, from Old High German sculdig. Equivalent to Schuld + -ig. The form shows (chiefly southern) blocking of umlaut in -ul- + consonant, as usually in modern German (exceptions gülden, gültig, Sülze). Cognate with Luxembourgish schëlleg, Dutch schuldig.

noun:Schach.tx: From Middle High German schāch, from Arabic شاه (šāh), from Classical Persian شاه (šāh), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”). Doublet of Check, Schah, and Scheck. Oriental words were usually borrowed into Middle High German through Italian or Old French. Therefore the final /x/ is remarkable, because this sound was replaced with /k/ in Italian …

noun:Sänger.tx: Inherited from Middle High German senger, from Old High German sangāri; Sang + -er.

noun:Sumpf.tx: From Proto-Germanic *sumpaz. Cognate with English swamp and sump.

noun:Stimme.tx: From Middle High German stimme, from Old High German stimma or stimna, from Proto-West Germanic *stebnu, from Proto-Germanic *stebnō or *stamnijō from Proto-Indo-European *stomen- (“mouth, muzzle”). Cognate with Hunsrik Stimm, English steven, Old English stefn, Old English stemn (“voice”), Old Frisian stifne, stemme (“voice”), Old Saxon stemna (“voice”) (Dutch stem), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌹𐌱𐌽𐌰 (stibna, …

adj:spät.tx: From Middle High German spǣte, from Old High German spāti, from Proto-West Germanic *spādī, from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz. Cognate with Hunsrik sped, from Low German späd, archaic Dutch spade (“late”). Probably related to sparen (“to spare, conserve”).

verb:stoppen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German stoppen, from Old Saxon *stoppōn. As in Dutch stoppen, the sense “to stop” is figurative from water flow being stopped by plugging. Only in this figurative meaning has the form been adopted into standard German proper, under the reinforcing influence of English to stop. Doublet of stopfen and staffieren.

noun:Sympathie.tx: Borrowed from Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).

noun:Symphonie.tx: Borrowed from Latin symphōnia. Doublet of Sinfonie.

noun:Spruch.tx: From Middle High German spruch, from Old High German *spruh, from Proto-West Germanic *spruki (“saying”), related to the verb *sprekan (“to speak”). Cognate with Dutch spreuk, German Low German Spröök.

noun:Schlampe.tx: Related to Middle High German schlampen (cp. Bavarian schlàmpen (Tirolisch), schlampen (Bayerisch), schlumpen (Bayerisch)); see schlampen for more. Cognate to English schlump.

noun:Stoff.tx: First attested in the mid 17th century. Most likely borrowed from Early Modern Dutch stof, from Middle Dutch stoffe, borrowed from Old French estophe, estoffe, from estoffer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”). The word is ultimately Germanic and was borrowed into Old French from Old High German stoffōn, itself from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn, making it a doublet of stopfen (“to stuff, to plug”).

adj:serpens.tx: Borrowed from Latin serpēns, present active participle of serpō (“crawl, creep”).

noun:Seife.tx: From Middle High German seife, from Old High German seifa, seiffa, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, dribble, strain, trickle”). Cognate with Dutch zeep, Low German Seep, West Frisian sjippe, English soap.

noun:Schloss.tx: From Middle High German sloȥ, from Old High German sloȥ, ablaut to the verb schließen. Cognate with Dutch slot (“lock”), Hunsrik Schloss (“lock”), English slot.

noun:Saft.tx: From Middle High German saf, saft, from Old High German saf, from Proto-West Germanic *sap (“juice, sap”).

verb:setzen.tx: From Middle High German setzen, from Old High German sezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *sattjan. Cognate with Hunsrik setze, English set, Dutch zetten, and Yiddish זעצן (zetsn).

adj:sauer.tx: From Middle High German sūr, from Old High German sūr, from Proto-West Germanic *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, from Proto-Indo-European *súHros. Cognate to Low German suur, Dutch zuur, English sour, Danish sur, Swedish sur.

noun:Schoß.tx: From Middle High German schōȥ, schōȥe, from Old High German scōȥo, from Proto-Germanic *skautaz. Compare Dutch schoot, Icelandic skaut, Danish skød ("lap", "womb").

noun:Sessel.tx: From Middle High German sëȥȥel, from Old High German sëȥȥal, from Proto-Germanic *setlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Cognates include English settle, Dutch zetel, Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐍄𐌻𐍃 (sitls).

noun:Schüssel.tx: From Middle High German schüȥȥel, from Old High German scuȥȥila, from Proto-West Germanic *skutilu (“small bowl, dish”).

verb:suchen.tx: From Middle High German suochen, süechen, from Old High German suohhen, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“seek out”). Originally Upper German form without umlaut on long rounded vowel before velar, reinforced against the umlauted Central German form (cf. Luxembourgish sichen) by the umlautless past forms (cf. cognate English seek …

verb:schmelzen.tx: From Middle High German smëlzen, from Old High German smëlzan, from Proto-West Germanic *smeltan, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną. Akin to Old Saxon smeltan. Cognate with English smelt, Danish smelte, Dutch smelten, German Low German smölten. Through the meaning of soften: compare Old Church Slavonic младъ (mladŭ) (whence младость (mladostĭ, “softness”)), Latin mollis (“soft”).

verb:schließen.tx: From Middle High German slieȥen, from Old High German slioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *sleutan, from Proto-Germanic *slūtaną, *sleutaną (“to lock, shut”). Cognate with Old Saxon slūtan, Dutch sluiten, English slot.

verb:schießen.tx: From Middle High German schieȥen, from Old High German skioȥan. Cognate with Low German scheten, Dutch schieten, West Frisian sjitte, English shoot, Danish skyde, Faroese skjóta.

noun:Stelze.tx: From Middle High German stelze, from Old High German stelza, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *staltijǭ, which is related to *stalljan (“to place, put”). Cognate with Middle Low German stelte, Dutch stelt, English stilt.

noun:Schürze.tx: First attested in the 17th century and hence hardly inherited within High German. Probably from Middle Low German schörte, from Old Saxon *skurtia, from Proto-West Germanic *skurtijā. Adapted to the High German consonantism by conflation with related Late Middle High German schurz (modern German Schurz), a nominalisation of the adjective schurz (“short”), from Old High German schurz, from …

verb:schaffen.tx: From Middle High German schaffen (strong verb), from Old High German scafan, scaffen, byform of skephen, from Proto-West Germanic *skappjan. The form with -f- was chiefly backformed from the past participle giscaffan, but was also influenced by the regular present conjugations du skeffis, er skeffit, and by the weak verb in etymology 2 below. The form skephen survives in the (now archaic) variant …

noun:Schweiß.tx: From Middle High German sweiz, from Old High German sweiz, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, *swaitaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), *sweyd-. Cognate with German Low German Sweet, Dutch zweet, English sweat, West Frisian swit, Danish sved, and Yiddish שוויצן (shvitsn); see sweat for more.

verb:schwitzen.tx: From Middle High German switzen, from Old High German swizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *swittjan, from Proto-Germanic *switjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *swidyéti (“to sweat”). Cognates (without gemination): Dutch zweten, Danish svede, English sweat.

noun:Scherz.tx: From Middle High German scherz, further etymology uncertain (but nearly certainly related to scherzen, and thus cognate with Middle English schurt(t)en (“to amuse or enjoy oneself”)).

noun:Schinken.tx: From Middle High German schinke, from Old High German scinco, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō, from Proto-Germanic *skinkô, *skinkō (“shank; thigh”). In the sense “tome” originally student slang (18th c.), from the use of pigskin leather to bind such books. Related to German Low German Schinken (also: skinken, sschinken (Westphalian; linguistic spelling; accusative)) Middle Dutch schenke (“shin, …

noun:Schrank.tx: From Late Middle High German schranc, from Old High German scranc, from Proto-West Germanic *skrank, from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“grid, barrier”), probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). Cognate with German Low German Schrank (“barrier, barricade”).

noun:Strumpf.tx: From Middle High German strumpf, from Proto-Germanic *strumpaz (“stem, stalk”). The semantic shift from "stalk, stump" to "leg clothing" came about as a result of a fashion development, where originally one-piece leg garments were separated into two parts, the trousers and the socks. The socks were interpreted as the "stump", i.e. the remainder of the leg garment. Related to stramm and strampeln.

noun:Stufe.tx: From Middle High German stuofe, from Old High German stuofa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōpā, related to the verb *stappjan (“to tread, step”). Akin to Old Saxon stōpo. Cognate with Dutch stoep. More at stoop.

noun:Sturm.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German sturm (“storm”). The retention of the u vowel is irregular; it was lowered to o due to a-mutation in all other West Germanic languages and even Old Norse, despite German being the one Germanic language where a-mutation most consistently occurred, especially of u to o. Cognates Compare Luxembourgish Stuerm, Low German Storm, Dutch storm, English storm, …

verb:sollen.tx: From Middle High German suln, soln, scholn, schuln, from Old High German sculan, skulan, scolan, from Proto-West Germanic *skulan. Cognate with English shall and should, Dutch zullen, Danish skulle, Swedish skall and skulle, Yiddish זאָלן (zoln).

noun:Storch.tx: From Middle High German storch, storc, from Old High German storah, *storc(h), from Proto-West Germanic *stork, from Proto-Germanic *sturkaz. Cognate to dialectal Dutch stork, English stork, Swedish stork. The expected German form is also Stork, which was indeed in wide use, but has not become standardized. The shifted variant Storch is probably due to the use of epenthetic vowels in Old High …

noun:Suizid.tx: Learned borrowing from New Latin suicidium. First attested in the 18th century, but in more regular use only since the mid-20th century.

pt: plural of Scheit (“log, stick of firewood”)
verb:scheitern.tx: Verbal formation from Middle High German schīt, synchronically analyzed as Scheiter (“plural of Scheit (“log, stick of firewood”)”) + -n (“verbal suffix”). The modern sense of "to fail" is derived from figurative usage of the verb as "to fall to pieces (logs)" > "to fail" (DWDS).

noun:Stroh.tx: From Middle High German strō, from Old High German strō. Cognate with Old Norse strá, Old English streaw, Dutch stro, English straw.

noun:Schwester.tx: From Middle High German swëster, from Old High German swëster, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr. Compare Low German swester, Dutch zuster, English sister, Danish søster, Swedish syster.

noun:Schaum.tx: From Middle High German schūm, from Old High German scūm, from Proto-West Germanic *skūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz. Cognate to English scum.

noun:Sohn.tx: From Middle High German sun, from Old High German sunu, from Proto-West Germanic *sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús. Compare German Low German Söhn, from Middle Low German sone, from Old Saxon sunu. Compare Dutch zoon, English son, Danish søn, Norwegian Bokmål sønn, Norwegian Nynorsk son, Swedish son, Yiddish זון (zun), Gothic 𐍃𐌿𐌽𐌿𐍃 (sunus).

noun:Schuld.tx: From Middle High German schult, from Old High German sculd, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldi, from Proto-Germanic *skuldiz. Cognate with obsolete English shild (“debt, fault, guilt”).

noun:Schriftsteller.tx: From Schrift + erstellen + suffix -er with the loss of the er- prefix.

noun:Sehne.tx: From Middle High German sën(n)e, sën(e)we, from Old High German senawa, from Proto-West Germanic *sinu, which see. The forms Sehne and Senne alternated widely, though on the whole the former was more northern, the latter more southern.

noun:Schwelle.tx: From Middle High German swelle, from Old High German swelli, swella, from Proto-Germanic *swalī, from Proto-Indo-European *swel-, *sel- (“piece of wood; beam, post, balk, board, threshold, sill”).

noun:Stier.tx: From Middle High German stier (“bull”), from Old High German stior (“bull, calf of a bull”), from Proto-Germanic *steuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros.

verb:steigen.tx: From Middle High German stîgen, from Old High German stīgan, from Proto-West Germanic *stīgan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stīganą. Cognate with obsolete English sty.

adj:schier.tx: From Middle High German schir (“immediate, quick”) (adv. schire), Old High German skeri (“sharp, acute, quick, rapid”), likely cognate with Old Church Slavonic скоръ (skorŭ, “rapid”) (Russian ско́рый (skóryj)), Lithuanian skėrỹs (“grasshopper”), Ancient Greek σκαίρειν (skaírein, “to jump”); if so, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to move, sway, swing, jump”). Grimm assumes partial …

adv:schier.tx: From Middle High German schir (“immediate, quick”) (adv. schire), Old High German skeri (“sharp, acute, quick, rapid”), likely cognate with Old Church Slavonic скоръ (skorŭ, “rapid”) (Russian ско́рый (skóryj)), Lithuanian skėrỹs (“grasshopper”), Ancient Greek σκαίρειν (skaírein, “to jump”); if so, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to move, sway, swing, jump”). Grimm assumes partial …

noun:Schreibtisch.tx: From schreiben (“to write”) + Tisch (“table”). Equivalent to Luxembourgish Schreifdësch, Hunsrik Schreibdisch. Both components are ultimately from Latin.

verb:spähen.tx: From Middle High German spehen, from Old High German spehōn, spiohōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

verb:schlafen.tx: From Middle High German slāfen, from Old High German slāfan, from Proto-West Germanic *slāpan. Compare Low German slapen, Dutch slapen, English sleep.

noun:Sonnenaufgang.tx: From Old High German sunnūn ūfgang, from West Germanic *sunnōn upgang. Cognate with Dutch zonsopgang, Old English sunnan upgang. Equivalent to Sonne (“sun”) + -n- + Aufgang (“rising”).

adv:sonst.tx: From Middle High German sunst, sust, sus, from Old High German sus (“thus”), from Proto-West Germanic *sus, from *swā (“so”), formally related to Proto-West Germanic *þus (“thus”). Cognate with Hunsrik sunst, Old Saxon sus (Middle Low German süs), archaic Dutch zonst (“otherwise”), Alemannic German sus and suscht.

adj:schmal.tx: From Middle High German smal, from Old High German smal, from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Cognate with Dutch smal, Low German small, English small.

noun:Steuer.tx: From Middle High German stiure, from Old High German stiura (“support”). Related with the "helm, rudder" sense of Etymology 2 below, via semantic shift "helm" > "supporting post" > "support" > "supporting money" > "tax" (DWDS).

noun:Siegel.tx: From Middle High German sigel and Middle Low German seg(g)el, both from Latin sigillum. Compare Dutch zegel.

adj:selig.tx: From Middle High German sælic, sælec, nominalized sælde, from Old High German sālīg, nominalized sālida, from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg, derived from *sāli.

noun:Stamm.tx: From Middle High German stam, from Old High German stam, from Proto-West Germanic *stamni, from Proto-Germanic *stamnaz, *stamniz, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, stay”). Cognate with English stem.

noun:Saum.tx: From Middle High German soum, from Old High German soum, from Proto-West Germanic *saum (“seam, hem”).

noun:Schauer.tx: From Middle High German schūr, from Old High German scūr, from Proto-West Germanic *skūr, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Cognate with Dutch schoer, English shower, Swedish skur.

adj:sanft.tx: From Middle High German semfte, senfte, sanfte, from Old High German semfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (compare Proto-Germanic *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *sóm-tu-, possibly from *sem- (“one, whole”). Doublet of sacht. Cognate with English soft.

adj:selten.tx: From Middle High German sëlten, sëlden, from Old High German sëltan, from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā. Cognate with English seldom, Saterland Frisian säilden (“seldom”), West Frisian selden, komselden (“rare, seldom”), Dutch zelden, Danish sjælden, Norwegian sjelden, Swedish sällan, Faroese sjáldan, Icelandic sjaldan.

adv:selten.tx: From Middle High German sëlten, sëlden, from Old High German sëltan, from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā. Cognate with English seldom, Saterland Frisian säilden (“seldom”), West Frisian selden, komselden (“rare, seldom”), Dutch zelden, Danish sjælden, Norwegian sjelden, Swedish sällan, Faroese sjáldan, Icelandic sjaldan.

noun:Schlaf.tx: From earlier Slaf, from Middle High German slāf, from Old High German slāf, from Proto-West Germanic *slāp. Cognate with Hunsrik Schlof, Luxembourgish Schlof, Low German Slaap, Dutch slaap, and English sleep.

noun:Stütze.tx: From Middle High German stütze, ultimately from the root of stützen (“to support”).

adj:streng.tx: From Middle High German strenge, from Old High German strengi (“strong”), strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangijaz (“tight, tense”), *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”); related to Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“stiff”). Cognate with Dutch streng, English strong, Danish streng.

adv:streng.tx: From Middle High German strenge, from Old High German strengi (“strong”), strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangijaz (“tight, tense”), *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”); related to Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“stiff”). Cognate with Dutch streng, English strong, Danish streng.
