noun:Spaß.tx: From earlier Spasso, borrowed from Italian spasso, deverbal from spassare or spassarsela, from Vulgar Latin *expassāre, from expandō (“to stretch out”). Compare Saterland Frisian Spoas.

noun:Spieß.tx: From Middle High German spieȥ (“pike”), from Old High German spioȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *speut (“spear”). Cognate with Middle Dutch spiet, Old Saxon spiot. Merged semantically with Middle High German spiȥ (“spit”), from Old High German spiȥ, from Proto-Germanic *spituz. Cognate with Dutch spit, English spit, Swedish spett. Etymological relation between the two merged words is possible, but uncertain.

noun:Stoß.tx: From Middle High German stōz, from Old High German stōz, ultimately from the root of stoßen (“to shove”).

noun:Steiß.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German stiuz, from the root of stoßen (“to push”).

noun:Spross.tx: Doublet of Sprosse (“rung, sprout”), which see. Middle High German sprozze was a weak masculine. The apocopated form adopted strong declension, while the fuller form became feminine. The semantic distinction between both was introduced and advocated by the grammarian Gottsched (18th c.). It remains vague, however, except insofar as the masculine form is no longer possible in the sense of “rung”.

noun:Schuss.tx: From Middle High German schuȥ, from Old High German scuȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *skuti; whence English shoot and skeet. Cognate with Dutch scheut, Old English scyte, Icelandic skutur. Related to schießen and Schoss.

noun:Schluss.tx: From late Middle High German sluz, ultimately from the root of schließen (“to close, shut”). Compare Dutch slot. Related to English slot.

noun:Schutz.tx: From Middle High German schuz. See the verb schützen (“to defend”).

noun:Schütze.tx: From Middle High German schütze, from Old High German scuzzo, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (“to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (“bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). Compare English shut.

noun:Sicht.tx: From Middle High German siht, from Old High German siht, from Proto-West Germanic *sihti. Cognate with English sight.

noun:Schule.tx: From Middle High German schuole, from Old High German scuola.

noun:Schraube.tx: From Middle High German schrūbe. The earlier developments seem not to be quite clear; see screw for more.

noun:Steinbock.tx: From Middle High German steinboc, synchronically analyzed as Stein (“stone”) + Bock (“buck, ram”).

noun:Säbel.tx: From Late Middle High German sabel, possibly from Old Polish szabla (cp. Polish szabla), from Hungarian szablya.

verb:säen.tx: From Middle High German sæjen, from Old High German sāen, sājen, sāwen, from Proto-West Germanic *sāan, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-. Compare Dutch zaaien, English sow, Danish så, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (saian). The expected modern spelling would be with an -h- to mark the hiatus (as in mähen, nähen), but this was avoided to distinguish säen from sähen, subjunctive of sehen (“to see”).

noun:Saite.tx: From Middle High German seite, from Old High German seita (also seito m), from Proto-West Germanic *saidā, *saidō, from Proto-Germanic *saidô (“string, cord”). In the 17th century, the ⟨ei⟩ was changed to the homophonous ⟨ai⟩, in order to distinguish this word from Seite. Derived from Seite originally.

noun:Samt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German samīt, borrowed from Old French samit, from Medieval Latin samitum, borrowed from Medieval Greek ἑξάμιτος (hexámitos), from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-, “six”) + μῐ́τος (mĭ́tos, “thread, strand”).

noun:Sattel.tx: From Middle High German satel, from Old High German satal, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz. Cognate with Old Norse sǫðull, Old English sadol, Dutch zadel, English saddle.

noun:Schabe.tx: From Middle High German schabe (“scraper, chaff, moulding; moth, cockroach”), from Old High German scaba (“scraper, plane”), from Proto-Germanic *skabō (“scraper”). Cognate with Dutch schaaf (“plane”). Also related to German Low German Schabbe (“mange, scabies”), English scab.

noun:Schacht.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German schacht, from Old Saxon skaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schaft.

noun:Schaft.tx: From Middle High German schaft, from Old High German skaft, scaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schacht.

noun:Schachtel.tx: 15th century, from Italian scatola, with metathesis from Latin castulum, itself a diminutive of Lombardic Old High German kasto. Hence a doublet of inherited Kasten as well as the later borrowing Schatulle. The -ch- is due to a Bavarian consonantal development, for which compare Spachtel.

noun:Schädel.tx: From Middle High German schedel (“skull”). Further origin uncertain. Borrowing from Middle Low German schêdel (“top of the head, head, skull”), cognate with German Scheitel (“top of the head, parting of the hair”), suggests itself, but is not embraced in most of the literature. If that theory is correct, then it would be derived from Proto-West Germanic *skaidilu (“part in the hair, top, crown, crest, summit”).

noun:Schäfer.tx: From Middle High German schæfære, from late Old High German scāphāre. Equivalent to Schaf (“sheep”) + -er. Compare Dutch schaper, scheper.

noun:Schaukel.tx: With -au- by artificial adaptation to standard German from Low German Schukel, a lengthened variant of Low German Schuckel (also early modern German Schuckel), deverbal from schuckeln, schockeln, iterative of Middle Low German and Middle High German schocken, from Proto-West Germanic *skokkōn. Related with English shock.

noun:Schaufel.tx: From Middle High German schūfele, schūvele, from Old High German scūvala, from Proto-Germanic *skuflō. Cognate with English shovel.

noun:Schall.tx: From Middle High German schal, from Old High German scal, from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Dutch schal and Swedish skall. Compare English low (“to moo”).

noun:Scham.tx: From Middle High German schame, from Old High German scama, from Proto-West Germanic *skamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European [Term?]. Compare Dutch schaamte, English shame, Danish skam.

noun:Schar.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō. Cognate with English share, Swedish skara.

verb:schenken.tx: From Middle High German schenken, from Old High German scenken, from Proto-West Germanic *skankijan (“to pour, serve”).

adj:scheu.tx: From Middle High German schiech, schiehe, schie, schiuch, schiuhe, schūche, from Old High German *skioh, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh. The modern form goes back to the Central German forms with -iu-, -ū-. These are usually interpreted as alterations based on Scheu (noun) and scheuen (verb), though this does not seem unquestionable in view of Middle Dutch schu, Middle Low German schǖ. The form …

adj:schief.tx: From northern Middle High German schief, schīf (etc.), from Middle Low German schêf, from Old Saxon *skêf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaib, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz. Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare Central Franconian scheif, northernmost Luxembourgish scheef. Otherwise it was borrowed from Low German into the colonial dialects, i.e. East …

adv:schief.tx: From northern Middle High German schief, schīf (etc.), from Middle Low German schêf, from Old Saxon *skêf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaib, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz. Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare Central Franconian scheif, northernmost Luxembourgish scheef. Otherwise it was borrowed from Low German into the colonial dialects, i.e. East …

adj:schlank.tx: From Middle High German slanc, Middle Low German slank, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist, wind”), the source of schlingen.

adj:schlau.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, whence probably also Dutch sluw. Further origin uncertain. Probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), which seems to trace back to a Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewǵ- (“to crawl, slide”) (albeit without any known extra-Germanic cognates), if the original sense referred to sneaking and sliding. Related to Dutch sluiken (“to creep, smuggle, act …

noun:Scharlach.tx: From Middle High German scharlach, backformation from northern Middle High German scharlachen, from Middle Dutch scarlaken, alteration (based on Middle Dutch laken = German Laken) of older *scarlaten (early modern Dutch schaerlaten, southern Middle High German scharlāt), from Old French escarlate, from Persian سقرلاط (saqerlât), from Latin sigillātum.

noun:Schau.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schouwe, equivalent to a deverbal from schauen.

verb:schauen.tx: From Middle High German schouwen, from Old High German scouwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”). Cognate with Old English scēawian (“to look at, examine, show”). Compare English show.

noun:Scheide.tx: From Middle High German scheide, from Old High German sceida, from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþiju. Compare Low German scheed, Dutch schede, English sheath, Danish skede, Norwegian Bokmål skjede, Icelandic skeið. The anatomical sense (16th c.) is a calque of Latin vagīna. The sense “partition” is attested since Old High German, but as it is not found in other Germanic languages, it is sometimes …

noun:Schein.tx: From Middle High German schīn, Old High German scīn, skīn (“shine, brightness, light, ray”), from Proto-West Germanic *skīn, from Proto-Germanic *skīną. Cognate with Old Norse skína, Old Saxon scīnan, Old English sċīn (“phantom, ghost”), Dutch schijn, English shine, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌽 (skeinan).

noun:Scheit.tx: From Middle High German schīt, from Old High German scīt (“log of wood”), from Proto-West Germanic *skīd (“piece of wood”). Cognate with West Frisian skīd, Old Norse skíð (“plank; billet; ski”), Old English sċīd, English shide, Ancient Greek σχίζα (skhíza, “splinter”), Latvian skaida (“chip”), Lithuanian skëdrà. Doublet of Ski.

noun:Schemel.tx: From Middle High German schemel, schamel, from Old High German scamal, from Proto-West Germanic *skamul, *skamil (“stool, bench”). Doublet of Stabelle.

noun:Schenkel.tx: From Middle High German schenkel, schinkel, akin to Old High German scanca. More at shank.

noun:Scherbe.tx: From Middle High German scherbe, from Old High German scirbi, from Proto-Germanic *skarbōjan-, related to *skrapōną (“to scratch”).

noun:Schere.tx: From Middle High German schære, from Old High German scāri, plural of scār, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran. The spelling with -e- (instead of Schäre) is East Central German, probably reinforced by the related verb scheren (“to shear”). Cognate with Dutch schaar, English shears.

noun:Scheune.tx: From Middle High German schiune, from Old High German scugin(n)a, from a Proto-Germanic *sku(w)enjō-, for which see Proto-Germanic *skūrō (“shelter, shack”) for more. The word was originally chiefly East Central German versus otherwise predominant Scheuer (Austro-Bavarian also Stadel). Scheune is reinforced by cognate Low German Schüün.

noun:Schicht.tx: From northern Middle High German schiht, from Middle Low German schicht, schichte, derived from the verb schichten (whence German schichten). Cognate with Dutch schicht, English shift.

noun:Schiene.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schine, from Old High German skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu. Cognate with Dutch scheen, English shin.

noun:Schilf.tx: From Middle High German schilf, from Old High German sciluf, from Proto-West Germanic *skilp, *skilup (“reed, rush”).

noun:Schindel.tx: From Middle High German schindel, from Old High German scintula, from Proto-West Germanic *skindulā (“roof-shingle”).

noun:Schirm.tx: From Middle High German schirm, scherm, from Old High German skerm, skirm (“screen”), from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi (“fur, pelt, covering, screen”). More at screen. Compare scrim.

noun:Schlacht.tx: From Middle High German slaht, from Old High German slahta, ultimately from the root of schlagen (“to strike, hit”). Compare Danish slag (“battle, strike”). Cognate of English slaughter.

noun:Schlacke.tx: From Middle Low German slagge (“slag”, older “splinter of hammered iron”, 14th c.), from slān (“to hit, strike”), the cognate of German schlagen. Compare Dutch slak, English slag, both also from Middle Low German.

adj:schlaff.tx: From Middle High German slaf, from Old High German slaf, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). The same word of Low German origin is schlapp, a synonym in modern standard German.

adj:schlecht.tx: From earlier slecht, from Middle High German slëht, from Old High German slëht (see also schlicht), from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz. Cognate with English slight, Dutch slecht, Afrikaans sleg, Icelandic sléttur, Faroese slættur, Swedish slätt, Danish slet, Gothic 𐍃𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (slaihts), and Norwegian slett.

adv:schlecht.tx: From earlier slecht, from Middle High German slëht, from Old High German slëht (see also schlicht), from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz. Cognate with English slight, Dutch slecht, Afrikaans sleg, Icelandic sléttur, Faroese slættur, Swedish slätt, Danish slet, Gothic 𐍃𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (slaihts), and Norwegian slett.

noun:Schlag.tx: From Middle High German slac, from Old High German slag, from Proto-West Germanic *slagi (“a blow, strike”). Perhaps cognate to English slug (“hard blow”).

noun:Schlamm.tx: From either Middle Low German slam or Middle High German slam, which Pfeifer derives from a Proto-Germanic *slambaz, to which he considers schlemmen and Schlampe related. He further derives the term from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lembʰ- (“to hang limply”), for which see Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, hang down”) for more.

noun:Schlauch.tx: From Middle High German slūch (“waterskin, snakeskin, slough”). Immediately cognate with Old Saxon slūk, also related with English slough. From the same root as schlüpfen (“to hatch, slip”).

noun:Schleim.tx: From Middle High German slīm, from Old High German slīm, from Proto-Germanic *slīmą. Cognate with Dutch slijm, English slime.

verb:schleppen.tx: From Middle High German slepen, from Middle Low German slēpen, related to Old High German sleifen (“to drag”) and slifan (“to slip”), from Proto-West Germanic *sleupan. Compare native High German schleifen, Dutch slepen, Yiddish שלעפּן (shlepn) and English schlep.

adj:schlimm.tx: From earlier slim, from Middle High German slimp (“slanting, awry”), from Old High German slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“oblique, crooked”). Compare English slim (“thin”), Dutch slim (“clever, smart”), Middle Dutch slim (“bad, crooked”).

adv:schlimm.tx: From earlier slim, from Middle High German slimp (“slanting, awry”), from Old High German slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“oblique, crooked”). Compare English slim (“thin”), Dutch slim (“clever, smart”), Middle Dutch slim (“bad, crooked”).

noun:Schleuse.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German slūse, from Middle Dutch slūse, sluise, from Old French escluse (French écluse).

noun:Schlinge.tx: From Middle High German slinge, from Old High German slinga, from Proto-West Germanic *slingwan, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist”). Compare schlingen and English sling.

noun:Schlitten.tx: From Middle High German slite, from Old High German slito, from Proto-Germanic *slidô. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schlitt, Dutch slee, English sled and sleigh, Swedish släde, Icelandic sleði, Italian slitta.

noun:Schlittschuh.tx: Originally in the obsolete form of Schrittschuh (“step shoe, pace shoe”), from Schritt + Schuh, an old compound already attested in Old High German scritescuoh and Middle High German schritschuoch. Remodelled in modern German by association with Schlitten (“sleigh”). Compare Swedish skridsko.

verb:schlucken.tx: From Middle High German slucken, from Old High German (attested in the derived noun slucko (“glutton”)), probably ultimately onomatopoeic. Cognate with Dutch slokken.

noun:Schlummer.tx: From Late Middle High German slummer. From the verb schlummern.

verb:schlummern.tx: An originally Low and Central German word, from northern Middle High German slummen and Middle Low German slummeren, slommen, from Old High German *slūmēn, from Proto-Germanic *slūm-. Cognate with Dutch sluimeren, English slumber.

noun:Schlund.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German slunt, from the root of schlingen (“to swallow, gulp”).

noun:Schmalz.tx: From Middle High German smalz, from Old High German smalz, from Proto-West Germanic *smalt (“(molten) fat, lard”), an ablaut derivative of *smeltaną. Doublet of Emaille. The figurative sense in part as a backformation from schmalzig.

noun:Schmied.tx: From Middle High German smit, from Old High German smid, from Proto-West Germanic *smiþ, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz.

noun:Schnalle.tx: From Middle High German snalle (“buckle”), an ablauting formation to schnell (“fast, quick”).

noun:Schnauze.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German snûte, whence also the later doublet Schnute (“pouting mouth”). Further from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt (“snout”). Cognate with Dutch snuit, English snout. The forms Schnauße and somewhat later Schnauze are artificial adaptations to High German consonantism, probably under the influence of schnäuzen (“to blow one’s nose”), from Proto-West …

intj:Schnauze.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German snûte, whence also the later doublet Schnute (“pouting mouth”). Further from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt (“snout”). Cognate with Dutch snuit, English snout. The forms Schnauße and somewhat later Schnauze are artificial adaptations to High German consonantism, probably under the influence of schnäuzen (“to blow one’s nose”), from Proto-West …

noun:Schnitt.tx: From Middle High German snit, from Old High German snit, from Proto-West Germanic *snidi, from Proto-Germanic *snidiz.

noun:Schnitzel.tx: From Schnitz (“cut-off piece”) + -el. Pertaining to schneiden (“to cut”). The culinary sense spread from Austria and was therefore adopted in the regional neuter gender.

noun:Schnorchel.tx: Early 20th century, deverbal from Low German schnorgeln, snörgeln (“to snore, snuffle”, attested 19th century). So called because of the stertorous sound. Related to schnarchen (“to snore”). Doublet of obsolete Schnörchel (“a certain disease of pigeons”).

noun:Schnepfe.tx: From Middle High German snepfe, from Old High German snepfa, from the root of Schnabel (“beak, pecker”). Related to Icelandic mýrisnípa.

noun:Schnupfen.tx: From Middle High German snupfen, an intensive formation related to schnauben (“to snort”) (DWDS).

noun:Scholle.tx: From Middle High German scholle m or f, from Old High German scollo m, scolla f. The feminine gender is chiefly Central and Low German. Cognate with Dutch schol, Middle Low German scholle.

noun:Schopf.tx: From Middle High German schopf, akin to Old High German scuft, from Proto-West Germanic *skuft, from Proto-Germanic *skuftą. Akin to Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍆𐍄 (skuft, “hair of the head”), compare English sheaf, scruff, Old Norse skopt (“hair of the head”), skauf (“fox's tail”), North Frisian skuft (“back of the neck of a horse”), Dutch schoft (“withers (of a horse)”).

noun:Schote.tx: From Middle High German schōte (“pod; pea”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *skaudō (“sheath, husk”), which is probably related to *hūdijaną (“to conceal”). Cognate with Middle Low German schōde, Old Norse skauð, and perhaps the first element in Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍀𐍃 (skaudaraips).

noun:Schranke.tx: From Middle High German schranke, related to Old High German firskrenken (“to prevent”), German schränken (“to put or pile things crosswise”), from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“barrier, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”).

noun:Schritt.tx: From Middle High German schrit, from Old High German scrit, from Proto-Germanic *skriþiz or *skridiz. Compare *skrīþaną (“to walk, crawl”), whence schreiten. Cognate with Dutch schrede.

noun:Schrot.tx: From Middle High German schrōt, from Old High German scrōt, from Proto-Germanic *skraudō.

noun:Schrott.tx: From Ripuarian and Low Franconian Schrott (“scrap”), which is the same word as German Schrot (“groats”). The regional form is not, however, derived from Middle High German schrōt, but from a variant Middle High German schrāt, Middle Dutch *scraet (compare attested scrāden, an eastern variant of scrōden, whence modern Dutch schrooien).

noun:Schuft.tx: According to Kluge, borrowed from Middle Low German schūvūt (“eagle owl”) (itself onomatopoeic in origin). The word may have been applied to criminals because, like the bird, they shy away from the light of day.

noun:Schuppe.tx: From Middle High German schuope, schuoppe, schuppe, from Old High German scuobba, scuopa, from earlier *skōbba, ultimately from the root of schaben (“to scrape”). Cognate with Middle Low German schōpe, schōve, schubbe. One of the rare words with a long vowel followed by an original geminate (compare Haken). Different simplifications of this cluster led to the great variety of forms.

noun:Schuppen.tx: A nominal formation related to Schopf (“tuft, crown (of feathers)”), as they were originally covered with bundles of straw. Cognate with dialectal English shippon (“cow-shed”),, also cognate with English shop.

noun:Schuster.tx: From Middle High German schuochsūtære, from Old High German *skuohsūteri, from Proto-West Germanic *skōhasūtārī (“shoemaker”).

noun:Schutt.tx: From Late Middle High German schut.

noun:Schwager.tx: From Middle High German swāger, from Old High German swāger, swāgur, from Proto-West Germanic *swāgr, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz (“husband's brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *swēḱurós (“brother-in-law”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“husband's father”).

noun:Schwall.tx: From Middle High German swal, from the root of schwellen (“to swell”).

noun:Schwamm.tx: From Middle High German swamme, swam, swamp, from Old High German swamp, from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz. See also Old English swamm.

noun:Schwan.tx: From Middle High German swan, from Old High German swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). Compare Low German Swaan, Dutch zwaan, English swan, Swedish svan.

adj:schwanger.tx: From Middle High German swanger, from Old High German swangar, from Proto-West Germanic *swangr (“heavy”), further origin unknown. Cognate with Old English swangor, Dutch zwanger (“pregnant”), Yiddish שוואַנגער (shvanger, “pregnant”), and Norwegian Bokmål svanger (“pregnant”); compare also Lithuanian sunkùs (“heavy; difficult”).

noun:Schwarm.tx: From Middle High German swarm, from Old High German swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”). Compare Dutch zwerm, English swarm, Danish sværm. The sense “crush” is a backformation from the verb schwärmen; see there.

noun:Schwindel.tx: From Middle High German [Term?]. Cognate with Hunsrik Schwinnel.

noun:Schwung.tx: From Middle High German swunc, ablaut derivation from swingen, modern schwingen (“to swing”). Originally infrequent, but in general use since the 18th century.

verb:schwingen.tx: From Middle High German swingen, from Old High German swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą. Cognate with Low German swingen, English swing. Doublet of swingen.

noun:Schwur.tx: From Middle High German swuor, from Old High German swuor, from Proto-Germanic *swōraz (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”). Compare English swear and Vilamovian śwür.

noun:Segen.tx: From Middle High German segen, from Old High German segan, from Latin signum. Cognate to Low German Siägen (Münsterländisch, Lippisch). Compare English sign.

noun:Seite.tx: From Middle High German sît(e), from Old High German sīta, from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ. Cognate with Dutch zijde, Low German Siede, English side, Swedish sida.

noun:Semmel.tx: From Middle High German semele, Old High German semala, from Proto-West Germanic *similā (“wheat flour”). Compare Yiddish זעמל (zeml).

noun:Seuche.tx: From Middle High German siuche, from Old High German siuhhī; equivalent to siech (“sick”) + -e (“ness”).

noun:Sichel.tx: From Middle High German sichel, from Old High German sihhila, from Proto-West Germanic *sikilu.

noun:Sieb.tx: From Middle High German sip, from Old High German sib, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi. Cognate with Dutch zeef, English sieve.

noun:Sieg.tx: From Middle High German sige, sic, from Old High German sigu, sigi, from Proto-West Germanic *sigi, from Proto-Germanic *segaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”).

noun:Silbe.tx: From Middle High German silbe < sillebe < sillabe, from Old High German sillaba, borrowed from Latin syllaba.

noun:Sippe.tx: From Middle High German sippe, from Old High German sibba, sippa, from Proto-West Germanic *sibbju. Cognate with English sib.

noun:Sitte.tx: From Middle High German site, from Old High German situ, from Proto-West Germanic *sidu, from Proto-Germanic *siduz.

noun:Sitz.tx: From Middle High German siz, from Old High German siz, ultimately from the root of sitzen (“to sit”). Compare Old Norse sæti.

noun:Socke.tx: From Middle High German socke, from Old High German soc, a West Germanic borrowing from Latin soccus (“a light shoe or slipper, buskin”), from Ancient Greek σύκχος (súkkhos, “a kind of shoe”), probably from Phrygian or from an Anatolian language. Cognate with Scots sok (“sock, stocking”), West Frisian sok (“sock”), Dutch sok (“sock”), English sock, Danish sok, sokke (“sock”), Swedish sock, socka …

noun:Spalt.tx: From Middle High German spalt, from Old High German spalt.

noun:Spaten.tx: The word was originally restricted to Low and Central German: from Middle High German spade, spate and Middle Low German spade, both from Old Saxon spado (possibly also Old High German *spato), from Proto-Germanic *spadô. Due to its northern origin the form has undergone open-syllable lengthening before -t- (which was generally blocked in Upper German). Cognate to English spade; see there for further cognates.

noun:Spatz.tx: From Middle High German spaz, spatze, from a diminutive of sparwe, from Old High German sparo + -izo (compare Wanze and names like Fritz, Heinz, Kunz). Related with Sperling.

noun:Speer.tx: From Middle High German spër, from Old High German spër, from Proto-West Germanic *speru, from Proto-Germanic *speru. Compare Dutch speer, English spear.

noun:Speiche.tx: From Middle High German speiche, Old High German speihha, ultimately from the root of spitz (“spike”). Cognate with Old Norse spik (“spike, sprig”), Old Saxon spēca (“spoke”), Old English spāce, Dutch spaak, English spoke.

noun:Speichel.tx: From Old High German speihhil, cognate with Dutch speeksel.

noun:Speicher.tx: From Middle High German spīcher, from Old High German spīhhāri, from Proto-West Germanic *spīkārī, borrowed from Late Latin spīcārium.

noun:Sperling.tx: From Middle High German sperlinc, from Old High German sperili(n)g, derived from sparo. Within High German, Sperling was north-eastern versus southern and western Spatz (western also Müsche, cf. Dutch mus, which was not standardised and has now been replaced with Spatz). Sperling was reinforced by Middle Low German sperlinc.

verb:sperren.tx: From Middle High German sperren, from Old High German sperran. Cognate with English spar (“to bolt, bar”), from Proto-West Germanic *sparrijan, from Proto-Germanic *sparrijaną (“to block, bar”).

noun:Sperber.tx: From Middle High German sperwære, from Old High German sparwāri. Cognate with Dutch sperwer, French épervier, Italian sparviere. Related with Sperling (“sparrow”).

noun:Sporn.tx: From Middle High German spore, from Old High German sporo, from Proto-West Germanic *sporō, from Proto-Germanic *spurô. Cognate with Dutch spoor, English spur. The final -n of the modern form is from the Middle High German inflected forms. The development of a singular in -n with plural in -en is unique, though somewhat similar to that in Herr.

noun:Spott.tx: From Middle High German spot, from Old High German spot.

verb:spritzen.tx: From Middle High German sprützen (“to squirt”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sprittōną (“to disperse”).

noun:Spule.tx: From Middle High German spuole, from Old High German spuola, spuolo, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ, *spōlô (“spool”). More at spool.

noun:Stapel.tx: From Middle Low German stāpel, from Old Saxon stapol, from Proto-West Germanic *stapul (“pillar, post, basis, foundation”). Doublet of Etappe and Staffel.

noun:Stärke.tx: From Middle High German sterke, from Old High German starchī. By surface analysis, stark (“strong”) + -e.

noun:Stätte.tx: From Middle High German stat, from Old High German stat, from Proto-West Germanic *stadi, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz. Doublet of Statt and Stadt.

noun:Staub.tx: From Middle High German stoup, stoub from Old High German stoub, from Proto-West Germanic *staub, from Proto-Germanic *staubaz, related to *steubaną (“to smoke, fume, fly about”) (compare also Gestüpp). Related to stieben. Cognate with Danish støv, Norwegian Bokmål støv, Norwegian Nynorsk støv, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌿𐌱𐌾𐌿𐍃 (stubjus).

noun:Stau.tx: First attested in the 18th century, from Low German Stau, from Middle Low German stouw, stouwe (“weir”), probably a back-formation from stouwen (“to stop, dam”), from Old Saxon *stōwa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōu, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *stōō (“place”). Cognate with Dutch stuw. Alternatively the Dutch and Low German forms could be inherited from the Germanic noun (like English …

verb:stauen.tx: From Middle High German stouwen, from Old High German stouwen, from Proto-West Germanic *stōjan.

noun:Steg.tx: From Old High German steg. Germanic cognates include Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌲𐌰 (staiga, “way”), non-Germanic ones: Russian стезя́ (stezjá), Lithuanian stiga, Ancient Greek στίχος (stíkhos), Albanian shteg.

noun:Stempel.tx: Low German and Central German in form (Middle Low German stempel). This northern form replaces Middle High German stempfel from Old High German stemphal. Pertaining to stampfen (“to stamp”).

noun:Stich.tx: From Middle High German stich, from Old High German stih, from Proto-West Germanic *stiki (“puncture, prick”). Cognate with Dutch steek (“prick, stitch”), English stitch (“needlework”), Old English stician (“stick, stab, pierce, prick”).

noun:Stiefvater.tx: From Middle High German stiefvater, from Old High German stioffater, from Proto-West Germanic *steupafader, from Proto-Germanic *steupafadēr. Cognate with Dutch stiefvader, English stepfather, Danish stedfar, Swedish styvfar, Icelandic stjúpfaðir. By surface analysis, stief- (“step-”) + Vater (“father”).

noun:Schwiegermutter.tx: Expanded from earlier Schwieger (“mother-in-law”), from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱruh₂- (“woman's mother-in-law”) (compare *swéḱuros (“woman's father-in-law”)). By surface analysis, schwieger- + Mutter.

noun:Stiel.tx: From Middle High German stil, from Old High German stil, from Latin stilus. Doublet of Stil and Style.

noun:Stift.tx: From Middle High German stift /steft, from Old High German stift /steft, from Proto-West Germanic *stift, from Proto-Germanic *stiftaz (“pin, nail”); likely derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *steyp- (“stiff, erect”), whence also German steif (“stiff”). Cognate with German Low German Stift.

verb:stiften.tx: From Middle High German stiften, from Old High German stiften, from Proto-West Germanic *stiftijan, from Proto-Germanic *stiftijaną. See also steif (“stiff, rigid”) and Stift (“pin; pencil”), both likely from the same root. Compare typologically Russian утверди́ть (utverdítʹ) (akin to твёрдый (tvjórdyj)).

noun:Stirn.tx: From Middle High German stirne, from Old High German stirna, from Proto-West Germanic *stirniju.

noun:Staubsauger.tx: From Staub (“dust”) + saugen (“to suck”) + -er. The word itself is attested since at least 1846, originally in the textile industry. (see quote)

noun:Stöpsel.tx: Derived from German Low German and Central German stoppen in the sense of “to plug”.

verb:stopfen.tx: Middle High German stopfen, from Old High German stopfōn (“to close”), from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn.

noun:Strang.tx: From Middle High German strank, stranc, strange, from Old High German stranc, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ-; related to Middle High German strange f, from Old High German stranga (“strand”). Cognate with Low German Strenge, Dutch streng, English string, Danish streng, Latin stringere, Swedish sträng.

noun:Strähne.tx: From Middle High German strëne, from Old High German strëno, from Proto-West Germanic *strenō, from Proto-Germanic *strinô (“strip, strand”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“strip, line, streak”). Cognate with Dutch streen and probably English strand. The spelling -ä- indicates the Middle High German low/open -ë- (as sporadically in other words, e.g. Bär).

noun:Strauch.tx: From northern Middle High German strūch, from Old High German *strūh, from Proto-West Germanic *strūk. Cognate with Dutch struik, Middle Low German strûk. Upper German originally lacked the word and some dialects still avoid it today.

noun:Strauß.tx: Inherited from Middle High German, related to strotzen (“to teem with”), Icelandic strútur, Old Norse strútr.

noun:Streich.tx: From Middle High German streich, from Old High German *streih, from Proto-West Germanic *straik (“stroke”). Compare Dutch streek, English stroke. In Middle High German the form strīch also occurs, which is either an adaptation to, or a new derivation from, the underlying verb streichen. In Modern Standard German both forms would have merged, but most dialects continue West Germanic ai.

noun:Streit.tx: From Middle High German strīt, from Old High German strīt, from Proto-West Germanic *strīd, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaz.

noun:Strich.tx: From Middle High German strich, from Old High German strih, from Proto-West Germanic *striki.

noun:Strick.tx: From Middle High German stric, from Old High German stric, from Proto-West Germanic *strikk, possibly related to *strang (“severe, strict, strong”), but the appearance of the -kk- would be unexplained. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, shear”), similar to Latin stringo (“to draw tight”). Cognate with Dutch strik and Hunsrik Strick.

noun:Striemen.tx: From Middle High German strieme, with -n from the oblique cases; borrowed from Middle Low German strieme (compare Dutch striem), ultimately from the root of Strahl (“beam, ray”). Displaced native Middle High German strīm, strīme (“stripe”) (whence dialectal German Streim, Streime (“stripe”)), from Old High German strīmo (see Swedish strimma).

noun:Strudel.tx: From strudeln, from Middle High German strëden, from Old High German strëdan (“to burn, glow, hiss, whiz”), from Proto-Germanic *streþaną (“to burn, seethe, whirl”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to stream, flow, run”).

noun:Stück.tx: Inherited from Middle High German stücke, from Old High German stucki, from Proto-West Germanic *stukkī, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją. Cognate with Hunsrik Stick, Dutch stuk, Luxembourgish Stéck, Yiddish שטיק (shtik), dialectal English steck (“piece”). Doublet of Stuck.

noun:Stummel.tx: From Middle High German stumbel, from a substantivized variant of Old High German stumbal (“mutilated, trimmed”), ultimately from a nasal-extended formation of the root of either Stab (“rod, staff”) or Stumpf (“stump”), the latter two which have been thought to be related.

noun:Stumpf.tx: From Middle High German stumpf, stump, from Old High German stumpf, stumph, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz (“stump, blunt, part cut off”). Cognate with English stump.

noun:Sturz.tx: From Middle High German sturz, from Old High German sturz, related to Old High German sturzen (“to hurl, plunge, turn upside down”) (German stürzen). See start § Etymology 2.

noun:Stute.tx: From Middle High German stuot, from Old High German stuot (“herd of horses”), from Proto-Germanic *stōdą.

noun:Suche.tx: From Middle High German suoche, from a merger of Old High German suocha, suohha and Old High German suochī, suohhī. Cognate with German Low German Söke, Söök. Compare also German suchen and English seek, soke, soken.

noun:Sühne.tx: From Middle High German süene, suone, from Old High German suona, from Proto-Germanic *swōnō. Cognate with Dutch zoen (“kiss”).

noun:Sünde.tx: From Middle High German sunde, from Old High German sunta, from Proto-Germanic *sundī. Compare Dutch zonde, English sin, Danish synd.

noun:Sprosse.tx: From Middle High German sprozze m, from Old High German sprozzo (“rung”), from Proto-Germanic *sprutô, from the root of *spreutaną, whence sprießen. Cognate with Dutch sport (“rung”), Middle Low German sprōte (“rung, sprout”), Old English sprot(a) (“sprout”). The sense “sprout” seems to be original, but is not attested in High German before the 15th century. Doublet of Spross, which compare. The …

noun:Stecken.tx: From Middle High German stëcke, from Old High German stëcko.

noun:Stille.tx: From Middle High German stille, from Old High German stillī; equivalent to still + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Schwere.tx: Middle High German swære, from Old High German swārī, from Proto-West Germanic *swārī, from Proto-Germanic *swērį̄; equivalent to schwer + -e. Cognate with British English sweer.

noun:Sodomie.tx: From Late Latin sodomia, from the Biblical town Sodom (Genesis 18f.), from Ancient Greek Σόδομα (Sódoma), from Hebrew סדם (səḏōm).

verb:strapazieren.tx: 17th century, from Italian strapazzare (“to handle roughly”). By surface analysis, Strapaze + -ieren.

verb:sägen.tx: From Middle High German segen, sagen, from Old High German segōn, sagōn. Equivalent to Säge + -en. The two vocalic forms are considered ablaut variants, not umlaut variants; the spelling with -ä- is a compromise form.

verb:saufen.tx: From Middle High German soufen (“to drink, slurp, sink, go down”), from Old High German sūfan, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną. Cognate with Dutch zuipen, Swedish supa (Old Norse súpa), English sup.

verb:sausen.tx: From Middle High German sūsen, from Old High German sūsōn, of imitative origin.

adj:sauber.tx: From Middle High German sūber, from Old High German sūbar, from Proto-West Germanic *sūbrī, from Latin sobrius (“sober”).

verb:sammeln.tx: From Middle High German sameln, samlen, samelen, regarded as being formed by dissimilation from samenen, which ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *samnōną. Alternatively, inherited from Old High German *samalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *samalōn (“to bring together, assemble”).

verb:schalten.tx: From Middle High German schalten, from Old High German scaltan, from Proto-West Germanic *skaldan (“to push, shove”); further etymology obscure; according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, separate”), in which case related to English shell. Cognate with Old Saxon skaldan (“to push”).

verb:schelten.tx: From Middle High German schëlten, from Old High German skëltan, from Proto-Germanic *skeldaną. Compare English scold.

adj:schüchtern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German schüchter, whence also Dutch schuchter. Cognate with scheu. The final -n is an original case ending, which was sometimes added to the stem in Low German (compare German albern).

adv:schüchtern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German schüchter, whence also Dutch schuchter. Cognate with scheu. The final -n is an original case ending, which was sometimes added to the stem in Low German (compare German albern).

adj:schwül.tx: Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German swōl, swūl, in Standard German since the 18th century, ultimately from the root of schwelen (“to smoulder”). The umlaut is possibly due to analogy with kühl (“cool”). The unumlauted form schwul is limited to the sense “gay, homosexual”. Cognate with Dutch zwoel (“sultry; sensual”), Old Norse svalr (“cold”), English sweal, swelter.

adj:seicht.tx: From Middle High German sīhte (“low, shallow”). Related with sinken (“to sink”).

adj:schräg.tx: 16th century; derived from Middle High German schrage (“grid of items arranged crosswise, e.g. of wooden pegs”), probably related with schränken (“to arrange crosswise”), from Old High German screnken (“to slant”), from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“barrier, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). Cognate with Dutch schraag, German Schranke (“gate, barrier”). Older derivatives …

verb:schielen.tx: From Middle High German schilhen, from Old High German scilihen, from Proto-West Germanic *skilhijan, from Proto-Germanic *skilhijaną, *skilhwijaną (“to squint”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to bend; crook”). Related to Dutch scheel (“squinty; squint-eyed”), Old English sċeolh (“slanted; oblique; wry”). More at skelly (“to squint”).

verb:schimmern.tx: Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German schēmeren or Middle Dutch schemmern, intensive form of schemen (“to flash, blink”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *skīnan (“to shine”).

verb:schimpfen.tx: From Middle High German schimpfen, from Old High German skimpfen, from Proto-West Germanic *skimpijan. Cognate with dialectal English skimp (“to make fun of, scoff at”), Dutch schimpen (“to mock, scold”).

verb:schieben.tx: From Middle High German schieben, from Old High German skioban, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuban, from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ-. Cognate with Low German schuven, Dutch schuiven, English shove, Danish skubbe.

verb:schmuggeln.tx: Borrowed from Low German smuggeln, from Middle Low German smugen, from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to slip through, creep”). Compare Swedish smyga. Cognate with English smuggle, also a borrowing.

verb:schmeicheln.tx: From Middle High German smeicheln, smeichelen, of uncertain origin. Possibly an iterative of Middle High German smeichen; or alternatively from Old High German *smeihhalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *smaikulōn (“to caress, flatter, stroke”), an iterative of Proto-West Germanic *smaikōn. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *smē(y)g- / *smī̌g-, a guttural extension of Proto-Indo-European *smē- / …

verb:schmeißen.tx: From Middle High German smīzen, from Old High German smīzan, from Proto-West Germanic *smītan, from Proto-Germanic *smītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *smeyd-. Cognate with Dutch smijten, Low German smieten, English smite, Danish smide, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌼𐌴𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (bismeitan).

verb:schützen.tx: From late Middle High German schützen (“to protect”, literally “to dam up, contain”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuttjan (“to shut, enclose, protect”), either from the root of schießen (“to shoot (advance a barrier)”) or schütten (“to pour [pile up a protective wall]”). Cognate with English shut. Compare typologically Latin prōtegō, prōtectus (whence English protect), from Latin prō- + tegō.

verb:schwören.tx: From Middle High German swern, from Old High German swerien, sweren, from Proto-West Germanic *swarjan, from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *swer-. Compare Low German swören, sweren, Hunsrik schweere, Dutch zweren, English swear, Danish sværge, Swedish svära.

verb:schneien.tx: From Middle High German snīen, from Old High German snīwan, from Proto-West Germanic *snīwan, from Proto-Germanic *snīwaną.

verb:schlingen.tx: From Middle High German slingen, from Old High German slingan, from Proto-West Germanic *slingwan, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist”). Compare English sling.

verb:schleichen.tx: From Middle High German slīchen, from Old High German slīhhan. Compare also English slink, though formally unrelated. Cognate with English slick.

verb:schleifen.tx: From Middle High German slīfen (strong verb), from Old High German slīfan, from Proto-West Germanic *slīpan, from Proto-Germanic *slīpaną (“to slide, to whet”). The strong verb was restricted in Modern German to the sense “whet”, the sense “slide” was redistributed to the weak verb (etymology 2), although the split is not entirely clear-cut in practice (see usage notes below). This development …

verb:schonen.tx: From Middle High German schōnen, akin to the adjective schön.

verb:schöpfen.tx: From Middle High German schepfen, from Old High German skephen, from Proto-West Germanic *skappjan, from Proto-Germanic *skapjaną, an originally weak verb. Likely denominal from *skapą, whence regional German Schaff (“wooden container or rack: tub, barrel; cupboard”). The rounding of the vowel was caused by the adjacent consonants (cf. zwölf and various other words with Middle High German /e/).

verb:schlüpfen.tx: From Middle High German slüpfen, slupfen, from Old High German *slupfen, from Proto-Germanic *slupjaną, related to *sleupaną (“to slip, sneak”).

verb:schlürfen.tx: An onomatopoeic formation, perhaps somehow related, or of similar formation logic, to Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ- (“to sip, suck in”). Cognate with Dutch slurpen (whence also English slurp).

verb:schmiegen.tx: From Middle High German smiegen, from Old High German smiogan (“to pull up, contract, snuggle”), from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan, from Proto-Germanic *smeuganą.

verb:schmieren.tx: From Middle High German smirn, from older smirwen, from Old High German smirwen, from Proto-West Germanic *smirwijan, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną, derived from *smerwą, whence dated German Schmer (“fat”). The loss of -w- is mostly a Central German development; compare fahl and falb, etc. Cognate with Dutch smeren, English smear.

verb:schnappen.tx: From Middle High German snaben (“to snap, snort”), ultimately imitative of clattering jaws (lautmalend); compare also schnaufen (“to snort, pant”). Cognate with Dutch snappen, English snap.

verb:schwanken.tx: From late Middle High German swanken, ultimately from the root of schwingen (“to swing”). See also Schwang.

verb:schweigen.tx: From Middle High German swīgen, from Old High German swīgēn, from Proto-West Germanic *swīgēn. The verb was originally weak, but developed strong forms in early Middle High German.

verb:sehnen.tx: Uncertain; compare Middle High German senen (“sadness, grief, heartache”). Has been considered a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-, though whether in the "sow (seed)" or "longlasting" sense is unclear.

verb:splittern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German splitteren, since the 16th century. By surface analysis, Splitter + -n.

verb:spalten.tx: From Middle High German spalten (strong verb), from Old High German spaltan, ultimately from or related to Proto-West Germanic *spilþijan (“to destroy, spoil, ruin”). Cognate with English spald (“to split”), Danish spalte (“to split”), Norwegian Bokmål spalte (“to split”), Swedish spalta (“to split”).

noun:Saat.tx: From Middle High German sāt, from Old High German sāt, from Proto-West Germanic *sādi, from Proto-Germanic *sēdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *sētis-, *seh₁tis, from *seh₁- (“to sow”). Compare English seed, Low German Saad, Hunsrik Soot, Dutch zaad, Danish sæd.

verb:stechen.tx: From Middle High German stëchen, from Old High German stëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *stekan.

verb:schwellen.tx: From Middle High German swëllen, from Old High German swëllan, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną. Compare Low German swellen, Dutch zwellen, English swell, Swedish svälla.

adj:schmutzig.tx: From Schmutz + -ig, whence also dialectal Dutch smotsig. Compare also English smutty.

adj:stumpf.tx: From Middle High German stumpf, from late Old High German stumph, from the root of Stumpf (“stump, stub”).

verb:sinken.tx: From Middle High German sinken, from Old High German sinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną. Compare Low German sinken, Dutch zinken, English sink, Danish synke, Swedish sjunka.

verb:senden.tx: From Middle High German senden, from Old High German senten, from Proto-West Germanic *sandijan. Compare Dutch zenden, English send, Danish sende, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (sandjan).

verb:sengen.tx: From Middle High German sengen, from Old High German *sengen, from Proto-West Germanic *sangijan (“to burn, torch”), from Proto-Germanic *sangijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *senk- (“to burn”).

verb:seufzen.tx: From Middle High German siufzen, alteration (after the suffix -zen as in ächzen etc.) of earlier siuften, sūften, from Old High German sūftēn, sūft(e)ōn, from Proto-West Germanic *sūftēn, *sūftōn. Cognate with Dutch zuchten, Middle Low German süchten, süften.

verb:senken.tx: From Old High German senken, from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną. Causative of sinken.

verb:sickern.tx: An iterative construction, seihen + -ern, with emphatic doubling of the consonant, preserving the original /k/. Exclusively dialectal until the 19th century.

verb:sprühen.tx: From Middle High German spræjen, spræwen, ultimately from some derivative of Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to sprinkle, scatter, strew”), see also Latin spargō, English sprout. Compare Middle Dutch sprayen, spraeyen, Dutch sproeien (“to spray”). See spray for more.

verb:spannen.tx: From Middle High German spannen, from Old High German spannan, from Proto-Germanic *spannaną.

verb:spazieren.tx: Inherited from Middle High German spazieren (13th c.), from Italian spaziare, from Latin spatiāri.

verb:spülen.tx: From Middle High German spüelen, from Old High German *spuolen (attested in Old High German irspuolen (“to wash”)), from Proto-West Germanic *spōlijan.

verb:spüren.tx: From Middle High German spüren, spuren, spurn, from Old High German spurien, spurren, from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną. By surface analysis, Spur + -en. Cognate with dialectal English speer, Scots speir, Swedish spörja.

verb:sprengen.tx: From Middle High German sprengen, from Old High German sprengen, from Proto-West Germanic *sprangijan, from Proto-Germanic *sprangijaną, causative of *springaną.

verb:spinnen.tx: From Middle High German spinnen, from Old High German spinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *spinnan. Compare Low German spinnen, Dutch spinnen, English spin, Danish spinde, Swedish spinna, Gothic 𐍃𐍀𐌹𐌽𐌽𐌰𐌽 (spinnan).

verb:sprenkeln.tx: Attested 16th century. Cognate with Dutch sprenkelen, English sprinkle. Possibly a frequentative of sprengen (“to spray, to water”), from Proto-Germanic *sprangijaną. Alternatively denominal from Sprenkel, from Middle High German sprenkel, sprinkel, which would then be a nasalised variant of spreckel (“spot”), from the root of Proto-Germanic *sprakô (“spark”). Compare Middle Dutch sprank (“spark” …

verb:stinken.tx: From Middle High German stinken, from Old High German stinkan, stincan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną. Compare Dutch stinken, English stink.

verb:stöhnen.tx: From northern Middle High German stenen and Middle Low German stȫnen, stēnen, from Old Saxon *stenan, from Proto-Germanic *stenaną. Cognate with Dutch steunen. The rounded vowel likely through merger with another verb, either Middle Low German stōnen, from Proto-Germanic *stunōną (English stun), or a descendant of *stunjaną (Old Norse stynja).

verb:stolpern.tx: Iterative verb form of archaic stopeln (“to be stiff”), according to Kluge, an imitative verb similar to holpern; this is considered possible by Pfeifer, though he expresses skepticism.

verb:stören.tx: From Middle High German stören, from Old High German stōren, from Proto-West Germanic *staurijan.

adj:stramm.tx: From Middle Low German stram. Cognate with Dutch stram (possibly also from Low German). Further origin uncertain.

adj:steif.tx: From Middle High German stīf, from Old High German *stīf, from Proto-West Germanic *stīf.

adj:starr.tx: From Middle High German star, from Old High German *star, from Proto-West Germanic *star.

adj:stumm.tx: From Middle High German stum, from Old High German stum, from Proto-West Germanic *stumm. Cognate with Dutch stom.

verb:staunen.tx: Attested since the 17th century, then introduced in the general written language by Albrecht von Haller (1708-1777), from Alemannic German stūnen, of uncertain origin. Probably related to stauen (“to dam, retain”). Alternatively—though less likely both on semantic and phonetic grounds—from Old French estoner, whence English astound, astonish. Probably not related to English stun (German stöhnen). …

verb:stampfen.tx: From Middle High German stampfen, from Old High German stampfōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, from Proto-Indo-European *stembʰ- (“to trample down”).

verb:stecken.tx: From Middle High German stecken, from Old High German steckōn, a geminated derivative of stëhhan, whence modern stechen.

verb:sticken.tx: From Middle High German sticken, from Old High German sticken, perhaps related to Stich (“prick, stab”) or stecken (“to stick, pin, insert”).

verb:summen.tx: From Middle High German summen, ultimately imitative. Compare German Low German summen (“to buzz, hum”), Saterland Frisian sumje (“to buzz, hum”), Middle English summen (“to buzz, hum”), Dutch zoemen (“to buzz”).

noun:Schokolade.tx: Borrowed from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.

adj:subtil.tx: From Middle High German subtīl (13th c.), from Latin subtīlis. It was fairly well integrated in Middle High German. Accordingly a diphthongised form subteil is attested (albeit rarely) and the word is also current in some dialects. Since the 18th century it has become less frequent and more restricted to learned parlance.

noun:Selbstmord.tx: selbst (“self”) + Mord (“murder”). Compare Dutch zelfmoord, English self-murder.

adv:selbst.tx: With excrescent -t (same: eins > einst, su(n)s > sonst etc.) fossilized from the neutral gendered Middle High German sëlbes, from the Old High German pronoun sëlb, sëlbo, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”). Compare Low German sulv, Dutch zelf, English self, Danish selv.

noun:Schnelligkeit.tx: From Middle High German snellecheit, an extended form of Middle and Old High German snelheit. Equivalent to schnell + -igkeit. The simpler form Schnellheit is now substandard, but may still be heard (chiefly as an ad-hoc formation); compare Dutch snelheid.

noun:Sonnenlicht.tx: From Middle High German sunnenlieht, from Old High German sunnūnlioht, equivalent to Sonne (“sun”) + -n- + Licht (“light”).

noun:Scheherazade.tx: Borrowed from Russian Шехераза́да (Šexerazáda), from Persian شهرازاد (šahrâzâd), alternative form of شهرزاد (šahrzâd, literally “child of the city”), from شهر (šahr, “city”) + ـزاد (-zâd, “child of”). The noun is a reference to the fictional character.

noun:Schaltjahr.tx: From Middle High German schaltjār, from Old High German scaltjār, from scaltan (“to push forward”).

noun:Steinzeit.tx: Shortening of Steinzeitalter. Equivalent to Stein (“stone”) + Zeit (“time; age”).

noun:Skalar.tx: Borrowed from Latin scālāris. from scāla (“ladder, stairs”).

adj:stolz.tx: From Middle High German stolz, from Old High German stolz, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz (“proud, stately, stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, stand”); cognate with English stout.

adj:spezifisch.tx: From French spécifique (with the suffix -ique replaced by -isch), from Late Latin specificus.

verb:streichen.tx: From Middle High German strīchen, from Old High German strīhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan. Cognate with Dutch strijken, English strike.

noun:Scharlatan.tx: Borrowed from French charlatan, from Italian ciarlatano.

noun:Süßigkeit.tx: From Middle High German süezecheit. Analyzable as süß (“sweet”) + -igkeit.

adj:satt.tx: From Middle High German sat, from Old High German sat, from Proto-West Germanic *sad, from Proto-Germanic *sadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂-. Compare Dutch zat, English sad, Danish sat.

noun:Sitzfleisch.tx: From sitzen (“to sit”) + Fleisch (“flesh”). Cognate with Yiddish זיצפֿלייש (zitsfleysh).

verb:starten.tx: Borrowed from English start + -en; compare with Dutch starten and native High German stürzen.

verb:stemmen.tx: From Middle High German stemmen, from Old High German *stemmen, from Proto-West Germanic *stammijan. Compare Old Norse stemma (“to halt, to dam”), Swedish stämma (“to block”), English stem and English stammer.

noun:Schrei.tx: From Middle High German schrei, schrē, from Old High German screi. First attested in the 9th century. Cognate with Hunsrik Schreu. Ultimately from the root of schreien (“to shout, cry out”).

noun:Schock.tx: Chiefly a borrowing (since 18th century), partly from French choc, partly from English shock, both derived from Old French choquer, from Frankish *skokkōn. There was also an uncommon native cognate, from Middle High German schoc (“wind gust”, rarely also “shock, thrust”), from Old High German scoc, which may have been merged with the borrowing.

noun:Störung.tx: From stören + -ung. Related to English stirring.

noun:Spektrum.tx: In the sense “range” (18th c.) after English spectrum, from Latin spectrum. The sense “spectre” (16th c.) was directly from the Latin; it remained rare and became fully obsolete after the emergence of the contemporary meaning.

noun:Schornstein.tx: From Middle High German schor(n)stein, Old High German scorrenstein. The first element is from schore (“support”), related to the root of scheren (“to cut”); the second element is from Stein (“stone”).

noun:Spiegelei.tx: From Spiegel (“mirror”) + Ei (“egg”). Probably a loan translation of earlier French œuf miroir, œuf au miroir, possibly through Dutch spiegelei.

noun:Seehund.tx: 15th century, alteration of Seelhund, explanatory compound from now obsolete Seel (“seal”) + Hund (“dog”). The first component seems to have been inherited from Middle High German sële, sëleh, from Old High German sëlah, from Proto-Germanic *selhaz (“seal”). For natural reasons it was a rare word, however, and was later reinforced by cognate Middle Low German sēl, also sēlhunt. Cognate with …

noun:Spielzeug.tx: Compound of Spiel (“game”) + Zeug (“stuff”) or spielen (“to play”) + Zeug (“stuff”).

noun:Schlüsselbein.tx: 17th century, from Schlüssel (“key”) + Bein (“bone”), after New Latin clāvicula (literally “little key”). Compare Dutch sleutelbeen, Swedish nyckelben, Czech klíční kost, etc., some of which may be loan translations of the German.

noun:Schimpanse.tx: From a Bantu language, probably via French chimpanzé.

verb:schnorcheln.tx: From Schnorchel + -n. The noun is itself deverbal (see the lemma), but the modern verb must be a new derivation from the noun.

noun:Spezialität.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin speciālitās. By surface analysis, spezial + -ität.

noun:Schlagsahne.tx: A compound of schlagen (“to beat”) + Sahne (“cream”).

noun:Salat.tx: 15th century, from earlier Italian salata, a variant of insalata, likely reinforced by Middle French salade.

noun:Schleife.tx: From Middle High German slöufe, from Old High German sloufa, from Proto-West Germanic *slaupijā. Cognate with Dutch sloop (“pillowcase”). Doublet of Schlaufe (“strap, noose”). Schleife exhibits unrounding, while Schlaufe exhibits Upper German lack of umlaut before a labial. The West Germanic noun is denominal to the verb at hand in Old High German sloufen, causative of sliofan (whence archaic …

noun:Spielsucht.tx: From Spiel (“game; play”) + Sucht (“addiction”). Compare Dutch speelzucht.

verb:stottern.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German stotteren, iterative of the verb stōten (“to bump, nudge (the tongue when speaking)”), from Old Saxon stotan.

verb:schwärmen.tx: From Middle High German swermen (“to swarm”), from Old High German swermen (“to swarm”), derived from swarm (“swarm of bees”), whence modern German Schwarm (“swarm; flock of birds”). The figurative senses developed in Early Modern German via “to deviate from the established dogma or school of thought”.

verb:schätzen.tx: From Middle High German schetzen (Duden), synchronically analyzable as a verbal formation from Schatz (“treasure”) (DWDS).

adj:steinen.tx: From Middle High German steinīn, from Old High German steinīn, from Proto-West Germanic *stainīn. By surface analysis, Stein + -en.

verb:säumen.tx: From Middle High German säumen, from Old High German saumen, from Proto-West Germanic *saumijan, from Proto-Germanic *saumijaną.

adj:schläfrig.tx: From Middle High German slæferic, slāferic, from Old High German slāfrag, slāferag. By surface analysis, Schläfer (“sleeper”) + -ig.

noun:Solidarität.tx: Based on French solidarité during the end of the 18th century.

adj:scheußlich.tx: From Middle High German schiuzlîch, reshaped under the influence of Scheusal; see scheuen for more.

noun:Soße.tx: Borrowed from French sauce, from Old French sauce, sause, sausse, salse, from Latin salsa.

noun:Sommersprosse.tx: 17th century, from Sommer (“summer”) + Sprosse (“sprout”). See the latter for more.

noun:Schraubstock.tx: 16th century, from schrauben (“to screw”) + Stock (literally “stick, trunk”). The latter word here probably continues the use of Middle High German stoc for a kind of wooden block used to shackle prisoners. Compare also French étau.

noun:Salbei.tx: From Middle High German salbeie, salveie f, from Old High German salbeia, salveia f, from Proto-West Germanic *salbejā (“sage”), from Late Latin salvegia, from Latin salvia. Cognate with English sage.

noun:Strapaze.tx: 17th century, from Italian strapazzo. The feminine form in -e probably by backformation from the more usual plural; perhaps also influenced by synonyms such as Anstrengung, Mühe, etc.

noun:Spende.tx: From Middle High German spënde, from Old High German spenta, either nominalized from spentōn (“to donate; to spend”), from Proto-West Germanic *spendōn (“to spend”), or borrowed from Medieval Latin spenda, spenta (“alms, charity”).

verb:spenden.tx: From Middle High German spenden, from Old High German spentōn (“to consume, use, spend”), from Proto-West Germanic *spendōn (“to spend”), from Latin expendō.

noun:Schreibmaschine.tx: From schreiben (“write”) + Maschine (“machine”). Cognate with Hunsrik Schreibmaschin, Plautdietsch Schriewmaschien.

noun:Schnurrbart.tx: A borrowing from German Low German Snurrbaart, equivalent to schnurren (“to purr”) + Bart (“beard”), thus the "purring beard", perhaps owing to its tendency to rustle when its owner speaks or "purrs", or perhaps due to its resemblance to the whiskers of a purring cat. Compare Schnurrhaar (“whisker”).

verb:schnurren.tx: From Middle High German snurren, ablaut variant of snarren (whence modern schnarren), ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend); compare Dutch snorren, as well as English snarl. Pfeifer ultimately connects these terms to an onomatopoeic Proto-Indo-European *(s)nur- (“to grumble, growl”), and adduces nörgeln (“to nag, grumble”) as a cognate.

noun:Schwindsucht.tx: From Middle High German swintsucht, translating Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis, “consumption, decline, wane”). Equivalent to schwinden + Sucht.

adj:stur.tx: Via German Low German stūr from Middle Low German stūr, stūre, ultimately from the root of stehen (“to stand”). The word is first attested in standard German in the 19th century, but speedily became part of the core vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch stoer (itself a form of dialectal origin), Swedish stursk and with Old High German stūr, stūri, stiuri (“strong, big, stately, proud”). Outside of …

verb:stärken.tx: Inherited from Middle High German sterken, from Old High German sterken, equivalent to stark + -en.

noun:Synagoge.tx: From Middle High German sinagoge, from Latin synagoga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ). Used in German texts since the 12th century, but mainly a learned word. The popular term was Judenschule; compare Yiddish שול (shul).

verb:sabbern.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German sabben, ultimately from the source of Saft (“juice, sap”). Closely related to sabbeln (“to babble”). Compare southern Dutch zabberen and standard Dutch sabbelen.

adj:schäbig.tx: From Middle High German schebic, equivalent to Schäbe + -ig or Schabe + -ig, both ultimately from schaben. Cognate with Middle Dutch schabbich, Middle Low German schabbich, schēvesch (“miserable”). More at shabby. See also paździerz in Polish.

noun:Soja.tx: Borrowed from Satsuma Japanese 醤油 (そや, soya).

noun:Stil.tx: 15th century, from Latin stilus. Doublet of Stiel and Style.

verb:studieren.tx: From Middle High German studieren, from Latin studeō + -ieren.

noun:Studium.tx: Borrowed from Latin studium (“study, university”), 15th century.

verb:schlachten.tx: From Middle High German slahten, from Old High German slahtōn (“slaughter, sacrifice”), from Proto-Germanic *slahtōną, related to *slahaną (“to hit, strike”). Cognate with Dutch slachten.

noun:Schurke.tx: Derived from Middle High German schurgen, schürgen (“to shove, push, egg on”) in the 16th century, from Old High German scurgen. This verb is related to (but probably not the direct ancestor of) modern schüren (“to stir, stoke up”); compare Old High German fiurscurio (“villain”, literally “he who stokes up fire”). Middle High German schurgen shows Upper German umlaut blocking in -ur- + consonant. …

noun:Savanne.tx: From French savanne, from Spanish sabana, from Taíno.

verb:sprießen.tx: From Middle High German sprieʒen, from Old High German spriozan, from Proto-West Germanic *spreutan, from Proto-Germanic *spreutaną. Cognate with English sprout.

verb:streiken.tx: In part denominally form Streik + -en, in part directly from English to strike. Doublet of native streichen through Proto-Germanic *strīkaną.

noun:Streik.tx: Earlier 19th century, borrowed from English strike. Doublet of Strike (“strike” in certain games). Related with native streichen.

noun:Standarte.tx: From Middle High German standert or stanthart (first attested in the 13ᵗʰ century), from Old French estandart (“standard”). Doublet of Standard.

noun:Schlumpf.tx: Alteration of French schtroumpf, itself probably from German Strumpf (“stocking”). Whether the form was coined at random by the German translator or whether it was influenced by the surname below or perhaps by some other word, appears to be unknown.

verb:siedeln.tx: From Middle High German sidelen, from Old High German sidalen, derived from sidila (“seat”), which is cognate with Old English setl. Related with sitzen (“to sit”) and hence eventually related with English settle, but not a direct cognate of this latter.

adj:schrecklich.tx: Schreck + -lich; from Late Middle High German [Term?].

adv:schrecklich.tx: Schreck + -lich; from Late Middle High German [Term?].

noun:Schreck.tx: From Middle High German schrecke, from Old High German screcko, formed from the noun screckōn (“to jump around, surge, flash out, rebound”), from where is also derived schrecken (“to frighten”), which see for further. Compare Dutch schrik.

verb:subventionieren.tx: Borrowed from French subventionner, 19th century. Equivalent to Subvention + -ieren.

noun:Stör.tx: From Middle High German stüre, störe, store, from Old High German sturio, sturo, from Proto-West Germanic *sturjō, from Proto-Germanic *sturjô. Cognate with Dutch steur and Latin sturio (a Germanic borrowing), whence English sturgeon. The ö-vocalism is expected in Middle Low German stȫre as well as in parts of East Central German, but it appears elsewhere too. This might be explained as a …

noun:Szepter.tx: From Middle High German zepter, cepter, scepter, from Latin scēptrum.

verb:schwindeln.tx: From Middle High German swindeln, from Old High German swintilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *swindilōn.

verb:schockieren.tx: Borrowed from French choquer. Doublet of schocken.

adj:steil.tx: From Middle High German steil, steigel, from Old High German steigal, *steigil, from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”). Though native in High German, the word was rare until it was reinforced in Early Modern German by Middle Low German steil, stegel, from Old Saxon stegil, from the same Proto-Germanic source. More at English stay (“steep”).

adv:sowieso.tx: Literally, “so like so”, that is "this way and that way", "anyway".

intj:sowieso.tx: Literally, “so like so”, that is "this way and that way", "anyway".

noun:Schizophrenie.tx: Coined 1908 by Eugen Bleuler, from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) + Ancient Greek φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”) + -ie (abstract noun suffix).

adj:schizophren.tx: From Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “I split”). The meaning of contradictory from the (medically incorrect) idea that schizophrenia equals split personality.

noun:Skelett.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σκελετόν (skeletón), neuter of Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós).

noun:Spitze.tx: From Middle High German spitze, from Old High German spizza, from Proto-Germanic *spitjaz, related to *spitō (“spike”). Compare English spit (“skewer”), Swedish spets (“point, tip; lace”).

verb:spitzen.tx: From Middle High German spitzen, from Old High German spizzen, spizzōn. By surface analysis, spitz + -en.

verb:schnüren.tx: From Middle High German snüeren, from Old High German *snuoren (in firsnuoren), possibly from Proto-Germanic *snōrijaną, from *snōrō, whence German Schnur. Cognate with Dutch and Middle Dutch snoeren, Middle Low German snȫren, Old Norse snœra.

verb:schäumen.tx: From Middle High German schoumen, schemen, schūmen, from Old High German scūmen, skūmen, from Proto-West Germanic *skūmijan (“to foam, froth”), from Proto-West Germanic *skūm (“foam”). Cognate with German Low German schumen, Dutch schuimen, English scum.

noun:Stinktier.tx: From stinken (“to stink”) + Tier (“animal”). Compare Dutch stinkdier.

noun:Schakal.tx: Borrowed from French chacal, from Turkish çakal, from Ottoman Turkish چقال (çakâl), from Classical Persian شغال (šaġāl), borrowed from Sanskrit शृगाल (śṛgāla, “jackal”), the alternative form of सृगाल (sṛgāla).

verb:streiten.tx: From Middle High German strīten, from Old High German strītan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīdan. Cognate with Low German striden, Dutch strijden, English stride.

noun:Sklave.tx: From Late Middle High German sklafe (15th c.), a relatinisation of older slave (13th c.), from Medieval Latin s(c)lavus, from Late Latin Sclavus, from Medieval Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that Greek entry and slave for more. Doublet of Slawe and ciao.

noun:Stolperstein.tx: From stolpern (“to stumble”) + Stein (“stone”). Sense 3 developed in the first decade of the 21st century, applying the figurative sense of "impediment, obstacle" back to literal blocks, though ones that cause passersby to pause and reflect rather than literally stumble.

noun:Scharlatanerie.tx: Borrowed from French charlatanerie, from charlatan, from Italian ciarlatano.

verb:salzen.tx: From Middle High German salzen, from Old High German salzan, from Proto-Germanic *saltaną.

verb:streuen.tx: From Middle High German ströuwen, Old High German strewen, from Proto-West Germanic *strauwjan. Cognate with Old Saxon strewian, Old English streowian, Dutch strooien, English strew, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (straujan).

noun:Spion.tx: 16th century, from Italian spione, in part through Middle French espion. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *spehōną, whence German spähen.

noun:Sauerteig.tx: From sauer (“sour; acidic”) + Teig (“dough”), from Middle High German sūwerteic.

verb:schrumpfen.tx: In this form attested since the 17th century. Possibly an alteration of obsolete schrimpfen, from Middle High German schrimpfen, from Old High German *skrimpfan, from Proto-West Germanic *skrimpan. The form would have originated in the strong past participle geschrumpfen and through intermediation of the rounded variant schrümpfen (16th c.). Alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *skrumpōn, a …

adj:schwierig.tx: From Middle High German swiric, sweric (“full of boils”), a derivative of Schwäre (“ulcer”). Cognate to dated Dutch zwerig (“full of boils”). Often connected to its synonym schwer, but unrelated.

noun:Schamane.tx: Borrowed from Russian шама́н (šamán). See English shaman for more.

noun:Stiftung.tx: From stiften (“to endow, donate”). Compare Dutch stichting.

noun:Sarkophag.tx: Borrowed from French sarcophage, from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos, “coffin of limestone”, noun), from σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos, “flesh-eating, carnivorous”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh, meat”) + -φάγος (-phágos).

noun:Sekte.tx: From Middle High German secte, from Late Latin secta (“a sect in philosophy or religion, a school, faction”), possibly from Latin sequī (“to follow”).

noun:Skandal.tx: Borrowed from French scandale. Doublet of Skandalon.

adj:skandalös.tx: Borrowed from French scandaleuse. By surface analysis, Skandal + -ös.

adv:sofort.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German so vōrt, from so (intensifier) + vōrt (“forth; soon”). Written as one word from the 16th century.

noun:Schubkarre.tx: Schub (“push”) + Karre (“cart”). First attested in a Central German form schuffkarrn (15th century).

noun:Szenario.tx: Borrowed from Italian scenario, from scena + -ario. Doublet of Szenerie (“scenery”).

noun:Schlussverkauf.tx: From Schluss (“end, ending, conclusion, finish”) + Verkauf (“sale”).

adj:saisonal.tx: From Saison + -al. A pseudo-Gallicism, perhaps modeled on English seasonal (compare French saisonnier).

noun:Seeräuber.tx: From See (“sea”) + Räuber (“robber”). Compare Danish sørøver, English sea rover, Norwegian sjørøver, Swedish sjörövare, Dutch zeerover.

noun:Stasi.tx: From Ministerium für Staatssicherheit (“Ministry for State Security”).

verb:scherzen.tx: From Middle High German schërzen, from Old High German *skërzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”), from Proto-Germanic *skertaną.

noun:Schotter.tx: From dialectal Central German, akin to German Schutt (“rubble, debris”), German schütten (“to pour, spill, cast, strew”).

adj:schick.tx: From French chic, itself from German Schick (“correct manners, correct clothing”).

adj:seltsam.tx: From Middle High German seltsām, seltzām, seltsæm, alteration (due to Middle High German -sam (“-some”)) of Middle High German seltsæn, seltsæne, from Old High German seltsāni. Cognate with Dutch zeldzaam and English seldom.

adv:seltsam.tx: From Middle High German seltsām, seltzām, seltsæm, alteration (due to Middle High German -sam (“-some”)) of Middle High German seltsæn, seltsæne, from Old High German seltsāni. Cognate with Dutch zeldzaam and English seldom.

noun:Staatsräson.tx: From Staat + -s- + Räson, a partial calque of French raison d'État.

adj:skeptisch.tx: From Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós), probably via Latin scepticus, with -isch instead of -icus.

noun:Steckenpferd.tx: Stecken (“wooden rod, staff”) + Pferd (“horse”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English hobby horse.

noun:Sibylle.tx: Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

noun:Stabilität.tx: 18th century, from Latin stabilitas, in part through French stabilité. By surface analysis, stabil + -ität.

noun:Schaumkrone.tx: From Schaum (“foam”) + Krone (“crown”). Compare Dutch schuimkraag (literally “foam collar”).

adj:silbern.tx: From Old High German silberīn, from Proto-Germanic *silubrīnaz.

noun:Sander.tx: Borrowed from Icelandic sandur (literally “sand”). Doublet of Sand.

noun:Schienbein.tx: From Middle High German schinbein, schinebein, from Old High German skinabein, from Proto-West Germanic *skinubain, from Proto-Germanic *skinōbainą. Equivalent to Schiene + Bein. Compare Hunsrik Schienbeen, Dutch scheenbeen, English shinbone, Danish skinneben, Swedish skenben.

verb:schnattern.tx: From Middle High German snateren (“to cackle, croak (of frogs), clatter (of storks), chatter”). Cognate with Dutch snater (“beak”), snateren (“to quack”), Swedish snattra.

noun:Schützengraben.tx: Compound of Schütze (“shooter”) + -n- (genitive infix in compounds) + Graben (“ditch; trench”).

noun:Selbstwertgefühl.tx: Selbstwert + Gefühl. Coined by Austrian psychotherapist Alfred Adler.

noun:Sims.tx: From Middle High German simez, from Old High German simiz. Lacking cognates in Germanic, therefore usually connected to Latin sima (“horizontal element at the top of a column”), perhaps through Late Latin simatus.

noun:Sentimentalität.tx: From French sentimentalité, with assimilation to nativized suffix -ität.

noun:Seitan.tx: From Japanese セイタン, possibly via English.

noun:Sirene.tx: In the mythological sense from Middle High German sirēne, from Latin Sirēn, in the acoustical sense from French sirène, in the botanical sense confused from Syringe from Latin sȳrinx which was before the introduction of the lilac to Europe in the 16th century the name of the plant now called Pfeifenstrauch (sweet mock orange, Philadelphus coronarius). Dutch sering developed likely simultaneously …

phrase:Sesam, öffne dich.tx: From its use in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, translating French Sésame, ouvre-toi in Antoine Galland's version of the Ali Baba story in the One Thousand and One Nights, possibly based on an oral Arabic source.

noun:Schwierigkeit.tx: From Late Middle High German swǣrecheit, equivalent of schwierig + -keit.

noun:Schwiegersohn.tx: schwieger- + Sohn; cognate with Hunsrik Schwieghersohn

noun:Schauspiel.tx: Schau (“view”) + Spiel (“play”). Compare Danish skuespil, Swedish skådespel, Norwegian Bokmål skuespill, Norwegian Nynorsk skodespel, Faroese sjónleikur, Dutch schouwspel.

adj:stetig.tx: From Middle High German stætec (“firm, constant, stable”), Old High German stāti; analyzable as stet + -ig.

noun:Subjekt.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin subjectum. Doublet of Sujet.

noun:Sodbrennen.tx: From Middle High German sote (“boil”) + brennen (“to burn”).

adv:schlechthin.tx: 17th century, from schlecht + hin. The first component here preserves the older sense “plain, simple”, otherwise now restricted to the variant schlicht (see there).

noun:Serie.tx: 18th century, from Latin seriēs, perhaps through French série.

noun:Schüler.tx: From Middle High German schuolære, from Old High German scuolāri, from Medieval Latin scholaris; analyzable as Schule + -er.

noun:Spionage.tx: 18th century, from spionieren or Spion + -age, after French espionnage.

adj:spontan.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin spontāneus, from Latin sponte (suā) (“of one's free will, voluntarily”).

noun:Sonnenblume.tx: From Sonne (“sun”) + -n- + Blume (“flower”). Compare English sunbloom.

noun:Separee.tx: 19th century. Shortened from now archaic Chambre séparée (“private room”), a German coinage from French chambre séparée (“separate room”), not used as a fixed term in French.

verb:schnitzen.tx: From Middle High German snitzen, from Proto-Germanic *snittōną (“to cut”).

noun:Sonderbehandlung.tx: From sonder- (“special”) + Behandlung (“treatment”). The Nazis used the word as code during the early stages of the Holocaust. By the time of the creation of the extermination camps it was already too widely understood and, as a codeword, replaced by terms such as Evakuierung (“evacuation”) and Durchschleusung (“channeling, passage”).

adj:sonderbar.tx: Inherited from Middle High German sunderbære, equivalent to sondern (“to separate”) + -bar (“-able”). Cognate to German absondern, aussondern.

adj:sonderlich.tx: From Middle High German sunderlīch, from Old High German suntarlīh (“‘singly, especially, distinguished”). Related to sondern (“to separate, distinguish”).

adj:schlicht.tx: Chiefly Low German, also to a lesser degree Central German variant of schlecht. From Middle Low German slicht and northern Middle High German sliht (both “flat, straight, simple”), from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz, which see for cognates.
