Since the Late Middle Ages, schlecht/schlicht developed the sense “bad”, which became predominant over time, but did not displace the original one entirely. By the …

verb:schlichten.tx: From Middle High German slihten, from Old High German slihten, from Proto-West Germanic *slihtijan, from Proto-Germanic *slihtijaną. By surface analysis, schlicht + -en.

verb:schaudern.tx: From Middle Dutch schuderen, schuyderen and/or Middle Low German schōderen, variants (with expressive lengthening?) of Middle Dutch schudderen and Middle Low German schodderen, respectively, themselves iteratives of the verb at hand in German schütten (“to pour”, originally “to shake”, compare schütteln). See English shudder for more.

adj:stechend.tx: Inherited from Middle High German stëchende, from Old High German stëhhanti, from Proto-West Germanic *stekandī.

adj:synchron.tx: Shortening of synchronisch; attested since the 1920s.

verb:schänden.tx: From Middle High German schenden, from Old High German skenten, from Proto-West Germanic *skandijan.

noun:Silvester.tx: From Pope Silvester I, whose feast-day has been the 31st of December since the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582. Compare Russian Сильвестров день (Silʹvestrov denʹ), Polish sylwester.

adj:seriös.tx: Borrowed from French sérieux, from Latin sēriōsus.

verb:sanieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin sānāre, sānō (“to heal”).

adj:saftig.tx: From Middle High German saftic, saffic, saffec, seffic. Equivalent to Saft + -ig.

adj:steinig.tx: From Middle High German steinec, from Old High German steinag, from Proto-West Germanic *stainag, from Proto-Germanic *stainagaz (“stony”), equivalent to Stein (“stone”) + -ig (“-y”).

adj:silbrig.tx: From Silber (“silver”) + -ig. Cognate with Hunsrik silvrich.

noun:Schnickschnack.tx: Reduplication; from schnacken or Low German schnacken (snacken) (“chatter”) (compare Plautdietsch schnaken (“chatter”)).

verb:steinigen.tx: Stein (“stone”) + -igen. Displacing Middle High German steinen, from Old High German steinōn.

adj:salopp.tx: 18th century, from French salope, adjectival use of salope (“slovenly woman”). Compare German schlampig.

noun:Schellack.tx: Borrowed from Dutch schellak. Cognate with English shellac (“scale lac, lac thin like scales”).

noun:Söldner.tx: From Middle High German soldener, soldenier, soldenære, derived from solt (modern Sold), likely after Medieval Latin soldonerius and Old Italian soldoniere, soldaniere, literally “salaried”, derived from soldo (“sold, salary”), used in the times of feudal militias, referring to hired or enlisted paid private (lowest rank) soldiers, and by extension mercenaries, as opposed to vassals, knights, and …

adj:sagenhaft.tx: 19th c., Sage + -n- + haft. Compare similar Middle High German sagehaft (“which is spoken of, famous”) which was not continued.

noun:Spitzhacke.tx: spitz (“pointed”) + hacke, inflection of hacken (“to chop”).

verb:stimmen.tx: From Middle High German stimmen, from Old High German *stimmen (attested in Old High German gistimmen), from the same source as German Stimme (“voice, vote”).

verb:segeln.tx: From Middle High German sëgeln, sigeln, sëgelen, sigelen, from Old High German *sëgalōn, *sigilen, from Proto-West Germanic *seglōn, *siglijan. Cognate with West Frisian sile, Low German seilen, Dutch zeilen, English sail, Swedish segla, Icelandic sigla.

noun:Serenade.tx: Borrowed from French sérénade, from Italian serenata.

verb:schikanieren.tx: From French chicaner + -ieren, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan. Doublet of schicken.

adj:sächlich.tx: From Sache + -lich. Cognate with Hunsrik sechlich.

noun:Salut.tx: Borrowed from French salut, from Latin salus.

noun:Schmiede.tx: From Late Middle High German smide (15th c.), alteration of older smitte, from Old High German smitta (early also smiththa, seldom smidda), from Proto-West Germanic *smiþþjā, from Proto-Germanic *smiþjǭ. Cognate with Dutch smidse, English smithy. The modern form, which had displaced Schmitte by the 18th c., is an adaptation to the related verb schmieden (“to forge”). It is of Central German …

verb:schwinden.tx: From Middle High German swinden, from Old High German swintan, from Proto-West Germanic *swindan. Cognate with Danish svinde (“to dwindle, vanish”), Dutch zwinden (“to disappear, vanish”), English swindle (“to take advantage of”), Hunsrik schwinne, Low German swinnen (“to decrease, shrink, vanish”), Norwegian svinne (“to disappear, vanish”), Swedish svinna (“to disappear, vanish”).

noun:Schlot.tx: With dialectal -ā- → -ō- from Middle High German slāt, from Old High German slāt, further origin unknown. Perhaps related with Middle High German slāte (“reed, cane”).

noun:Schwarzarbeiter.tx: schwarz (“black (i.e., illicit, illegal, clandestine, undocumented)”) + Arbeiter (“worker”)

noun:Strategie.tx: From Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “I lead, I conduct”).

noun:Stratege.tx: From Latin stratēgus, from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós), possibly influenced by French stratège.

noun:Spekulation.tx: Inherited from Middle High German speculâcie, from Latin speculātio.

noun:Spore.tx: New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá).

adj:sesshaft.tx: From Middle High German sëȥhaft, derived from sëȥ (“abode, residence”), from Old High German sëȥ, related with sizzen, whence modern German sitzen (“to sit”).

verb:scheffeln.tx: Denominative from Scheffel + -n, originally in the sense “to fill bushels”.

noun:Scheffel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German scheffel, from Old High German sceffil. Compare Schaff.

noun:Stolz.tx: From Middle High German stolz, from Old High German stolz, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz (“proud, stately, stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, stand”); cognate with English stout.

noun:Sünder.tx: From Middle High German sünder, sündære, sündāre, suntære, suntāre, from Old High German suntāri, from Proto-Germanic *sundārijaz, equivalent to Sünde + -er. More at sinner.

verb:sündigen.tx: From Middle High German sündigen, sundigen, alteration (due to Middle High German sundic, sundec, suntic (“sinful”) > German sündig) of Old High German suntōn, sunteōn. Compare Old Saxon sundiōn (“to sin”), Old English syngian (“to sin”), Old Norse syndga (“to sin”).

noun:Strenge.tx: From Middle High German strenge, from Old High German strengī. By surface analysis, streng (“strict”) + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Substanz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German substanz, substanzje, from Latin substantia.

noun:S-Bahn.tx: Abbreviation of Stadtschnellbahn, from Stadt (“city”) + schnell (“fast”) + Bahn (“rail”).

verb:schoppen.tx: Intensive formation to schieben. Compare Alemannic German schoppe.

noun:Saatkrähe.tx: From Saat (“seed”) + Krähe (“crow”), partially translating the Latin Corvus frugilegus.

noun:Satin.tx: Borrowed from French satin, from Arabic زَيْتُون (zaytūn, “Zayton; olive”).

noun:Schläfe.tx: Originally the plural of Schlaf (“sleep”), so called because one lies on one’s temple when sleeping on one’s side.

noun:Sellerie.tx: Borrowed from French céleri, from Lombard selleri, from Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon). Introduced in the 17th century as a culinary term; celery was unusual in German cuisine before that time.

pron:solch.tx: From Middle High German sulich, from Old High German sulīh, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz.

noun:Sammelsurium.tx: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from Low German sammelsūr/Sammelsūr (“[sour] dish made from various leftovers”) + Latin -ium.

noun:Schwiele.tx: From Middle High German swil, from Old High German swil, from Proto-West Germanic *swili, from Proto-Germanic *swiliz, related to German schwellen.

noun:Seezunge.tx: See (“sea”) + Zunge (“tongue”). Compare Dutch zeetong, German Low German Seetung, Swedish sjötunga, Danish søtunge.

adj:sexuell.tx: Borrowed from French sexuel in the 18th century, from Latin sexuālis, from Latin sexus (“sex; gender”).

adv:sexuell.tx: Borrowed from French sexuel in the 18th century, from Latin sexuālis, from Latin sexus (“sex; gender”).

noun:Statistik.tx: Derived from New Latin statistica (compare Italian statistica) or statisticus (“of the state”), from obsolete Statist (“statesman”), compare English statist. Coined by Gottfried Achenwall.

noun:Schmiergeld.tx: From schmieren (“to bribe”) + Geld (“money”). First attested 1616.

noun:Sägemehl.tx: From sägen (“to saw”) + Mehl (“flour”). The loss of the final -n is regular in compounds from verb stems. Alternatively analysable as Säge (“a saw”) + Mehl.

noun:Sinfonie.tx: Borrowed from Italian sinfonia. Doublet of Symphonie.

noun:Spreu.tx: From Middle High German, from Old High German spriu. Related to sprühen (“to spray”).

noun:Schmuggel.tx: Either a deverbal from schmuggeln or directly borrowed from Low German smuggeln.

verb:stagnieren.tx: 18th century, learned borrowing from Latin stagn(āre) + -ieren.

noun:Seifenoper.tx: Seife + -n- + Oper, calque of English soap opera.

adj:sorgfältig.tx: From Middle High German sorcveltic, sorgeveltic. By surface analysis, Sorgfalt + -ig. Cognate with Dutch zorgvuldig.

noun:Sujet.tx: Borrowed from French sujet. Doublet of Subjekt.

verb:schlechtreden.tx: schlecht (“bad”) + reden (“to talk”), akin in construction to schlechtmachen. Entered wider usage in the 1990s. Possibly building on the older intransitive usage of "schlecht von/über etwas reden" (to speak badly of something).

verb:stammen.tx: Stamm (“main stem”) + -en (“verbal infinitive suffix”); compare also English stem.

noun:Sonnenbrand.tx: From Sonne (“sun”) + -n- + Brand (“fire, burn”). The word originally meant the burning heat of the sun. As such it was also commonly used in the context of sunburnt skin. However, the use of Sonnenbrand to refer this skin condition itself (meaning that one can “have a sunburn”, Sonnenbrand haben) seems to be a development of the 20th century.

adj:sumpfig.tx: Sumpf + -ig. Compare English swampy and sumpy.

prep:samt.tx: From Middle High German sament, Old High German samant, ultimately from the root of sammeln. Compare Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌸 (samaþ).

adv:samt.tx: From Middle High German sament, Old High German samant, ultimately from the root of sammeln. Compare Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌸 (samaþ).

verb:sinnen.tx: From Middle High German sinnen, from Old High German sinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinnan.

noun:Steinmetz.tx: From Middle High German steinmetze, from Old High German steinmezzo.

verb:schwelen.tx: 18th century, from Low German swelen, from Middle Low German swēlen, from Old Saxon *swelan, from Proto-West Germanic *swelan, from Proto-Germanic *swelaną (“to smoulder, burn slowly”), from Proto-Indo-European *swel- (“to shine, warm, burn”). Cognate with Dutch zwelen, Old English swelan. Also related to German schwül (“sultry”), Old Norse svalr (“cold”), whence Danish sval.

adj:steinalt.tx: From Stein + alt, literally “stone-old”, later reanalyzed as stein- (“very-”) + alt.

verb:sträuben.tx: From Middle High German strūben, from Old High German strūbēn / strūben, from Proto-West Germanic *strūbijan. Related to struwwelig and struppig; outside of Germanic, compare perhaps Ancient Greek στρυφνός (struphnós, “sour, harsh”), Lithuanian strùbas (“cut short, curtailed”), and Russian струп (strup, “scab”).

noun:Stellvertreter.tx: 17th century, from Stelle (“place”) + vertreten (“to represent, fill in”) + -er (“-er”), probably after French lieutenant, Latin locum tenēns.

noun:Schlafentzug.tx: From Schlaf (“sleep”) + Entzug (“deprivation”, verbal noun of entziehen (“to deprive, take away, withhold, revoke”)).

noun:Stecknadel.tx: From steck(en) (“to stick, pin”) + Nadel (“needle, pin”)

adj:schneeweiß.tx: From Middle High German snēwīz, from Old High German *snēwīz, from Proto-Germanic *snaiwahwītaz, equivalent to Schnee + weiß.

noun:Sachse.tx: From Middle High German Sahse, from Old High German Sahso, from Proto-West Germanic *Sahsō (“Saxon”).

noun:Schöpfer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schepfære, from Old High German skephāri; equivalent to schöpfen + -er.

noun:Schneewittchen.tx: Partial calque of German Low German Sneewittken (from Snee (“snow”) + witt (“white”) + -ken). The Brothers Grimm only adapted the diminutive suffix to -chen, thus entitling the tale Sneewittchen. Over time the first word also came to be adapted to Schnee. Full calquing to Schneeweißchen, however, was hindered by the fact that it already occurred in an unrelated tale called Schneeweißchen und Rosenrot.

noun:Staatsanwalt.tx: From Staat (“state”) + -s- + Anwalt (“lawyer”) (“lawyer of the state”).

verb:stippen.tx: From Middle Low German stippen; cognate with steppen.

noun:Stratosphäre.tx: From Latin stratum (“covering, blanket”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).

noun:Stiefsohn.tx: From Middle High German stiefsun, stīfsun, from Old High German stiofsun, stiofsunu, from Proto-West Germanic *steupasunu, equivalent to stief- (“step-”) + Sohn (“son”). Cognate with English stepson.

noun:Stieftochter.tx: From stief- (“step-”) + Tochter (“daughter”). From Middle High German stieftohter, from Old High German stioftohter, from Proto-Germanic *steupaduhtēr (“stepdaughter”), equivalent to stief- + Tochter.

noun:Schreiner.tx: From Middle High German schrīnære, derived from schrīn (“cupboard”). Analysable as Schrein + -er.

noun:Schrein.tx: From Middle High German schrīn, from Old High German skrīni, skrīn, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīnī (“shrine, chest”). In older German, Schrein meant exclusively a case or box; the sense “sanctuary” is likely influenced by the English word.

noun:Schurkenstaat.tx: From Schurke + -n- + Staat, calque of English rogue state.

adj:sonnig.tx: From Middle High German *sunnec (suggested by derivative sunneclich), from Proto-West Germanic *sunnig; equivalent to Sonne + -ig. Compare English sunny.

noun:Strafraum.tx: From Strafe + Raum, a calque of English penalty area.

verb:schaben.tx: From Middle High German schaben, from Old High German skaban, from Proto-West Germanic *skaban, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scrape, scratch”). Cognate with Dutch schaven, English shave, Danish skave, Swedish skava, Icelandic skafa, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (skaban).

verb:schauern.tx: From Middle High German schawern (“hail, thunderstorm”); see Schauer.

verb:scheuern.tx: An originally Central and Low German word, from northern Middle High German schiuren and Middle Low German schǖren (both 14th c.). Further origin uncertain, but probably from Old French escurer (“to clean off”), from Late Latin excurare (literally “to treat thoroughly”), from Latin ex- + curare. If so, borrowed through Middle Dutch schuren (13th c., modern schuren), otherwise cognate with it. See …

verb:schlendern.tx: From Middle High German lenderen, from Old High German landteri, from Proto-Germanic *land-, ultimately from the root of schlingen (“to wind, twist, coil”). Cognate with Dutch slenteren (“to loiter”).

verb:schmieden.tx: From Middle High German smiden, from Old High German smidōn, from Proto-West Germanic *smiþōn. Cognate with Dutch smeden, English smith.

verb:schmücken.tx: From Middle High German smücken, smucken (“to press against oneself, contract”), from Old High German *smucken (whence firsmucken (“to crush”)), from a formation related to modern German schmiegen (“to nestle up”); see there for more.

verb:schreiten.tx: From Middle High German schrīten, from Old High German skrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīþan (“to step; stride”).

verb:schulden.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schulden, from Old High German skuldōn, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldōn.

verb:schütteln.tx: From Middle High German schütelen, schütteln, from Old High German scutilōn; synchronically analyzable as an iterative formation from schütten.

verb:segnen.tx: From Middle High German segenen, segen, from Old High German seganōn, from Latin signō, signāre. Compare English sain, Dutch zegenen, Hunsrik seghne, Old Norse, Faroese, and Icelandic signa.

noun:Schmaus.tx: Unknown, early 17ᵗʰ century’s student language. The Etymological Dictionary of the German Language claims a cognate with Dutch smullen (“to eat or drink immoderately, carouse”) and Low German smudderen, smodderen (“to feast”). Any connection to Schmer (“fat, lard”) is likely folk etymology.

verb:schmausen.tx: Originating in student academic speech. Probably originally meaning "to eat and drink uncleanly".

verb:schachern.tx: 17th century, borrowed from Yiddish סחרן (sakhern, “to do business”), derived from Hebrew סחר (sáḥar, “trade”). The form was influenced by now obsolete schachen (“to plunder”, with long [aː]), itself from Proto-West Germanic *skāk (“robbery”). The synonymous Yiddish שאַכערן (shakhern) may be a reborrowing.

adj:schneidig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German snīdec, by surface analysis, Schneid + -ig.

noun:Sakko.tx: From Sack (“sack”), which was used in the 19th century to refer to an unwaisted jacket; compare English sack coat. This name was due to the loose fitting, possibly reinforced by the idea of it being unpretentious and humble (compare Sack und Asche, English sackcloth). The later alteration of the form on the basis of Italian sacco was intended to have the opposite effect, namely to make it sound fashionable.

adv:stets.tx: From Middle High German stetes, from Proto-Germanic *stēdi-; cognate with Dutch steeds. Synchronically analyzed as an adverbial formation stet (“steady, constant”) + -s; see there for more.

noun:Schwaden.tx: From Middle High German swadem, from Old High German swedan (“to burn smolderingly”), from Proto-West Germanic *swīþan (“to singe, burn”). Cognate with Middle Low German swadem, dialectal Dutch zwadem.

adj:säuerlich.tx: From Middle High German sūrlīche, from Old High German sūrlīhho. By surface analysis, sauer + lich.

noun:Schoppen.tx: Borrowed from dialectal French chopenne, from Old French chopine, itself of Germanic origin, from Middle Low German schōpe(n) (corresponding to Middle High German schuofe), ultimately from the root of Schaff (“ladle”).

noun:Schiffbruch.tx: Compound of Schiff + Bruch. Perhaps a calque of Latin naufragium.

noun:Schotte.tx: From Middle High German Schotte, Schote. Probably from Old English Sċott, perhaps borrowed through Middle Dutch Scotte. In any case, ultimately from Latin Scōtus.

noun:Sorgfalt.tx: Back-formation from sorgfältig. Equivalent to sorgen + -falt.

noun:Stippvisite.tx: Stipp + Visite, related to Dutch stip (“dot”).

noun:Schlägel.tx: From Middle High German slegel, from Old High German slegil, ultimately from the root of schlagen (“to hit, beat”).

adj:stier.tx: Since the 15th century, probably from Middle Low German stūr(e) with influence from German Stier. Doublet of stur.

verb:stieren.tx: From the verbalization of Stier (“bull”), due to the stare of a bull, from Middle High German stier (“bull”), from Old High German stior (“bull, calf of a bull”). From Proto-Germanic *steuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros.

noun:Schablone.tx: 18th century, from Low German Schablun, Schabbelun, from Middle Low German schaplūn, earlier schampeliōn (“pattern, shape, model”), from Middle Dutch schampelioen, from Middle French eschantillon, from Old French eschandillon (“standard”), from Vulgar Latin *scandiculum, derived from Latin scandula (“shingle”). Compare modern French échantillon.

noun:Strohfeuer.tx: From Stroh (“straw”) + Feuer (“fire”), typically burning very quickly. Compare French feu de paille.

noun:Sexualität.tx: Borrowed from New Latin sexuālitās, from sexual + -ität.

noun:Steckrübe.tx: From stecken (“to stick, insert”) + Rübe (“turnip, root vegetable”).

noun:Säugling.tx: From Middle High German sūgelinc, equivalent to säug(en) + -ling. Cognate with English suckling, Dutch zuigeling (“suckling”).

verb:stammeln.tx: From Middle High German stamelen, from Old High German stamalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stamlōn. Compare English stammer, Dutch stameren, and Old Norse stammr.

noun:Skalpell.tx: Borrowed from Latin scalpellum via Old High German [Term?].

noun:Skorbut.tx: 18th century, from New Latin scorbutus, itself from Middle Low German schorbuk, in turn probably from Old Norse skyrbjúgr. Replaced the more native Scharbock, which is directly from the Low German.

noun:Schweizer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German swīzer. Equivalent to Schweiz + -er. The senses "doorman" and "milker" arose because Swiss people were commonly employed in Germany in those professions; the sense "sacristan" arose because sacristans' garb resembled that of the Swiss Guards. For the sense development compare also French Suisse (“Swiss”): suisse (“doorman”).

adj:Schweizer.tx: Inherited from Middle High German swīzer. Equivalent to Schweiz + -er. The senses "doorman" and "milker" arose because Swiss people were commonly employed in Germany in those professions; the sense "sacristan" arose because sacristans' garb resembled that of the Swiss Guards. For the sense development compare also French Suisse (“Swiss”): suisse (“doorman”).

verb:schrauben.tx: From Late Middle High German [Term?]; cognate with Hunsrik schrauve.

noun:Saibling.tx: Originally Bavarian variant of Sälmling, equivalent to Salm (“salmon”) + -ling. The form shows -a- from secondary umlaut, vowelisation of -l-, and dissimilation -ml- > -bl-. Especially the former two are typically Bavarian developments.

verb:schubsen.tx: 19th c., denominal from Schubs, Schupps (“push”), from Schupp (“push”) + -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.), in turn, is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. Doublet of now colloquial German schuppen and schupfen. Also cognate with Bavarian …

noun:Skript.tx: From Latin scriptum (“that which is written”).

noun:Statist.tx: From Latin status + -ist, compare English statist.

verb:sorgen.tx: From Middle High German sorgen, from Old High German sorgēn, from Proto-Germanic *surgāną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”). Cognate with English sorrow.

verb:sonnen.tx: From Middle High German sunnen, from the root of Sonne.

adj:speziell.tx: From older spezial, with French influence analogous to general → generell.

verb:starren.tx: A merger of two related verbs: # Middle High German staren, from Old High German starēn (“to stare”), from Proto-West Germanic *starēn (“to be fixed, be rigid”); # Middle High German starren, from Old High German storrēn (“to be stiff”), from Proto-Germanic *starjaną (“to be fixed, be rigid”).

noun:Schah.tx: Borrowed from Persian شاه (šâh). Doublet of Schach, Scheck, and Check.

noun:Stillleben.tx: still + Leben, calque of Dutch stilleven.

adj:schwindelig.tx: By surface analysis, schwindeln + -ig or Schwindel + -ig.

noun:Sparte.tx: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from late Medieval Latin sparta, from Ancient Greek σπάρτη (spártē, “hereditament”).

verb:schlurfen.tx: Originally an alternative form of schlürfen (“to slurp”), of imitative origin; compare Dutch slurpen and English slurp.

noun:Stechpalme.tx: stechen (“to prick”) + Palme (“palm”), acquiring this name in the 16th century for being a common replacement plant for Palm Sunday, compare the history of Polish ożanka (“germander, Teucrium”), Poland being outside the range of the European holly, earlier also called Stechbaum, Stechdorn, Stechlaub, Stecheiche, Stechwinde, Stechapfel, Stacheleiche, Walddistel, Zwieseldorn, Mäusedorn, Myrtendorn, …

noun:Süßholz.tx: süß + Holz, inherited from Middle High German süezholz, a calque of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza) from γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”).

adj:steinhart.tx: From Stein (“stone”) + hart (“hard”). Also equivalent to stein- + hart (the prefix developed from formations such as this).

noun:Stuten.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German stūt, stute (literally “thigh, rump”), hence “thigh-shaped bread”. Compare Middle Dutch stuyt, regional Dutch stoet (“bread”). Cognate with German Steiß from Old High German stiuȥ.

verb:stützen.tx: Attested as a simplex since the 17th century. Probably after Middle Low German stütten as a backformation from inherited unterstützen, from Middle High German understüzzen, from Old High German untarstuzzen, eventually from Proto-West Germanic *stuttijan. See also Dutch stutten (“to support”), and, by borrowing from Low German, Norwegian støtte, Swedish stötta, and (probably) dialectal English …

noun:Sturmgewehr.tx: From the Maschinenpistole 44, called the Sturmgewehr 44, whence it was renamed to represent the separate class of firearm it represented. From Sturm + Gewehr, hence English assault rifle.

noun:Spengler.tx: From Late Middle High German speng(e)ler, from Spengel/Spängel (a diminutive form of Spange) + -er.

noun:Seeungeheuer.tx: From die See (“sea”) / der See (“lake”) + Ungeheuer (“monster”).

noun:Szene.tx: From Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

noun:Sandsack.tx: By surface analysis, Sand (“sand”) + Sack (“sack”). Compare Danish sandsæk, Norwegian Bokmål sandsekk, Swedish sandsäck, Dutch zandzak

verb:schweißen.tx: From Middle High German sweiʒen, sweizen (“to roast, to weld”), from Old High German sweizen (“to roast”), from Proto-Germanic *swaitijaną, causative of etymology 2.

adj:stattlich.tx: Partial calque of Middle Low German statelīk, from state. Compare Dutch statelijk, Swedish ståtlig and Norwegian statelig.

adj:strikt.tx: 17th century, at first as an adverb from Latin stricte, from strictus.

verb:streicheln.tx: From streichen (“to stroke”, as a single action) + -eln (frequentive suffix).

noun:Schwarte.tx: From Middle High German swarte, Old High German *swarta, from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind, tough skin”). Cognate with Middle English sward, West Frisian swarde, Old Norse svǫrðr, Old English sweard, Danish svær, Dutch zwoerd, English sward, Gothic *𐍃𐍅𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (*swardus).

noun:Sprecher.tx: From Middle High German sprecher, sprechære, from Old High German sprechāri, sprehhāri (also as sprāchāri, sprāhhāri), an alteration (with change of suffix) of Old High German sprecho, sprehho, from Proto-Germanic *sprekô (“speaker”), equivalent to sprechen + -er. Compare English speaker.

noun:Sattler.tx: From Middle High German sateler, from Old High German satulāri. By surface analysis, Sattel (“saddle”) + -er.

noun:Skepsis.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σκέψις (sképsis, “examination, observation, consideration”).

noun:Stieglitz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German stigliz, stigelitze, from Old Czech stehlec, derived from Proto-Slavic *ščegъlъ. Cognate with modern Czech stehlík, Slovak stehlík, Polish szczygieł, Ukrainian щи́голь (ščýholʹ), Russian щего́л (ščegól), all referring to the same bird.

verb:satteln.tx: From Middle High German sateln, satelen, satlen, from Old High German satulōn, from Proto-West Germanic *sadulōn, from Proto-Germanic *sadulōną. By surface analysis, Sattel (“saddle”) + -n.

verb:schwafeln.tx: Originally dialectal, from East Central German [Term?].

verb:schwänzen.tx: From Middle High German swenzen (“to swing”), related to schwenken. The modern sense is from 18th c. student language.

noun:Schwippschwager.tx: Probably from regional schwippen (“to sway, slant”) + Schwager (“brother-in-law”), thus “deviating, indirect brother-in-law”. For the verb compare Schwips (“tipsiness”). Alternatively a reduplicative ablaut derivation like Mischmasch, Schnickschnack, etc., but the -pp- is more readily explained by the first-mentioned theory.

noun:Schlips.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Slips, derived from Middle Low German slip, slippe (“flap, lappet, tail”), probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *slīban (“to split”). Cognate with Dutch slip, whence possibly also English slip (“twig, strip”).

noun:Spätlese.tx: From spät (“late”) + Lese (“harvest”). Cognate with lesen (“to read, select, pick”), which yields a high-quality connotation.

noun:Schalmei.tx: From Middle High German schalemīe (13th century); from Old French chalemie, a suffixal variant of chalemel (compare French chalumeau), from Latin calamellus.

noun:Sittich.tx: From Middle High German sitich, from Medieval Latin sittacus, from Latin psittacus (“parrot”), from Ancient Greek ψιττακός (psittakós).

verb:speisen.tx: From Middle High German spīsen (“to feed”), deverbal from spīse (“food”). By surface analysis, Speise + -en; see this noun for more.

noun:Schorf.tx: From Middle High German schorf, from Old High German scorf (in compounds), from Proto-Germanic *skurf-, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”) Compare English scurf, scurvy, scruffy.

verb:schellen.tx: Merged from an Early New High German strong verb, Middle High German schellen, Old High German skellan, from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, together with an Early New High German causative verb, Middle High German schellen, Old High German skellen, Proto-Germanic *skallijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skel-, from *kelh₁- (“to call, to shout, to make noise, …

adj:suizidal.tx: From Suizid + -al. Possibly calqued on, but certainly reinforced by English suicidal.

verb:schwätzen.tx: From Middle High German swetzen, swatzen, akin to Middle High German swaz (“talk, chatter”), from swateren (“to clatter, rustle”), probably ultimately of imitative origin. Cognate with Pennsylvania German schwetze, Luxembourgish schwätzen, Dutch zwetsen.

adj:scheel.tx: From Middle Low German schēle and northern Middle High German schel, from Old High German skelah, from Proto-West Germanic *skelh, from Proto-Germanic *skelhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to lean, bend; joint”). The predominant High German form was Middle High German schelch, -hes, Old High German skelah, whence obsolete German schelch.

noun:Stichwort.tx: From Stich (“sting, prick, stitch, stab”) + wort (“-word”).

noun:Schlick.tx: From Middle Low German slik, slīk. Akin to Dutch slik, slijk.

adj:sporadisch.tx: Borrowed from French sporadique, assimilated to the native suffix -isch. This is in turns borrowed from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós), cognate with Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros) and Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma).

adv:sporadisch.tx: Borrowed from French sporadique, assimilated to the native suffix -isch. This is in turns borrowed from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós), cognate with Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros) and Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma).

noun:Schellfisch.tx: From Middle Low German schellevisch, from schelle (“peel, outer layer”) + visch (“fish”), due either to the relatively large scales or to the layered meat of the fish. The former component is related to German Schale (“peel”), the latter is cognate to Fisch. Compare Dutch schelvis.

noun:Strophe.tx: Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “a turn, bend, twist”).

noun:Sitzung.tx: Attested 15th century, meaning "sitting down," equivalent to sitzen + -ung, similar to English sitting.

verb:schmusen.tx: 18th century, borrowed via Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant) from Yiddish שמועסן (shmuesn). Cognate with English schmooze. The sense “to cuddle” developed (via “to flirt”) over the course of the 20th century and appears to have become predominant around 1980.

verb:schämen.tx: From Middle High German schamen, schemen, from Old High German scamēn, from Proto-West Germanic *skamēn, from Proto-Germanic *skamāną (“to be ashamed”), equivalent to Scham (shame) + -en.

adj:süßlich.tx: From Middle High German süeȥlich, suoȥlich, sūȥlich, from Old High German suoȥlīh, swuoȥlīh, equivalent to süß (“sweet”) + -lich. Cognate with Dutch zoetelijk (“mawkish; sentimental”), Middle English swetly, sweetly (“pleasant; lovely”, adjective).

verb:schwängern.tx: From Middle High German swengern, from Old High German swangaren, from swangar (“pregnant”), from Proto-West Germanic *swangr (“heavy”). Cognate with Yiddish שווענגערן (shvengern).

noun:Sauerbraten.tx: A compound of sauer (sour) and Braten (roast).

noun:Schwärmerei.tx: Derived from schwärmen (schwärm- + -erei) or from Schwärmer (Schwärmer + -ei).

noun:Schimäre.tx: From Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira, “chimera; female goat”).

verb:schüren.tx: From Middle High German schürn, from Old High German scuren, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran, from Proto-Germanic *skeraną, see also Old English sċieran, Old Frisian skera, Old Saxon sceran, Old High German skëran.

prep:sonder.tx: From Middle High German sonder, sunder, from Old High German suntar, from Proto-West Germanic *sundr, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“isolated, particular, alone”), from Proto-Indo-European *snter-, *seni-, *senu-, *san- (“apart, without, for oneself”). Cognate to English sunder (“separate, different”), Latin sine (“without”).

adj:spärlich.tx: From Middle High German sperlīche, from Old High German sparalīhho, ultimately from the root of sparen (“to save up”).

noun:Schlagbaum.tx: 16th century, from schlagen + Baum. The former word refers to the “slamming down”. The latter is used in the dated sense of “stem, beam, pole”; compare cognate English beam.

pt: appearance, that which only seems to be
adj:scheinheilig.tx: A word of the Reformation, first attested ca. 1580, from Schein (“appearance, that which only seems to be”) + heilig (“holy”), likely after Dutch schijnheilig (1557).

noun:Schneebesen.tx: Schnee (“snow”) + Besen (“broom”), referring to Eischnee (“egg white foam”, literally “egg snow”).

verb:stauben.tx: From Middle High German stouben, from Old High German stouben, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan (“to sprinkle”). Equivalent to Staub + -en. Cognate with Hunsrik staave.

verb:säubern.tx: From Middle High German siubern, sūbern, from Old High German sūbaren, sūbiren, sūbarōn. By surface analysis, sauber + -n.

noun:Scheck.tx: Borrowed from American English check. Doublet of Schach, Schah, and Check.

noun:Staude.tx: From Middle High German stūde, from Old High German stūda, probably related to stauen.

noun:Seelenwanderung.tx: Seele + -n- + Wanderung. Compare Danish sjælevandring and Swedish själavandring.

verb:sabbeln.tx: Related to sabbern (“to drivel, drool”). This word entered standard German alongside sabbern from Low German [Term?]. Subsequently, the meaning of this term shifted; sabbern retains the original meaning, "drool". Compare southern Dutch zabberen, standard Dutch sabbelen. The nouns Sabber and Sabbel are also closely related.

noun:Schaschlik.tx: Borrowed from Russian шашлы́к (šašlýk), from Turkic; compare Turkish şişlik.

noun:Sperma.tx: Borrowed from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”).

noun:Schätzung.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schetzunge (“tax”). By surface analysis, schätzen (“to estimate, guess”) + -ung. Compare also Swiss German Schatzung.

verb:schimmeln.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schimmelen, from Old High German scimbalōn; equivalent to Schimmel (“mould”) + -en (denominative suffix).

verb:schaufeln.tx: From Middle High German schūveln, synchronically analyzed as Schaufel + -n.

noun:Semit.tx: Sem + -it. Coined by members of the Göttingen School of History in the 1770s, after the biblical name Sem (“Shem”).

noun:Streu.tx: From Middle High German ströuwe, ströu, strewe. By surface analysis, deverbal from streuen.

noun:Sintflut.tx: From Middle High German sinvluot, sintvluot, from Old High German sinfluot, sintfluot, from sin- (“great, eternal”, prefix) + fluot (“flood”), whence modern German Flut. The variant Sündflut is due to association with Sünde (“sin”), as also in cognate Dutch zondvloed. The i-form was almost fully obsolete for 200 years, until it was revived in the early 19th century after the scientific study of …

noun:Seelachs.tx: From See (“sea”) + Lachs (“salmon”). So called because it was used as a substitute for salmon in the production of smoked salmon (“lox”) in the first half of the 20th century. This use is no longer common, but the name has been kept for marketing reasons.

adj:scheiße.tx: The adjective comes from predicative use of the noun, while the adverb is from its interjective use, e.g.: Scheiße, bin ich besoffen! → Er ist scheißbesoffen. (“He's completely plastered.”)

verb:scannen.tx: Borrowed from English scan, eventually from Latin scandere. Doublet of skandieren.

verb:schmoren.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German smôren, from Proto-Germanic *smurōną (“to suffocate, strangle”), probably related to *smallijan (“to burn”) or Old English smoca (“smoke”). Cognate with Dutch smoren, English smother.

noun:Spender.tx: From Middle High German spendære, from Old High German spentāri. Equivalent to spenden + -er.

noun:Schlamassel.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שלימזל (shlimazl, “unlucky, clumsy person”).

adj:splitternackt.tx: From Middle High German splitternāket. By surface analysis, Splitter + nackt.

noun:Spind.tx: From Middle Low German spint, spinde, borrowed from or reinforced by Middle Dutch spinde, spende. Eventually related with German spenden, from Late Latin spendere, from Latin expendere; either through Medieval Latin spenda, the existence of which is doubted however, or a Germanic derivation from the verb.

noun:Schlappe.tx: Partially from German Low German Slappe (“slap”). Probably imitative. Compare English slap and Russian шлёпанец (šljópanec).

noun:Schlappen.tx: Attested from dialects as a footwear since the 17th century, developing Middle High German slappe, slape (“the part of a head-covering hanging down like a pouch; klappen- oder beutelförmig herunterhängender Teil der Kopfbedeckung; Kopfbedeckung; Art Kappe”), hence in dialects a “loose shoe made by separating the front part of a shoe (der durch Abschneiden der Kappe zum Pantoffel gemachte Schuh; Pantoffel)”.

noun:Schwarzpulver.tx: From schwarz (“black”) + Pulver (“powder”). A popular folk etymology claims the legendary alchemist and alleged inventor Berthold Schwarz as origin.

noun:Schwemme.tx: From Middle High German swemme, deverbal from swemmen, whence modern schwemmen (“to sweep, to wash ashore”), which see for more. The sense “part of a beer hall” derives via “simple tavern” (16th c.) from the formerly current expression die Zunge in die Schwemme reiten (“to booze”, literally “to ride one’s tongue to the bathing place”).

noun:Song.tx: Borrowed from English song. Doublet of inherited Sang.

noun:Schlager.tx: From schlagen (“to hit”) + -er, formally a doublet of Schläger. Attested since the late 19th century and thus older than English hit (early 20th century).

noun:Schlagader.tx: schlagen (“to beat”) + Ader (“blood vessel”). Exact cognate with Icelandic slagæð.

verb:spleißen.tx: From Middle High German splīzen, from Old High German *splīzan, from Proto-West Germanic *splītan, which see for cognates. Within High German, the word was restricted to Central German, but even here far from general, and therefore did not establish itself in the modern standard language. The nautical sense after Low German splissen, splitzen, a related (but not identical) form.

noun:Staffel.tx: From Middle High German staffel, from Old High German staffal, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *stapul (“pillar, post, basis, foundation”). Doublet of Etappe and Stapel. Compare English staple.

noun:Siebenschläfer.tx: From Middle High German siben slāfære, referring to the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus. Univerbation since the 15th century. Use for “one who sleeps a lot” since the 17th century. The biological sense since the 18th century because of the animal's hibernation, which may last more than seven months.

verb:stocken.tx: From Proto-Germanic *stukkōną (“to stop, stick”). Though a surface analysis as Stock (“stick, broken-off twig”) + -en (“infinitive suffix”), as suggested by Pfeiffer, is not exactly correct, said analysis does trace back to the same root as *stukkōną.

verb:schmerzen.tx: From Middle High German schmërzen, from Old High German smërzan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with Dutch smarten, English smart, Low German smerten, Danish smerte, Swedish smärta.

noun:Stängel.tx: From Middle High German stengel, from Old High German stengil, stingil. Related to Stange.

noun:Staatsstreich.tx: Calque of French coup d'État (literally “stroke (or blow) of state”), from Staat + -s- + Streich.

noun:Scharia.tx: Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيعَة (šarīʕa, literally “path, way”).

noun:Schafgarbe.tx: From Schaf (“sheep”) + Garbe (“yarrow”). The second element may derive from Old High German garwa, garawa, from Proto-Germanic *garwo; see Garbe (“yarrow”). Compare Dutch gerw, English yarrow.

verb:schnäuzen.tx: From Middle High German sniuzen, from Old High German snūzen, snūzōn, from Proto-Germanic *snūtijaną. The ä was introduced in 1996 due to an alleged folk-etymological connection to Schnauze, as also in Greuel / Gräuel, but such spellings are even controversial to many a voice who adheres to the reformed rules.

verb:süßen.tx: From Old High German suozen, from Proto-Germanic *swōtijaną, derived from *swōtuz (“sweet”), whence German süß (“sweet”).

adj:somatisch.tx: From Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós) + -isch, from σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

adj:spröde.tx: Uncertain. Possibly connected with West Flemish sprooi and Middle English sprēth, sprēþe (“spiritually weak, inadequate”).

intj:schachmatt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schāch mat, from Classical Persian شَاهمَات (šāh-māt). By surface analysis, Schach + matt. The alternative form with intervening und is also already attested as Middle High German schāch unde mat.

adj:schachmatt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schāch mat, from Classical Persian شَاهمَات (šāh-māt). By surface analysis, Schach + matt. The alternative form with intervening und is also already attested as Middle High German schāch unde mat.

verb:suppen.tx: Related with Middle Low German besubben (“to soil, sully, bedabble”), dialectal Swedish subba (“to soil”), perhaps also sabbern (“to dribble, slaver”). Further possibly onomatopoeic, but also comparable with the root of Saft, English sap, or that of Sieb, Seife, English sieve, soap, seep. With regard to the latter, compare especially Dutch sijpelen (“to trickle, seep, drip”) and similar verbs in …

noun:Schwingen.tx: Verbal noun, substantivation of schwingen. The sense "Swiss wrestling" is attested from the 16th century, often in the phrase "Ringen und Schwingen".

noun:Schwachkopf.tx: schwach (“weak”) + Kopf (“head”). Compare with weakheaded, weakminded, Russian слабоу́мный (slaboúmnyj, “imbecile, weakminded”).

verb:stunden.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German stunden.

verb:sprinten.tx: Borrowed from English sprint + -en, since the 1930s. The modern pronunciation is a spelling pronunciation.

noun:Siff.tx: From Syph f (“syphilis”), clipping of Syphilis, either directly or as a back-formation from versifft (also spelt versypht). The use for “filth” has existed in slang since at least the 1960s; it became more widely accepted during the 1980s. While the origin from Syphilis is not in doubt, note that dialectally (e.g. Rhineland, parts of Hesse) there is a verb seifen, siffen, siefen (“to ooze, …

verb:schliefen.tx: From Middle High German sliefen, from Old High German sliofan, from Proto-West Germanic *sleupan.

adj:sechste.tx: From Old High German sehsto, from Proto-Germanic *sehstô. Equivalent to sechs + -te.

noun:Schrotflinte.tx: From Schrot (“small shot charge”) + Flinte (“flintlock rifle”). Since all guns of the type Flinte are used to deliver small shot charges, the combination is a pleonasm.

verb:schrecken.tx: From Middle High German schrecken, from Old High German skreckōn (“to jump”), from Proto-Germanic *skrikkōną; the ultimate origin is uncertain, possibly related to *skeraną (“to shear”) (thus "make sudden cutting movements" > "scare") or *skrīaną (“to scream”). Also compare Old Norse skaga (“to jut out”). Cognate with Dutch schrikken (“to be startled”). Danish skrække and Swedish skräcka are …

verb:spiegeln.tx: From Middle High German spiegeln, spiegelen; compare Middle Dutch spiegelen (Dutch spiegelen). By surface analysis, Spiegel + -en.

adj:spitze.tx: From Spitze (“of the highest grade, quality”, literally “peak, point”). See the adjective spitz (“sharp, pointy”).

noun:Schmu.tx: Rotwelsch, perhaps from Yiddish שמועס (shmues). Compare Dutch smoes, English schmooze.

noun:Simse.tx: Alteration of older Semde, from Middle High German semde, semede, from Old High German semid, semida. Related to Middle Low German semende, sēm (“bent, rush”).

verb:simsen.tx: From SMS (“short message service”) + -en, with excrescent -i-.

noun:Syndrom.tx: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).

noun:Solarium.tx: Ultimately from Latin solarium. Doublet of Söller.

noun:Schuhmacher.tx: From Middle High German schuochmacher. By surface analysis, Schuh (“shoe”) + Macher (“maker”).

adj:siebte.tx: Syncope of siebente, from Middle High German sibente, sibende, from Old High German sibunto, from Proto-West Germanic *sebundō, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô. Equivalent to sieben + -te.

noun:Stuss.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שטות (shtus, “nonsense”), from Hebrew שְׁטוּת (sh'tút, “nonsense”).

noun:Stockente.tx: From Stock + Ente. Cognate with Norwegian stokkand.

verb:scheuchen.tx: From Middle High German schiuhen (see there for more), making it a doublet of scheuen. The fortified pronunciation of word-finally and preconsonantally in Middle High German is generalized into all forms, first as a byform of scheuen, then becoming specific to certain senses.

noun:Serval.tx: Borrowed from French serval, from Portuguese (lobo) cerval (“Iberian lynx”).

noun:Seppuku.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 切腹/せっぷく (seppuku).

verb:splitten.tx: Borrowed from English split, itself from Middle Dutch and/or Middle Low German splitten, an intensive form of splîten, cognate of German spleißen. The borrowed word may have been reinforced or merged with modern Low German splitten, from the same source. Related with German Splitt (“grit, stone chips”), Splitter (“splinter”), and splittern (“to sliver”), which are all directly from Middle Low German.

noun:Schnitte.tx: From Middle High German snitte, snite, from Old High German snita. By surface analysis, deverbal from schneiden.

verb:stutzen.tx: From Middle High German stutzen (“to scare away”). Cognate with Dutch stuiten (“to check, rebound”).

noun:Schütz.tx: From the verb schützen (“to protect, shelter”)

noun:Sumach.tx: From Middle High German sumach, from Old French sumac, probably through Old Spanish (modern Spanish zumaque) or alternatively Old Italian (modern Italian sommacco), from Arabic سُمّاق (summāq), from Classical Syriac ܣܘܡܩܐ (summāqā, “red; sumac”).

adj:schnurz.tx: Attested since the 19th century, of unknown origin, probably purposefully combined to remininisce a number of terms for various lowly matters such as Schnurre, Schnodder, Rotz, Furz.

noun:Sexappeal.tx: Earlier 20th century, borrowed from English sex appeal.

verb:soufflieren.tx: Borrowed from French souffler, from Old French sofler, from Latin sufflāre.

noun:Spill.tx: From Middle Low German spille, from a contraction of Proto-West Germanic *spinnilu (“spindle”). Doublet of Spindel.

verb:stibitzen.tx: Uncertain, attested since the 18th century. Possibly from Serbo-Croatian štipati (“to pinch, nib”).

noun:Stack.tx: Borrowed from Low German Stack, from Middle Low German stak. Probably related with stāke (“stake”). Possibly influenced by stacket (“stockade, picket fence”), itself from also related Old French estakete.

noun:Strolch.tx: Related to Alemannic German strollen, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Italian astrologo (“astrologer”). Related also to German strolchen.

noun:Station.tx: From Late Middle High German *staziōn (attested as statziān), from Latin statio; see there for cognates.

noun:Spital.tx: From Middle High German spitāl, hospitāl, from Old High German *hospitāl (attested in hospitālhūs (“hospital”)), from Latin hospitale.

verb:stählen.tx: From Middle High German stælen, contraction of earlier stehelen. By surface analysis, Stahl (“steel”) + -en.

noun:Schulze.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German sculdheizo, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldihaitijō.

noun:Schwammerl.tx: From Bavarian Schwammerl, from Middle High German swamme, swam, swamp, from Old High German swamp, from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz.

noun:Schisma.tx: From Middle High German zisma, from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).

noun:String.tx: Borrowed from English string. The sense "G-string" is a pseudo-anglicism.

noun:Schweif.tx: From Middle High German sweif, from Old High German sweif; related to schweifen.

noun:Seitensprung.tx: From Seite (“side”) + -en- + Sprung (“jump, hop”). Compare Danish sidespring.

noun:Spendierhosen.tx: From spendieren (“to be generous”) + Hosen (“trousers”), literally “generosity trousers, treating trousers”.

noun:Sauce.tx: Borrowed from French sauce, from Old French sauce, sause, sausse, salse, from Latin salsa.

noun:Schuldiger.tx: From Middle High German schuldigære (“debtor, accused” as well as “creditor, accuser”). Equivalent to the obsolete verb schuldigen + -er. Compare Schuldner (“debtor, one who owes money”). In the Lord's Prayer a calque of Latin debitor.

verb:schludern.tx: From Middle High German slūdern (“to sway”), related with schleudern (“to swing, hurl”). Perhaps ultimately from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Compare also Dutch slodderen (“to be sloppy”). The form with -u- follows Low German sludern and other non-diphthongising dialects.
