noun:Stammlager.tx: From Stamm (“stem, trunk”, and hence “origin, root, center”) + Lager (“camp”).

noun:Scharmützel.tx: 14th century, from Middle High German scharmützel, diminutive in -el of scharmutz, from Italian scaramuccia and/or Middle French escarmuche, ultimately derived from Proto-West Germanic *skirmijan, whence German schirmen (“to protect”).

verb:schallen.tx: From Middle High German schallen, from the root of Schall (“sound”). The Grimms have it as corrupt form of Middle High German schëllen (inflected schal, geschollen), from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).

noun:Schneise.tx: From Middle High German sneise, sneize (first attested as sneyße, 14th c.), from Old High German *sneisa, from Proto-West Germanic *snaisu, from Proto-Germanic *snaisō. Related to German schneiden.

verb:streifen.tx: From Middle High German streifen, from Old High German *streifen (in abastreifen > modern abstreifen), from Proto-Germanic *straipijaną, *stripōną (“to touch”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Pokorny derives the word from Proto-Indo-European *ster-, *strē- (“strip, streak”), for which see Strahl (“beam, ray”), while Pfeifer instead takes the word as related to Streifen (“strip”), with semantic …

noun:Schabracke.tx: 17th century, from Hungarian csábrák. Some sources derive it further from Ottoman Turkish چاپراق (çaprak), while others suggest that the Ottoman is itself from Hungarian.

verb:stürzen.tx: From Middle High German stürzen, from Old High German sturzen, from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan. See also the doublet starten, descended from the same source. Compare English start.

pron:selber.tx: From Middle High German sëlber, fossiled strong masculine nominative of sëlp (“the same”). Thus identical to etymology 2 below with loss of inflection. Doublet of selbst, which is a fossiled genitive (with paragogic -t).

noun:Schlafrock.tx: From Schlaf (“sleep”) + Rock (“coat, robe”). Compare Yiddish שלאָפֿראָק (shlofrok).

verb:spuken.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German spōken; equivalent to Spuk + -en. Cognate with English spook and Dutch spoken.

noun:Spuk.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German spōk, from Old Saxon *spōk, from Proto-Germanic *spōk. Cognate with Dutch spook, whence English spook.

verb:stigmatisieren.tx: From Medieval Latin stigmatizō + -ieren, from Medieval Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō).

noun:Schwabe.tx: Possibly from Latin Suēbus, plural Suēbi.

verb:schirmen.tx: From Middle High German schirmen schërmen, from Old High German skirmen.

verb:schweren.tx: From Middle High German swæren, from Old High German swārēn, from Proto-West Germanic *swārēn, from Proto-Germanic *swērāną.

noun:Statt.tx: A mere orthographic variant of Stadt (“city”). Doublet of Stätte and Stadt. Cognate with English stead.

noun:Spanne.tx: From Middle High German spanne, from Old High German spanna, from Proto-Germanic *spannō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to stretch”). Cognate with Dutch span, spanne, English span.

noun:Spange.tx: From Middle High German spange, from Middle Low German spange, from Old High German spanga.

verb:strömen.tx: An old derivation of Strom (“stream”). Cognate with Old Norse streyma, Danish strømme and English stream.

noun:Streusel.tx: From streu- + -sel, literally “something strewn”. Related to English strew.

noun:Schmier.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שמירה (shmire), from Hebrew שמירה (šəmīrā, “guard”). Compare Schmiere stehen.

noun:Soda.tx: Borrowed from Spanish soda. Beverage uses are from semantic loan from English soda.

adj:sekundär.tx: 18th century, from Latin secundarius, chiefly through French secondaire.

noun:Sockel.tx: Borrowed from French socle, from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”).

noun:Steuerbord.tx: Equivalent to Steuer (“helm, steering wheel”) + Bord (“board”), because early Germanic ships were steered with a paddle over the right side.

adj:skurril.tx: Borrowed from Latin scurrīlis, from scurra (“jester, joker”). Compare Italian scurrile and English scurrilous.

noun:Schub.tx: From Middle High German schub, schup, ultimately from the root of and a deverbal from schieben (“to shove”). Cognate to English shove.

noun:Schubs.tx: From Schupp (“push”) + -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.) is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schubsen for more.

noun:Schabernack.tx: From Middle High German schabirnack, from Middle Low German schavernak (14th c.). Further etymology unknown.

noun:Steig.tx: From Middle High German stīc, from Old High German stīg, from Proto-Germanic *stīgaz (“path”), related to German steigen. Cognate with Old English stīġ (“path; footpath; narrow way”), English sty (“ladder”), Danish sti, Norwegian Bokmål sti.

noun:Steige.tx: From Middle High German steige, from Old High German steiga, from Proto-Germanic *staigō. Related with (but not identical to) more usual Steig, Stieg m, from Middle High German stīc. Related with steigen.

noun:Spat.tx: From Middle High German spāt (less often also spăt, possibly by confusion with etymology 2 below). There are no known cognates, but probably related to Span (“shaving, clipping”).

noun:Sorte.tx: In general use since the 16th century. Borrowed from Middle Low German sorte (14th c.), from Old French sorte, and from chiefly independent Upper German sorta, sort (15th c.), from Italian sorta; all eventually from Latin sors. See English sort for more.

noun:Schreibtischtäter.tx: Schreibtisch (“writing desk”) + Täter (“criminal”), adapted from English desk murderer, initially used to describe Nazi bureaucrats involved in the planning of genocide, in particular Adolf Eichmann during the Eichmann trial in 1961.

noun:Stumpen.tx: From a merger of two interrelated forms: 1.) Stump(en), a Central and Low German variant of Stumpf, from northern Middle High German stumpe and Middle Low German stump; 2.) Stumpen, Stumpel, an Upper German variant of Stummel, from Middle High German stumbel, from Old High German stumbal. The use in standard German is predominantly based on southern dialects (word 2).

verb:schichten.tx: From northern Middle High German schihten, from Middle Low German schichten, from Old Saxon *skiftian, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną. Cognate with Dutch schiften, English shift.

verb:schnaufen.tx: An old variant of schnauben (“to snort, to pant”), documented in Middle High German snūfen. The fricative -f- (or -v-) instead of -b- is expected for Low German (compare Middle Low German snûven) as well as West Central German (compare Luxembourgish schnauwen). However, such forms are also old in Upper German dialects, it not being sure whether the latter have borrowed them from the North, or …

noun:Schilling.tx: From Middle High German schillinc, from Old High German skilling, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz.

noun:Safran.tx: From Middle High German safrān; derived from French safran, from Arabic زعفران (zāfarān). Cognate with English saffron, Spanish azafrán, Italian zafferano.

adj:sämig.tx: Central and Low German form which (since the 19th c.) has displaced the slightly earlier seimig (18th c.). Equivalent to archaic Seim (“viscous liquid”, especially “syrup, honey”) + -ig. The spelling with -ä- (instead of -e-) could represent West Central German dialects, but is more probably analogous with adjectives in -ig showing umlaut of -a-.

noun:Spiritus.tx: 15th century, borrowed from Latin spiritus. Doublet of Esprit, Spirit, and Sprit.

noun:Slawe.tx: From Middle High German Slave, from Medieval Latin Sclavus. Distinguished from the doublet Sklave since the 18th century, probably influenced by descendants of Proto-Slavic *slověninъ. Also a doublet of ciao.

adj:splitterfasernackt.tx: Blend of splitternackt + fasernackt, since the 17th century.

noun:Symmetrie.tx: Borrowed from Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

noun:Strippe.tx: From a merger of two words: 1.) Middle Low German strippe (“strip, cord”), cognate with Dutch strip, English strip, and related with German Streifen, and 2.) Middle High German struppe, strüppe, northern variant of strupfe, strüpfe (“leather loop”), borrowed from Latin struppus (“strap, band”), cognate with Dutch strop.

verb:schmettern.tx: From Middle High German smetern (“to chatter, rattle”). In several dialects the word also means “to make a smacking sound”, which is perhaps the original meaning. Probably related with English smatter, Swedish smattra, though in all languages the word is attested rather late. Compare also German schnattern.

verb:schwirren.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German swirren in the 17th century, from Old Saxon *swirrian, from Proto-West Germanic *swirrijan, from Proto-Germanic *swirrijaną, *swerrōną, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum, whistle, sound, speak”). Cognate with Dutch zwieren, West Frisian swiere, Danish svirre, Swedish svirra.

noun:Slawistik.tx: From Slawist, modelled on Romanist, Romanistik. By surface analysis, Slaw(en) + -ist + -ik.

verb:schummeln.tx: There are two main theories, which need not be mutually exclusive but may complement each other. * From dialectal schummeln, originally probably “to move back and forth”, whence various attested senses: “waver, totter; rock, swing, push; chase off; abscond, steal away; take clandestinely; rummage; bustle about; do housework”, etc. In favour of this derivation speaks that the sense “to cheat” was …

noun:Schwatz.tx: From Middle High German swaz; see schwatzen (“to chat”).

noun:Spitzel.tx: The first sense derives from the second, because dogs of this breed were used as police dogs. From Spitz + -el, called so because of their pointy tail.

noun:Schmackes.tx: From the Low and Central German verb schmacken (“to hit hard”), ultimately of imitative origin; compare Middle Low German smacken. This verb is cognate with English smack, which see for more.

noun:Stuka.tx: From Sturzkampfbomber m. Hence the masculine gender. Alternative feminine gender from the common use of the feminine for ships and airplanes, as well as by analogy with most nouns in -a.

noun:Schapp.tx: From Low German Schapp, from Middle Low German schap, from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Doublet of Schaff.

verb:säuseln.tx: Since the 17th century, as a diminutivizing iterative sausen + -eln. Compare Dutch suizelen.

verb:schütten.tx: From Middle High German schütten, schüten (“to shake; to pour”), from Old High German scuttēn (“to shake”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuddjan. Cognate with Bavarian schittn, Hunsrik schidde, Dutch schudden (“to shake”); perhaps cognate with Lithuanian kutė́ti (“to shake up”) and Russian скитаться (skitatʹsja, “to wander, stray”).

verb:steppen.tx: From Middle High German steppen, itself either borrowed from Old Saxon steppon (“to pierce, mark with stitches”) or inherited from a Central German cognate of the same. Closely related with stippen, which see.

noun:Stimulans.tx: From Latin stimulāns (“stimulating”), present participle of stimulō (“to stimulate”). By surface analysis, stimulieren + -ans.

adj:semitisch.tx: Semite/Semit + -isch, named after Sem (a son of Noah)

noun:Schließung.tx: From schließen + -ung; cognate with Hunsrik Schliesung.

verb:schwären.tx: From Middle High German swërn, from Old High German swëran, from Proto-Germanic *sweraną.

adj:schicker.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שיכּור (shiker, “drunk”), from Hebrew שיכור / שִׁכּוֹר (shikór, “drunkard”).

verb:schnauben.tx: From dialectal Middle High German snūben, related to Middle Low German snûven, Middle High German snūfen (“to gasp, pant”), which is part of a group of interrelated forms (see below), ultimately from a Germanic base imitative of the sudden drawing of breath. The verb was originally strong, but developed weak forms as early as the 16th century, which have then predominated since the 18th century. …

adv:seinerzeit.tx: Univerbation of seiner + Zeit, originally an adverbial genitive, literally "of its time".

verb:servieren.tx: Borrowed from French servir + -en, from Latin serviō (“to serve, be a slave to”), from servus (“slave”).

adv:sogleich.tx: Univerbation of so + gleich, with "so" as an emphasizer, 18th century. Compare sofort, sodann.

verb:streben.tx: From Middle High German strëben, from Old High German strëbēn, from Proto-West Germanic *stribēn, from Proto-Germanic *stribāną.

adj:schlüpfrig.tx: From Middle High German slipferec, from Old High German sleffarag (influenced by Old High German slipfīg), from Old High German sleffar (“slippery”), from Proto-Germanic *slipraz (“slippery”). Figurative sense from 17th c.

adv:seinetwegen.tx: Shortened from von seinetwegen, which can be traced through two developmental routes. One route is from von seinentwegen / von seinent wegen, from von seinen wegen, from Middle High German von sînen wegen, in which wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and sînen was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural. Another route can be traced from von seintwegen / von seint wegen, from Middle …

noun:Suff.tx: Secondary ablaut formation (16th or 17th c.) from saufen (“to drink, swig”).

noun:Schemen.tx: From Middle High German scheme m or f, from Old High German *skemo m, skema f, from Proto-Germanic *skīmô, *skimô, *skimō. The word meant “mask” in Upper German, but “shadow, silhouette” in Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German schēme, from Old Saxon skimo. The modern meaning is based on the northern usage, in part after Luther. Cognate with Middle Dutch scheme alongside the stem …

noun:Satzung.tx: From Middle High German satzunge f.

noun:Sinneswahrnehmung.tx: From Sinnes + Wahrnehmung, from wahrnehmen, from wahr + nehmen.

verb:schrumpeln.tx: Derivative of schrumpen + -eln (itself not used in standard German), the German Low German and West Central German form of schrumpfen (“to shrink”).

noun:Sprinkler.tx: 20th century, from English sprinkler, from sprinkle. Associated in German with the cognate verb sprenkeln and therefore always pronounced like a native word.

verb:schürfen.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]. Cognate to Dutch schorpen (“to rip open; to saw”).

adj:sacht.tx: 16th c., borrowed from Low German sacht, sachte (“soft”), from Middle Low German sachte, from Old Saxon *sāfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (compare Proto-Germanic *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *sóm-tu-, possibly from *sem- (“one, whole”). Doublet of sanft. Cognate with English soft.

adv:sacht.tx: 16th c., borrowed from Low German sacht, sachte (“soft”), from Middle Low German sachte, from Old Saxon *sāfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (compare Proto-Germanic *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *sóm-tu-, possibly from *sem- (“one, whole”). Doublet of sanft. Cognate with English soft.

verb:schnuppern.tx: From schnuppen + -ern, with schnuppen (or snuppen) being the German Low German and Central German form of schnupfen (“to sniff”).

noun:Städter.tx: From Middle High German stäter, steter. Equivalent to Stadt + -er.

noun:Selbstanzeige.tx: From selbst (“self”) + Anzeige (“report to the authorities”).

noun:Schippe.tx: A Central and Low German word, from northern Middle High German *schüppe (attested 15th c.) and Middle Low German schüppe, from Proto-Germanic *skupjō. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schëpp (“shovel”), Dutch schop (“shovel, spade”).

verb:sprudeln.tx: Likely sprühen + -eln, influenced by brodeln (“to seethe”).

verb:schippern.tx: From Low German, from Schipper (“captain, one in charge of a boat”), from Middle Low German schipper, alteration of schēper, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz, whence also German Schiffer. Compare Dutch schipperen (“to manoeuvre, sort out, cope”).

noun:Schalthebel.tx: From Schalter + Hebel or schalten + Hebel.

noun:Schmand.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German smand. There are two theories as to the origin of the Middle Low German word: * Duden and some other authorities think it derives from Proto-West Germanic *smanþī (“smooth, soft”) and is thus cognate to English smooth. * Jacob Grimm and Václav Machek think it derives from Slavic (whence also Schmetten and English smetana). See смета́на (smetána) for more.

noun:Stegreif.tx: From Middle High German stegereif (“stirrup”), from Old High German stegareif (“stirrup”), from stegōn (“to ascend”, related with stīgan, whence modern steigen) + reif (“rope, ring”, whence modern Reif). Cognate with English stirrup. The contemporary sense is from the idea of someone going to task “from the stirrup”, that is immediately after their arrival and without further arrangements. …

noun:Sasse.tx: From Middle High German sāʒ, from Old High German sāʒo, from the root of sitzen (“to sit”) similar to Etymology 2 below. Compare Insasse (“passenger of a vehicle, inhabitant of a building”).

noun:Schandmaul.tx: From Schande (“disgrace, shame, shending”) + Maul (“muzzle, mouth”).

noun:Sigrist.tx: Middle High German sigrist, from Medieval Latin sacrista.

verb:schlemmen.tx: From Middle High German slammen, possibly from slampen by influence from Schlamm; see schlampen for more. Compare Dutch slempen, English slam.

verb:schlecken.tx: From Middle High German slecken, from Old High German *slikkon, from Proto-West Germanic *slikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *slikkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Cognate with Bavarian schleckn and Dutch slikken.

noun:Sprit.tx: 19th century, short for Spiritus, probably of dialectal origin, though some assume influence by French esprit. Ultimately from Latin spiritus (“spirit”). The original meaning is “brandy”, later extended to petrol, perhaps from the idea of a “potent liquid”. This sense is now predominant and also widely used in media parlance, such that contemporary speakers may actually think it the original one.

noun:Spedition.tx: Borrowed from Italian spedizione, from Latin expeditiō.

adj:schmuddelig.tx: From German Low German, synchronically analyzed as schmuddeln + -ig.

verb:scharren.tx: From Middle High German scharren, intensive of scherren, from Old High German scerran (“to scrape off”), from or related to Proto-West Germanic *skeran (“to cut”).

adj:schlapp.tx: From Middle Low German slap (“flaccid”), from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), and from the same family of words as German *slēpaną (“to sleep”); see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). Doublet of schlaff, which is often interchangeable in modern German. Also cognate with Dutch slap.

noun:Salto.tx: From Italian salto (“jump, leap”), from Latin saltus (“jump, leap”). Compare French salto, Dutch salto, Hungarian szaltó.

noun:Sang.tx: From Middle High German sanc, from Old High German sang, ultimately from the root of the verb singen (“to sing”).

noun:Schelle.tx: From Middle High German schelle, from Old High German scella, from Proto-Germanic *skellǭ (“bell”), from Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to sound; resound; ring”); see the related schellen (“to ring”) for more.

noun:Schiebetür.tx: From schieben (“to push, to shove”) + Tür (“door”).

noun:Schott.tx: Borrowed from Low German Schot in the 18th century, from Middle Low German schot, ultimately from the root of schießen (“to shoot”). Cognate with Dutch schot.

verb:schnacken.tx: Borrowed from German Low German snacken, from Middle Low German snacken, from Proto-Germanic *snakkōną (“to open the mouth”). Cognate with Dutch snakken, whence English snack, whence the German doublet Snack. Also related with English snatch and probably (with a different geminate) German schnappen, Dutch snappen, both originally “to snatch”.

noun:Sezession.tx: Borrowed from Latin sēcessiō (“withdrawal, secession”), with influence from English secession.

noun:Schnipsel.tx: Variant of Schnitzel, which used to be the dominant form before it became common in the sense of “cutlet” (to which it is now often restricted). Compare the verbs schnippeln (“to snip”) and schnipsen (“to nip off”). Ultimately all these forms pertain to schneiden (“to cut”).

noun:Sigel.tx: From French sigle, from Latin sigillum. Doublet of Siegel.

noun:Stiege.tx: From Middle High German stiege, from Old High German stiega, a variant (with an unusual ablaut grade) of Proto-Germanic *stigǭ (“path, way, staircase, ladder”). Related with German steigen and English stair. See also Bavarian Stiagn.

noun:Schwätzer.tx: From Middle High German swetzer. By surface analysis, schwatzen (“jabber, prattle”) + -er (agentive suffix).

noun:Schnuckel.tx: Probably related to a group of chiefly German Low German [Term?] and Central German dialect verbs schnucken, schnuckeln, and variants. These verbs mean “to eat sweets”, “to suck (like a baby)”, occasionally “to kiss”, all of which senses suit the noun perfectly. Compare English snookums.

noun:Saitenspiel.tx: From Middle High German seitspil, seitespil, seitenspil. By surface analysis, Saite (“string”) + -n- + Spiel (“play”).

verb:schwatzen.tx: From Middle High German swazzen. See schwätzen.

verb:shoppen.tx: Borrowed from English shop with suffix -en.

noun:Spacken.tx: Spacken and Spacko possibly derive from Spastiker, paralleling English spacko and spack coming from English spastic (and e.g. German Mucki from Muskel, etc). Alternatively, they might derive from Northern German spack (“thin, scrawny; brittle”), with -en, the Low German masculine nominative ending.

verb:swingen.tx: Borrowed from English swing. Doublet of schwingen.

noun:Stoppel.tx: From Middle High German stupfel, stoppele, from Old High German stuphila, *stuppila from Latin stipula (also attested as stupula). The modern form with -pp- is of Central and Low German origin; compare Middle Low German stoppel. Compare also Dutch stoppel, English stubble.

noun:Schluffen.tx: Borrowed from Central Franconian Schluff, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *sleupaną (“to slip”). Compare Dutch slof (“slipper”).

noun:Stützpunkt.tx: 19th century, from stützen (“to support, lean, hold”) + Punkt (“point”).

noun:Schmach.tx: From Middle High German smāch, smāhe, from Old High German smāhi (“small”), from Proto-Germanic *smēhaz. Related to schmähen.

verb:stürmen.tx: From Middle High German stürmen, from Old High German sturmen, from Proto-Germanic *sturmijaną. Equivalent to Sturm + -en.

noun:Songtext.tx: From Song + Text; compare English songtext.

adj:schmierig.tx: From Middle High German smerwic, smerewic, from Old High German *smerwīg, *smerewīg, from Proto-West Germanic *smerwig, equivalent to Schmiere + -ig. Perhaps also influenced by earlier Middle Low German smērich, which is directly from smēr, cognate of German Schmer.

noun:Schweinchen.tx: Schwein + -chen. In the sense of "jack-ball", a semantic loan from French cochonnet.

noun:Statthalter.tx: Late Middle High German stathalter, calque of Medieval Latin locumtenens (“lieutenant”). Compare Dutch stadhouder.

verb:signieren.tx: From Latin signō (“I mark, I sign”) + -ieren.

noun:Siel.tx: 18th century, from Low German Siel, from Middle Low German and Old Saxon sīl. Cognate with Dutch zijl, West Frisian syl.

noun:Schnitz.tx: From Middle High German sniz (“cut, slice”), from root of Old High German snīdan (“to cut”). Related to schneiden.

verb:stapfen.tx: From Middle High German stapfen, from Old High German staphōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stappōn. Related with *stappjan, whence English step. Compare also Dutch stappen. The word had died out in the written language around 1600, but survived in dialects. It was reintroduced by Wieland in his Oberon (1780-96).

verb:schwenken.tx: From Middle High German swenken, Old High German swenken, from Proto-West Germanic *swankijan, from Proto-Germanic *swankijaną (“cause to swing”).

noun:Spinnwebe.tx: From northern Middle High German spinnenwebe f, alteration of older spinnenweppe n, from Old High German spinnūnwebbi n. Compare Spinne (“spider”), weben (“to weave”).

phrase:Stein des Anstoßes.tx: Literally, “stone of stumbling”. This phrase originates from the Bible translation made by Martin Luther, in particular from the passage of Isaiah 8:14 in which אֶבֶן נֶגֶף (ʾeven neḡef) is mentioned in the original Hebrew version. Compare Dutch steen des aanstoots.

verb:schmunzeln.tx: From Late Middle High German schmuntzelen, smonczeln (15th c.), diminutive-iterative of smunzen, nasalized byform of smutzen (ca. 1300), all meaning “to smile, laugh slightly”. Further origin unknown.

noun:Spesen.tx: Borrowed from Italian spese, plural of spesa (“expense, expenditure”), from Latin expēnsa (“idem”). The word was borrowed into the German merchant's jargon of the 17th century, receiving a native plural ending -n. Earlier attestations (15th, 16th century) exist in Upper German sources in varying forms such as despessa, spesa, spessa, speise, speiz. Compare German Speise (“meal, foodstuff”), an …

adj:sturm.tx: From Middle High German sturm (“stormy”), from Old High German sturm.

noun:Sangria.tx: Borrowed from Spanish sangría, from sangre (“blood”).

verb:scheuen.tx: From Middle High German schiuhen, from Old High German sciuhen, from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhan, from the Proto-Germanic adjective *skiuhaz (“shy”). By surface analysis, scheu + -en. Doublet of scheuchen. Compare Dutch schuwen.

noun:Schnute.tx: 18th century, from Low German Snute, from Middle Low German snûte, from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt. Doublet of Schnauze (“snout, muzzle”), which is an earlier (adapted) borrowing from the Low German.

verb:schmatzen.tx: From Middle High German smatzen, from older smackezen, from the root of Schmackes (“force, power”).

verb:schröpfen.tx: From Middle High German schrepfen, schreffen, from Old High German *skrepfan, from Proto-West Germanic *skrappjan (“to scrape, scratch”). Belongs to the strong verb *skrepan (Middle High German schrëffen, Old English screpan), of which it is an intensive, as is the stem variant *skrapōn, whence Middle High German schraffen and (via Middle Low German) modern schrap(p)en (“to scrape”). The various …

noun:Schachspiel.tx: * (chess set): By surface analysis, Schach (“chess”) + Spiel (“game”).

verb:schmachten.tx: First attested in the 17th century, from Schmacht + -en, after Middle Low German smachten. The noun and the prefixed verb verschmachten are also attested in northern Middle High German (smaht, versmahten). Ultimately derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“small, little”). Related with Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós), Latin mica.

noun:Spelunke.tx: Borrowed from Latin spēlunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave, cavern, grotto”). Cognate to English spelunk

noun:Schwachmat.tx: Clipping of the older forms above, themselves from schwach (“weak”) blended with medical terms like Rheumatiker/Rheumatikus (“rheumatic”), Phlegmatiker/Phlegmatikus (“phlegmatic”), originally in student slang.

adj:schnöde.tx: From Middle High German snoede, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *snauþuz (“bald, naked, poor”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksnéw-tu-s, from the root *ksnew- (“to scrape, sharpen”). Cognates include Dutch snood, sneu and Old Norse snauðr.

verb:schwarzsehen.tx: From schwarz (“black”) + sehen (“to see, to watch”).

noun:Scherge.tx: From Middle High German scherge, from Old High German skerio (“troop leader”), from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō.

noun:Sud.tx: From Middle High German sut, from Old High German *sut, from Proto-Germanic *sudą (“brew, soup”); related to sieden (“to boil”). Cognate with Old English ġesod (“cooking, boiling, seething”), Old Frisian soth (“cooking, boiling”), Danish sod, Icelandic soð.

verb:schnupfen.tx: From Middle High German snupfen; equivalent to an intensive form of schnauben (“to pant, snort”).

noun:Steiger.tx: From Middle High German stīger, stīgære, equivalent to steigen + -er. Cognate with Middle Low German stīgære, stēgære.

verb:seihen.tx: From Middle High German sīhen, from Old High German sīhan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīhwan, from Proto-Germanic *sīhwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to filter”).

phrase:so Gott will.tx: The word so is used in the dated sense “if”.

noun:Sachertorte.tx: From Sacher + Torte (“cake”), named after Austrian confectioner Franz Sacher (1816–1907), who invented it in 1832.

verb:schwadronieren.tx: From Schwadron (“squadron”) + -ieren, 18th century, modern sense from student slang related to fencing.

noun:Stele.tx: Ca. 1800, from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē, “upright rock, pillar, column”).

noun:Spekulatius.tx: Unknown. Various theories have been proposed: * Latinized form of Low German (especially East Frisian) Spikelātsje, Spekelātsje and Rhinelandic Spekulaties (19th c.), from Dutch speculatie meaning "plastically formed goodies" and later referred to "figured biscuits". One possible explanation for the Latinization of the Low German and Rhinelandic forms is that they were believed to be derived from …

noun:Seidel.tx: From Middle High German sīdel, borrowed in the 13th c. from Medieval Latin situlum, from Latin situla.

noun:Schiffer.tx: From Middle High German schiffære, schiffere, from Old High German *skiffāri, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz (“sailor”). Doublet of Schipper and Skipper.

adj:siech.tx: From Middle High German siech, from Old High German sioh, siuh, from Proto-West Germanic *seuk, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz. Cognate with English sick, Dutch ziek, Swedish sjuk.

noun:Stracciatella.tx: Unadapted borrowing from Italian stracciatella, from stracciare (“to rip, to tear up”), of ultimate Latin origin.

noun:Sternenbanner.tx: Sterne (“stars”) + -n- + Banner (“banner”), a calque of English Star-Spangled Banner.

noun:Studentenfutter.tx: From Student (“student”) + -en- + Futter (“fodder”). Compare Polish mieszanka studencka.

noun:Sparren.tx: From Middle High German sparre, from Old High German sparro, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô.

noun:Spachtel.tx: Originally a Bavarian variant of Spatel (“scoop, applicator”) (see for more). Compare the same Bavarian development in Schachtel.

noun:Skate.tx: From English skate, itself from Dutch schaats.

noun:Synkope.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin syncope, from Ancient Greek σῠγκοπή (sŭnkopḗ).

noun:Spielmann.tx: From the Middle High German spilman, from the Old High German spiliman, from spil + man.

noun:Staatsmann.tx: Late 17th century. From Staat (“state”) + -s- + Mann (“man”), calque of French homme d'État, perhaps after English statesman (late 16th century).

noun:Seim.tx: From Middle High German seim (“honey, syrup”), from Old High German seim, from Proto-West Germanic *saim, from Proto-Germanic *saimaz (“raw honey”). Cognate with Dutch zeem, Old Saxon sēm (“fresh honey”), and Old Norse seimr (“honeycomb”). It may be a cognate of Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma), see there for more.

noun:Schalk.tx: From Middle High German schalc, from Old High German skalk, from Proto-West Germanic *skalk.

verb:schmähen.tx: From Middle High German smæhen, from Old High German smāhen, from Proto-Germanic *smēhijaną (“to reduce; belittle; despise”), from Proto-Indo-European *smēyg- (“small, thin, delicate”). See also Dutch smaad (“slander”), Proto-Germanic *smikraz (“fine, fair”), Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“little”).

noun:Spätzle.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Spätzle, unclear if. # a diminutive of Spatz (“sparrow”), comparing the name of the dish Rindsvögel # or in another ablaut to the family of Spitze (“cusp, peak”), German Spieß (“spit”), comparing to the Italian spirelli (literally “little spires or coils”); compare its other name Knöpfli from Knopf (“knob”) # or of even more obscure orgin possibly related to German …

verb:schnalzen.tx: From Middle High German snalzen (“to move with a noise peculiar to the rapid movement of the fingers or the tongue”).

noun:Stulle.tx: Perhaps from Dutch stul, or a variant of Stollen.

intj:sapperlot.tx: Borrowed from French saperlotte (17th century), euphemistic modification of sacredieu, from sacré (nom de) Dieu (literally “holy (name of) God”).

noun:Sakristei.tx: Inherited from Middle High German sacristīe, from Medieval Latin sacristi|a, ~ae.

noun:Scheu.tx: From Middle High German schiech (“despondent, frightening, ugly”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh (“shy, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, fearful”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian skjou (“shy”), Dutch schuw (“shy”), English shy, Danish sky (“shy”), and doublet of schiech.

noun:Sakrament.tx: From Middle High German sacrament, from Latin sacramentum.

noun:Sonntagsstaat.tx: From Sonntag (“Sunday”) + -s- + Staat. The latter word is used in the archaic sense “condition, appearance, clothing”.

noun:Stoffel.tx: From the German given name Stoffel, a pet name for Christoph. A short form of the surname Christoffel

noun:Stelldichein.tx: stell dich ein, a calque of French rendez-vous.

noun:Senn.tx: Inherited from Middle High German senne, from Old High German senno, from Proto-West Germanic *sannjō (“herdsman, dairyman”), from Vulgar Latin saniō (“herdsman, dairyman”), deemed a borrowing from Celtic languages, the stem preserved in Old Irish sine (“nipple, teat”), reconstructing Proto-Celtic *sɸenyos (“teat, nipple”) corresponding to Proto-Germanic *spenô (“nipple”).

noun:Schabbes.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שבת (shabes), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת.

noun:Skipper.tx: Borrowed from English skipper, from Middle English skippere, from Middle Dutch schipper, from Old Dutch *skipāri, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz. Doublet of Schiffer and Schipper.

noun:Schupp.tx: Deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną.

noun:Splitt.tx: From German Low German Split, Splete (“splinter, kindling, stone chip”), from Middle Low German *split, splēte. Related with Middle Low German splîten, German spleißen, and eventually also English split.

noun:Siphon.tx: From French siphon, from Latin sipho, from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”).

noun:Strunk.tx: A Central and Low German word from northern Middle High German strunc and Middle Low German strunk, ultimately from the root of starren (“to be stiff”). Cognate with Dutch stronk.

noun:Schenk.tx: From Middle High German schenke, from Old High German scenco, from Proto-West Germanic *skankijō.

noun:Stocker.tx: From Middle High German stocker. By surface analysis, stocken + -er or Stock + -er.

noun:Schaub.tx: From Middle High German schoup, from Old High German scoub, from Proto-West Germanic *skaub, from Proto-Germanic *skauba-. Ultimately related to schieben (“to shove”). Doublet of Schof.

noun:Schick.tx: From the reflexive verb sich schicken (“to be appropriate”).

noun:Sandler.tx: Borrowed from Bavarian Sandler, from Middle High German seinen. By surface analysis, sandeln + -er

noun:Stuck.tx: Borrowed from Italian stucco in the 18th century. Doublet of Stück.

noun:Session.tx: Borrowed from Latin sessiō or French session.

noun:Schaff.tx: From Middle High German schaf, from Old High German scaf, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Doublet of Schapp. Cognate with Dutch schap and Swedish skåp.

noun:Schreier.tx: From Middle High German schrīære, schrīer. By surface analysis, schreien + -er.

verb:siechen.tx: From Middle High German siechen, from siohhēn, from Proto-West Germanic *seukēn. Cognate with Low German süüken, seeken and Swedish sjukna.

noun:Schimpf.tx: From Middle High German schimpf, from Old High German skimpf, from Proto-West Germanic *skimp (“mockery, joke”). Cognate with Middle Low German schimp, Dutch schimp (“taunt, railing”).

noun:Scheuer.tx: From Middle High German schiure, from Old High German skiura, from Proto-West Germanic *skūru, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Originally the predominant High German word, except in the north-east. Cognate with Dutch schuur.

adj:schlagfertig.tx: Mid-17th century, equivalent to Schlag (“hit, blow”) + fertig (“ready, capable”). Probably a calque of Dutch slagvaardig. For this speak the slightly earlier attestation (1625), the invariably nautical context of the earliest German attestations, and the fact that Dutch slag means “battle”. (The proper German form would thus be schlachtfertig, which makes more sense semantically and is indeed attested.)

noun:Schierling.tx: From Middle High German schirlinc, with irregular raising from older scherlinc, from Old High German skerling, itself with dissimilation from older skerning. Cognate with Dutch scheerling. Derived from Proto-Germanic *skarną (“dung”) due to the plant’s preferred habitat. Compare dialectal English sharn.

noun:Schur.tx: From Middle High German schuor, schür, from Old High German *skuora, from Proto-Germanic *skōrō (“shearing”). Cognate with Old English scora (“a hairy garment”).

adj:schleunig.tx: From Middle High German sliunec (“hastily”), from Old High German sliumo, sniumo (“immediately”, literally “moving quickly”), from or related to Proto-West Germanic *sniumijan (“to hurry”). The -l/n replacement seems to have been produced by assimilation on account of the suffix -n (DWDS).

adj:schmählich.tx: From Middle High German smæhelich, smāhelich, smāhlich, smēlich, from Old High German smāhlīh, from Proto-West Germanic *smāhalīk, *smāhīlīk, equivalent to schmähen + -lich.

adj:schnieke.tx: From Low German snikke (“pretty”), influenced by schniegeln (“to spruce up”).

adj:schnuppe.tx: From Schnuppe (“[worthless as] the burnt remains of a wick”).

noun:Schussel.tx: Probably cognate to German Schusser (“clacker, bullet; wound”), as if by surface analysis, Schuss (“shot”) + -el, literally one who is shot, amorous verschossen (“have a crush; miss a shot”). Maybe related to schudeln, compare hudeln. Older dictionaries gloss this specifically feminine, mismatching the supposed derivation which requires neuter gender, matching Ripuarian neuter inflection on …

noun:Stake.tx: 15th century, borrowed from Middle Low German stāke m, from Old Saxon *stako, from Proto-West Germanic *stakō, from Proto-Germanic *stakô. Cognate with Dutch staak, English stake.

adj:schwülstig.tx: Schwulst + -ig. Doublet of schwulstig, which has developed slightly different meanings. Compare Swedish svulstig.

adj:schütter.tx: With sporadic rounding after sch from Middle High German schiter, from Old High German skitir, sketar, with regular preservation of t before r from Proto-Germanic *skit(a)raz. Cognate with Ancient Greek σκιδαρός (skidarós, “thin, fine, weak”). The word was widely obsolete in standard German until the 19th century, when it was revived on the basis of Upper German dialects.

adj:sittsam.tx: Middle High German sitsam, Old High German situsam, corresponding to Sitte + -sam

adj:solitär.tx: From French solitaire (“solitary”), from Latin sōlitārius.

adj:spartanisch.tx: Latin Spartānus with -isch replacing Latin -us. Analysable as Sparta + -isch with -an- from Latin -ānus and analogy

adj:sportiv.tx: Borrowed from French sportif, equivalent to Sport + -iv.

adj:stämmig.tx: Stamm + -ig, from the idea of being "built like a tree trunk". Cognate with English stemmy.

adj:substanziell.tx: From Latin substantialis, partly through French substantiel. Equivalent to Substanz + -ell with an additional i.

noun:Schlappschwanz.tx: From schlapp (“limp”) + Schwanz (“cock, dick, penis”, literally “tail”).

noun:Schlauberger.tx: 19th century. From schlau (“smart”) + Berg + -er, as if being the demonym of an imaginary town Schlauberg (“Smartville”, literally “smart mountain”). Compare English wisenheimer.

verb:schwelgen.tx: From Middle High German swëlgen, from Old High German swëlgan, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą (“to gulp (down); swallow; devour”). Cognate with Old English swelgan (English swallow).

noun:Schlehe.tx: From Middle High German slēhe, from Old High German slēha, from Proto-West Germanic *slaihā, from Proto-Germanic *slaihǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *sléh₃ikos (“bluish”). Cognate with Dutch slee, English sloe, Swedish slån, and probably with Proto-Slavic *sliva (“plum”), whence Russian сли́ва (slíva) etc.

noun:Strike.tx: Late 20th century, borrowed from English strike.

adv:sperrangelweit.tx: Blend of the earlier synonymous emphatic forms of sperrweit and angelweit.

noun:Schlaufe.tx: Upper German form of Schleife (“bow, tie”), which see for more. The semantic distinction between both variants is secondary.

noun:Schramme.tx: From Middle High German schramme, schramm, cognate to Old English scrama (cf. scramasax), Middle Dutch scramme, Dutch schram (“scratch”), Old Norse skráma (“wound”), Swedish skråma (“scratch”). Possibly related to Middle Irish screm, Welsh cramen (“crust”), Russian крома́ (kromá, “crust”), Latvian kri̇̀mst, Lithuanian krim̃sti (“to gnaw”).

noun:Schwebezustand.tx: schweben (“to hover, to float”) + Zustand (“state, condition”)

noun:Schwarzkopf.tx: Compound of schwarz (“black”) + Kopf (“head”), from black hair being observed to be rare among ethnic Germans.

noun:Steinhaus.tx: Stein + Haus; cognate with Hunsrik Steenhaus

noun:Schwengel.tx: From Middle High German swengel (“something which swings or flings”), thus related to schwingen (“to swing, to fling”) and schwenken (“to swivel, to slew”).

verb:stufen.tx: Asynchronically analyzable as denominal of Stufe

verb:schäkern.tx: Of unclear origin. A relation has been proposed with Yiddish חק (khek, “bosom, womb”), from Hebrew חֵיק (khék, “bosom”).

noun:Stichel.tx: From Middle High German stichel, from Old High German stihhila.

verb:schuften.tx: Probably borrowed from Middle Low German schoft (“a quarter day's work”), related to Schub (“batch (work that can be performed in one run)”) and schieben (“to shove”). Unrelated to Schuft (“scoundrel”).

verb:skandieren.tx: First attested 1523. Either directly from Latin scandere or through French scander (1516). Doublet of scannen.

noun:Siebensachen.tx: Univerbation of sieben + Sachen. Literally, “seven things”.

noun:Strafbataillon.tx: From Strafe + Bataillon or strafen + Bataillon.

noun:Suhle.tx: 17th-century alteration (after the related verb suhlen) of older Sole f, Sol m, n, from Middle High German sol, from Old High German sol, from Proto-West Germanic *sol, from Proto-Germanic *sulą.

verb:schwarzfahren.tx: From schwarz + fahren. Compare Dutch zwartrijden.

verb:stöbern.tx: 16th century, iterative of stäuben, stauben, from Middle High German stöuben, stouben (“to swirl up, raise dust”), from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan, factitive of *steuban (whence stieben). The ö-vocalism is East Central and Low German (Middle Low German stö̂ven). The sense “to browse” is in part derived through the noun Middle High German stöuber, Middle Low German stö̂ver (“small hound used …

verb:schlitzen.tx: From Middle High German slitzen, from Old High German slizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *slittjan, from Proto-Germanic *slittjaną.

noun:Stümper.tx: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German stümper. Derived from the cognate of Stumpf (“stump”). Cognate with Dutch stumper.

verb:schweifen.tx: From Middle High German sweifen, from Old High German sweifan, from Proto-West Germanic *swaipan, from Proto-Germanic *swaipaną.

verb:schunkeln.tx: 18th century, from a nasalised byform of Schaukel (“swing”), which see.

noun:Stutzen.tx: From Middle High German stutz, stutze (“shock, thrust; something compressed, stub; glass without a foot and stem”), from stutzen (“to butt, shock, stall”). Compare modern German stutzen (“to stall, pause, be perplexed; to trim, shorten”), related with stoßen (“to push, butt”).

verb:schmollen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German smollen, ablaut form of Middle High German smielen (whence ultimately English smile).

verb:schiefgehen.tx: schief (“slanted, awry”) + gehen (“to go”). Compare English go awry and go sideways.

verb:schmarotzen.tx: 15th c. Middle High German smorotzen (“to beg”), further origin unclear; whether or not the word is from Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant) cannot be proven with certainty. Possibly a blend of schnorren (“to beg”) and late Middle High German mutzen (“to cut off, trim”).

noun:Showmaster.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from show + master, equivalent to Show + Master.

noun:Supplement.tx: Borrowed from Latin supplementum, or French supplément.

noun:Schmauch.tx: From northern Middle High German smouch (13th c.), from Old High German *smouh, from Proto-West Germanic *smauki. Originally restricted to Central German, later reinforced by cognate Middle Low German smôk, but not fully established in the standard language (apart from the specialist use in weaponry). Further cognate with dated Dutch smook, dialectal English smeech. Also related to smoke, which compare.

noun:Schleudersitz.tx: From schleudern + Sitz or Schleuder + Sitz.

noun:Strass.tx: After its inventor, the 18th-century Alsatian jeweler Georg Friedrich Strass.

noun:Sodomist.tx: From Sodomie + -ist. Alternatively analysable as Sodom + -ist.

noun:Schlemihl.tx: 19th century, from Yiddish שלימיל (shlimil). Further origin uncertain; see the Yiddish for more. The rather odd spelling with -ih- follows the use of Adelbert von Chamisso in his well-known novella Peter Schlemihl (1813). Von Chamisso probably avoided Schlemiel because it could have suggested a trisyllabic pronunciation as in Gabriel (though he might have spelt *Schlemil).

verb:strotzen.tx: From Middle High German strotzen, ultimately from the root of starren (“to be covered”). Cognate with Old Norse þrútenn (“swollen”), English strut.

verb:spicken.tx: From Middle High German spicken, from Middle Low German specken, analyzable as Speck + -en. The meaning “cheat at an exam” was possibly influenced by spähen (“to peek, spy”).

noun:Schmatz.tx: Late Middle High German smaz, related to schmatzen.

noun:Sortiment.tx: 17th century, from Italian sortimento, derived from sortire. Analysable in German as Sorte or sortieren + -ment. Borrowed from German into various languages of northern and eastern Europe; compare Swedish sortiment, Czech sortiment.

noun:Schlafittchen.tx: 18th century, but probably older. Generally explained as a reinterpretation (as a diminutive) of Schlafittichen, dative plural of obsolete Schlafittich, itself from an underlying *Schlagfittich, from schlagen (“to strike, thrash”) + Fittich (“wing of a bird”), from the way a bird is grabbed by its thrashing wings. This requires that the word is of Central or Low German origin and that southern …

noun:Schrebergarten.tx: Schreber + Garten (“garden”), named after German physician Moritz Schreber (1808–1861), who was known for advocating allotment gardens for recreational usage, particularly for children.

noun:Streitgespräch.tx: From Streit (“quarrel, dispute, fight, argument”) + Gespräch (“talk”).

noun:Scherflein.tx: Diminutive of Scherf, from Middle High German scherf, scherpf (“a coin of small value, esp. a halfpenny”), from Old High German scerf, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skrapōną (“to scratch”). Related to modern Scherbe (“shard”) and Middle High German scharben (“to notch, to nick”) (from Old High German scarbōn, cognate with Old English sceorfan (“to gnaw, to bite”)), because the coins were …

noun:Stutzflügel.tx: stutzen (“to cut short, to trim”) + Flügel (“grand piano”)

verb:schnallen.tx: Denominal verb of Schnalle in the 17th century.

adv:stracks.tx: From Middle High German strackes, from strac, whence rare German strack (“straight”). Compare Dutch straks.

noun:Schwadron.tx: 17th century, borrowed from Italian squadrone. The onset developed after Schwader, Geschwader, an earlier borrowing from related Italian squadra.

noun:Selfie.tx: Borrowed from English selfie. Cognate literally in structure with rare German Selbstchen (“selfie, self-photo”), probably calqued from English.

noun:Schutzhaft.tx: 19th century, from Schutz (“protection”) + Haft (“custody”). The law was first used to detain opponents between 1914 and 1919. The Nazi government revived and greatly escalated this practice, often giving the pretext that the arrested had to be protected from the wrath of the general population.

verb:schächten.tx: 17th century, from Hebrew שָׁחַט (šāḥaṭ). The umlaut possibly spread from the derivative Schächter (“Jewish butcher”), where it may have sprung from analogy with unrelated Schlächter (“butcher”), but a verb form with -a- seems unattested.

verb:schlingern.tx: From Middle Low German slingeren, iterative of slingen, which latter is cognate with German schlingen, English sling. The iterative also in Dutch slingeren.

verb:salben.tx: From Middle High German salben, from Old High German salbon, from Proto-West Germanic *salbōn, from Proto-Germanic *salbōną. Equivalent to Salbe + -en.

noun:Schlawiner.tx: From Slawonier (“Slovene”), a reference to Slovene door-to-door salesmen, who were considered very cunning. Austrian German, 19th c.

noun:Stenz.tx: Rotwelsch, or from older dialectal stenzen, compare stanzen.

verb:sühnen.tx: From Middle High German süenen, suonen (“to reconcile, balance”), from Old High German suonen (“to judge, bring about compensation”). By surface analysis, Sühne (“atonement”) + -n (“verbal suffix”).

noun:Strohwitwe.tx: From Stroh + Witwe. First attested in the early 18th century.

noun:Schöngeist.tx: Calque of French bel esprit, schön + Geist.

noun:Schmöker.tx: From Low German Smöker, from the verb smöken (“to smoke”), from Middle Low German smöken, from Proto-West Germanic *smaukijan. The semantic motivation is unclear. Some compare Schinken (literally “ham”) and thus interpret Schmöker as “smoked ham”. Others compare Swedish lunta (literally “fuse”) and derive it from the practice of using pages from old books for lighting pipes. It could also refer …

verb:schnippeln.tx: Frequentative of schnippen + -eln, from Central and Low German dialects (18th century). Compare Dutch snippen (“to chop”).

noun:Schlendrian.tx: schlendern + Jan, compare Liederjan, Dummerjan, or also with Latin -iānus as in Grobian.

verb:stauchen.tx: Uncertain. Perhaps from Middle High German stūchen (“to cup, bleed”), from Middle High German stūche (“cupping glass”). Alternatively, perhaps from Middle Low German stûken (“to push, compress, arrange flax in small bundles for drying”), from Middle Low German stûke (“bundle of flax set up to dry, bunch of grain”).

verb:schinden.tx: From Middle High German schinden, schinten (“to cheat; swindle; torment; peel off; skin”), from Old High German skinden, skinten (“to skin; flay; peel off”), derived from the noun Middle High German schint (“fruit peel”), all ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skinþą (“fruit peel”). Cognate with German Low German schinden, schinnen (“to torment; afflict; harass”). Related to English skin.

noun:Samariter.tx: From Latin Samarites. By surface analysis, Samaria + -iter

verb:saunen.tx: From Sauna (“sauna”) + -en, after the plural Saunen (“saunas”) and by analogy with duschen (“to shower”) and baden (“to bathe”), which exhibit the same alternation between intransitive and reflexive use.

verb:scheppern.tx: 17th century, of onomatopoeic origin, apparently first in Upper German dialects.

noun:Schnodder.tx: Northerly Central German or Low German consonantism from Proto-Germanic *snuttuz.

noun:Sachwalter.tx: From late Middle High German sachwalter. By surface analysis, Sache + Walter or Sache + walten + -er.

noun:Schändung.tx: From Middle High German schendunge. Equivalent to schänden + -ung.

noun:Selbstverwirklichung.tx: selbst (“self”) + Verwirklichung (“actualization, realization”). Compare Swedish självförverkligande.

noun:Schelte.tx: From Middle High German schëlte, from Old High German skëlta.

noun:Schani.tx: From an Austrian colloquial form of French Jean (given name).

noun:Schwulst.tx: From Middle High German swulst f (“tumor, growth”), from swellen (“to swell up, bulge”), from Old High German swellan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).

verb:stiefeln.tx: 16th century, from Stiefel + -en in the reflexive sense. The sense “stride, walk” since the 18th century.

noun:Schmarrn.tx: From Bavarian Schmårrn, from the root of schmieren (“to smear”) and Schmer (“lard”), thus ultimately from Proto-Germanic *smerwą (“grease, fat”).

noun:Siegrune.tx: First attested as a translation of Old Norse sigrún (victory rune). It was popularized as the name of the ᛋ-rune by Guido von List in his book Das Geheimnis der Runen.

noun:Schickeria.tx: From schick, influenced by Italian sciccheria (“elegance”).

noun:Schnitter.tx: From Middle High German snitære, from Old High German snitāri. By surface analysis, Schnitt + -er.

noun:Schurz.tx: From Middle High German schurz (“apron”), substantivization of schurz (“short”), from Old High German scurz, from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz. Compare Schürze.

noun:Spielhaus.tx: From Middle High German spilhūs, from Old High German spilehūs, spilahūs, spilohūs (“theater, playhouse, gymnastics field, ring field, sports school”), equivalent to Spiel + Haus.

noun:Spanferkel.tx: From Middle High German spenvarch, from Old High German spunnifarah, from spunna (“teat”) + farah (“pig”). See spean and farrow for more.

noun:Schwang.tx: From Middle High German swanc. Doublet of Schwank.

noun:Sänfte.tx: From Middle High German senfte, semfte, from Old High German samfti. Equivalent to sanft + -e.

pt: appearance, that which seems to be
noun:Scheinehe.tx: From Schein (“appearance, that which seems to be”) + Ehe (“marriage”).

verb:suhlen.tx: From Middle High German süln, suln, soln, from Old High German *sullen, *solōn (attested in bisullen), from Proto-West Germanic *sulwijan, from Proto-Germanic *sulwijaną (“to soil, make dirty”), from Proto-Germanic *sulwō, from Proto-Germanic *sulą (“mud”). Cognate with English sully.

noun:Schnack.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German snak (“speech, chatter”), from Middle Low German snacken (“to speak, talk, chatter”), akin to Middle High German snacken (“to chatter, chat”).

noun:Stadel.tx: From Middle High German stadel, Old High German stadal, related to stehen. Cognates include English staddle, Czech stodola and Polish stodoła.

noun:Staupe.tx: 13th century, from northern Middle High German stūpe, from Middle Low German stûp, staup, from Polabian staup, from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”).

noun:Schwank.tx: From Middle High German swanc. Doublet of Schwang.

noun:Seekuh.tx: From See (“sea”) + Kuh (“cow”). The sense "hippopotamus" is a calque of Afrikaans seekoei.

verb:schwärzen.tx: From Middle High German swerzen, from Old High German swerzen. Equivalent to schwarz + -en.

noun:Schultheiß.tx: Inherited from Middle High German schultheize, from Old High German sculdheizo.

noun:Sentenz.tx: From Middle High German sententie, from Latin sententia. Masculine gender predominated until the mid-18th century, probably after Spruch and/or Satz.

noun:Stiftungsvermögen.tx: From Stiftung (“foundation, endowment”) + -s- + Vermögen (“fortune, assets, wealth, capital”).

noun:Schlich.tx: From Middle High German slich, from Old High German slich, from Proto-Germanic *slīką. Doublet of Schleich and Schlick.

noun:Sojus.tx: Borrowed from Russian Союз (Sojuz), from союз (sojuz, “union”).

noun:Spielverderberin.tx: Spiel (“game”) + Verderberin (“spoiler, corrupter (female)”), or rather from Spielverderber (“game spoiler”) + -in (“female”)

verb:streunen.tx: Old High German striunen, related to Old English strēon (“gain, wealth”), English strain.

noun:Schtetl.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish שטעטל (shtetl, “small town, townlet”).

noun:Stammgast.tx: Stamm (“trunk, stem”) + Gast (“guest”), Cognates include Swedish stamgäst and Dutch stamgast.

noun:Stabhochspringerin.tx: Stab (“rod, staff”) + Hochspringerin (“high jumper (female)”), or rather from Stabhochspringer (“pole vaulter”) + -in (“female”)

verb:straucheln.tx: From Middle High German strūcheln, iterative of strūchen, from Old High German strūhhōn. Equivalent to obsolete strauchen + -eln. Cognate with Dutch struikelen.

noun:Schecke.tx: Derivational nominalization of the adjective scheckig (“dappled”). (First attested in the late 16th century.)

noun:Senkel.tx: From Middle High German senkel (“net weighed down with lead balls, anchor, lace”), from Old High German senkil (“anchor, cast net”), from an extension of senken with nominalizing suffix -ila, originally meaning "device that one lets sink down"; see Stachel for an analogous noun formation.

noun:Spritzkuchen.tx: spritzen (“to pipe [with a pastry bag]”) + Kuchen (“cake”)

noun:Straßenmusiker.tx: From Straßenmusik (“street music”) + -er (“-ian”); analyzable as Straße (“street”) + -n- + Musiker (“musician”).

adj:scheckig.tx: Middle High German schecke, from Old French eschec (“check”), thus “checkered”.

noun:Spliss.tx: 20th century, from Low German Spliss, Spließ, from the nautical verb splissen (“to splice; to fray the ends of ropes and tie them together”). The latter is cognate with Dutch splitsen (“to split”, older also splissen) and related with Proto-Germanic *splītaną, whence regional German spleißen (also used in the nautical sense above), Dutch splijten, English split.

noun:Sachlichkeit.tx: sachlich + -keit. Cognates include Swedish saklighet, Dutch zakelijkheid.

verb:schnarren.tx: From Middle High German snarren, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *snarkōną, of imitative origin (lautmalend). Compare Middle Low German snarren, snarren, English snar, snarl, German schnurren.

noun:Schwieger.tx: From Middle High German swiger, from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō.

noun:Sixpack.tx: Late 20th century, from English six pack.

noun:Supermann.tx: super- + Mann, on the model of English superman.

noun:Schund.tx: Derived from schinden (“to strip, peel, skin”). Originally applied to rubbish from shaving.

noun:Schwitzkasten.tx: From schwitzen (“to sweat”) + Kasten (“case, chest, box”).

noun:Schnösel.tx: 19th century, from Low German Snösel, Snäsel (18th c.). The sense “snotnose”, which Pfeifer considers original, is of very limited attestation and not mentioned at all by early sources such as the Low German dictionaries of Dähnert (1780) and Schütze (1806). Nevertheless it is plausible to associate the onset S(ch)n- with words like Schnabel (“beak”, cf. Grünschnabel), Schnute (“snout”), …

noun:Schindluder.tx: Low German, schinden (“to skin”) + Luder (“carrion; bait”)

noun:Schmauchspur.tx: From Schmauch (“thick smoke; gunshot residue”) + Spur (“trace”).

noun:Simulant.tx: Borrowed from Latin simulans, or synchronically fromsimulieren (“simulate”) + -ant (noun suffix).

noun:Seevogel.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German sēfogal; equivalent to See + Vogel.

verb:strudeln.tx: An ablaut variant with iterative suffix of Middle High German strëden, from Old High German strëdan, from Proto-West Germanic *streþan, from Proto-Germanic *streþaną. By surface analysis, Strudel + -n.

noun:Sankt-Nimmerleins-Tag.tx: From Sankt Nimmerlein + -s- + Tag, literally “St. Little Never’s Day”. Compare an equivalent in Portuguese no Dia de São Nunca and Italian il giorno di San Mai, further also Dutch met sint-juttemis, French à la Saint-Glinglin.

noun:Stadtbild.tx: From Stadt (“town, city”) + Bild (“image”), perhaps influenced by Weichbild (“city area”), in which the component -bild is, however, not immediately equivalent to German Bild.

noun:Spreißel.tx: From Middle High German sprīzel, perhaps related to spleißen (“to split”).

adj:schadlos.tx: From Middle High German schadelos; equivalent to Schaden (“damage”) + -los (“-less”). Cognate with English scatheless.

verb:speiben.tx: From dialectal Bavarian speibn. See this and the lemma form for more. For the Upper German development -īw- > -eib- compare Eibe.

noun:Schaumschläger.tx: Schaum (“foam”) + Schläger (“whipper”), the latter from schlagen (“to whip”).

noun:Seersucker.tx: Borrowed from English seersucker, from Hindi शीरशक्कर (śīrśakkar), from Persian شیر و شکر (šir o šekar, literally “milk and sugar”).

noun:Skilanglauf.tx: From Ski (“ski”, noun) + lang (“long”, adjective) + Lauf (“run”, noun).

verb:scrollen.tx: Borrowed from English scroll. Doublet of schrotten.

noun:Spreize.tx: From Middle High German spreitze, from Old High German spriuʒa.

intj:salü.tx: Borrowed from French salut (“hello”, greeting), from Latin salūs (“health”).

noun:Sech.tx: From Middle High German sech, from Old High German seh, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], derived from Latin secare (“to cut off”).

phrase:so sicher wie das Amen in der Kir.tx: Literally, “as certain as the Amen in church”, that is, with the same certainty that service participants will say “amen” when required; e.g. in Catholic services, whenever the priest says in Ewigkeit (“forever”). Compare Polish jak amen w pacierzu.

phrase:Sauer macht lustig.tx: Literally, “sour makes merry”. Refers to the positive effects of sour foods on appetite and digestion. Generally, German cuisine is fond of and rich in sour dishes, compare Sauerkraut, Sauerbraten, Saurer Hering, etc. Probably originated in Czech (kyselo dělá veselo), where it rhymes.

pt: blocked or dammed mass of water
noun:Staumauer.tx: From Stau (“blocked or dammed mass of water”) + Mauer (“wall”).

noun:Saftladen.tx: From Saft (“juice”) + Laden (“shop”), a 19th century term meaning “pharmacy”.

noun:Spatel.tx: Middle High German spatel, spatl, Latin spatula

noun:Schäferstündchen.tx: Calque of French heure du berger, Schäfer + Stündchen

noun:Schorle.tx: Clipping of Schorlemorle, originally a dialect word of southwest German origin.

noun:Schliff.tx: From Middle High German slif, from Old High German slif.

noun:Stemmeisen.tx: From stemmen (“to press, to brace”) + Eisen (“iron”).

noun:Schlüsselreiz.tx: Coined by Konrad Lorenz in 1935, Schlüssel + Reiz

noun:Steuerruder.tx: From steuern (“to steer”) + Ruder (“oar, rudder”), an explanatory compound to specify the meaning “rudder”.

verb:strampeln.tx: 15th century, iterative of Middle Low German strampen. Related with stramm, Strumpf, and Dutch strompelen.

adj:stockkonservativ.tx: From stock- + konservativ. Compare Swedish stockkonservativ.

noun:Schulung.tx: schulen + -ung First attested in the 19th century.

adj:schwindlig.tx: By surface analysis, schwindeln + -ig or Schwindel + -ig.

noun:Sup.tx: Borrowed from English sup, or independently clipped in German from Supplement.

noun:Schmirgel.tx: From Middle High German smirgel, smergel, from Italian smeriglio.

prep:seitens.tx: From prepositional phrases with Seite with a calcified inflectional -en (compare e.g. aufseiten) with a secondary adverbial -s.

noun:Standgericht.tx: From Stand (“standing”) + Gericht (“tribunal, court of justice”).

noun:Speis.tx: See Speise. The use for “larder” is from the Bavarian above.

noun:Schneewehe.tx: From Schnee (“snow”) + Wehe (“drift”), from wehen (“to blow”).

noun:Schmeichler.tx: From Middle High German smeicheler, by surface analysis, schmeicheln + -er.

noun:Schwund.tx: Early 19th century, analogical ablaut formation from the verb. Compare the participle geschwunden and deverbal nouns like Bruch, Bund, Fund, Sprung.

noun:Scharlachfieber.tx: Calque of New Latin febris scarlatina: Scharlach + Fieber.

verb:schlampen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German slampen, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lembʰ- (“to hang loosely”), for which see Schlamm (“mud”) for more. See also Schlampe.

noun:Stola.tx: Relatinization of older Stole, from Middle High German stōl(e), from Old High German stōla (since ca. 800), borrowed from Latin stola, from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ).

verb:sputen.tx: 17th century, at first alongside spuden, both secondary adaptations of Middle Low German spôden, from Old Saxon spōdian, from Proto-West Germanic *spōdijan, derived from *spōdi (“prosperity, success”), itself from the verb *spōan, from Proto-Germanic *spōaną (“to prosper, succeed, be happy”), from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to prosper, turn out well”). The West Germanic verb had a cognate in …

noun:Sprint.tx: Borrowed from English sprint, since the start of the 20th century. The modern pronunciation is a spelling pronunciation.

noun:Schrippe.tx: Documented since the 18th century, a derivative of the verb schripfen (“to tear open”).

noun:Scheibenhonig.tx: From Scheibe (“slice, disc”) + -n- + Honig (“honey”). Use as a minced oath probably due to phonetic similarity to Scheiße.

intj:Scheibenhonig.tx: From Scheibe (“slice, disc”) + -n- + Honig (“honey”). Use as a minced oath probably due to phonetic similarity to Scheiße.

noun:Scheibenkleister.tx: From Scheibe + -n- + Kleister, alteration of Scheibenhonig.

intj:Scheibenkleister.tx: From Scheibe + -n- + Kleister, alteration of Scheibenhonig.

noun:Sliwowitz.tx: 19th century, from Czech slivovice and/or Slovene slivovica, derived from Proto-Slavic *sliva (“plum”).

noun:Schwertfeger.tx: Middle High German swertveger, by surface analysis, Schwert + Feger, from fegen (“to polish”).

noun:Schulschwänzer.tx: From Schule + Schwänzer, from schwänzen (“to skip (school)”).

verb:schrubben.tx: From Middle Low German schrubben, schrobben (“to scratch, remove by scraping”), from a formation related to schrappen (“to scrape”), see there for more.

noun:Senke.tx: Inherited from Middle High German senke.

noun:Shop.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English shop. Doublet of Schober, Schupfen, and Schuppen

noun:Schonfrist.tx: schonen (“to spare from harm”, verb) + Frist (“time period”)

noun:Schulmeister.tx: From Middle High German schuolemeister. By surface analysis, Schule + Meister.

adv:sodann.tx: From Middle High German sōdanne, from Old High German sōdanne. By surface analysis, univerbation of so + dann.

noun:Spund.tx: From Late Middle High German spunt m or n (meaning both bung-hole and bung), probably (ultimately) from Latin expūnctum (expungere), whence Middle Low German spunt, Middle Dutch spond (→ spondgat), Dutch spon. Originally only with the meaning of bung-hole (German Spundloch, Anstichöffnung). Possibly through an Italian intermediate spunta.

noun:Stag.tx: From German Low German Stag, from Middle Low German stach, from Old Saxon stag, from Proto-West Germanic *stag from Proto-Germanic *stagą.

noun:Sparring.tx: From English sparring with a spelling pronunciation.

noun:SS-Mann.tx: From SS + Mann, with SS being the initialism of Schutzstaffel.

noun:Schmacht.tx: From rare, northern Middle High German smaht, later reinforced by Middle Low German smacht. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“little, small”). Related to Schmach.

noun:Schampus.tx: 19th century, from a clipping of Champagner + derivational pseudo-Latin -us.

verb:schlottern.tx: Middle High German slotern, intensive form of sloten (“to tremble, hang down loosely”). Perhaps related to a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber.

noun:Serail.tx: 17th century, from French sérail, from Italian serraglio, from Ottoman Turkish سرای (seray, saray), from Persian سرای (sarây).

verb:sterbien.tx: From sterben, made to rhyme with Serbien for the WWI propaganda slogan Serbien muß sterbien (“Serbia has to die”).

noun:Straßenfeger.tx: From Straße (“street”) + -n- + Feger (“sweeper”). The television sense from the notion that it empties the streets of people.

noun:Schnellgericht.tx: From schnell (“fast, quick”) + Gericht (“court of law/justice”).

noun:Segnung.tx: From Middle High German segenunge. Equivalent to segnen + -ung.

verb:skalpieren.tx: From English scalp + -ieren, from Middle English scalp, skalp, scalpe (“crown of the head; skull”).

noun:Superwahljahr.tx: super- + Wahljahr. Popularized in 1994, when many state elections as well as national and European parliamentary elections coincided in Germany.

noun:Schwimmabzeichen.tx: From schwimmen + Abzeichen. Compare with Swedish simmärke.

verb:scheiteln.tx: From Middle High German scheiteln, from Old High German skeitilōn.

verb:schnetzeln.tx: Since the 16th century. A by-form of schnitzeln.

verb:siegeln.tx: From Middle High German sigelen, from Old High German sigilen, from Proto-West Germanic *siglijan, from Latin sigillō (“to seal”).

noun:Schmolle.tx: From late Middle High German smole (“crumb”). Possibly related to mahlen. Compare Old Norse moli (“crumb”) and Swedish smula (“crumb”).

noun:Schra.tx: From Middle Low German schrā, itself probably from Old Norse skrá (“parchment”), though it might also be inherited from the underlying Proto-Germanic *skrahō.

noun:Shoppingcenter.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English shopping center.

adj:stylisch.tx: Borrowed from English stylish, equivalent to Style + -isch.

noun:Stolperdraht.tx: From stolpern (“to stumble, to trip”) + Draht (“wire”).

pt: to strew, to scatter, to sprinkle
noun:Streubombe.tx: From streuen (“to strew, to scatter, to sprinkle”) + Bombe (“bomb”).

noun:Softeis.tx: From English soft + Eis (“ice cream”). Compare Dutch softijs.

verb:schwemmen.tx: From Middle High German swemmen, from Old High German *swemmen, from Proto-Germanic *swammijaną. Equivalent to a causative of schwimmen, thus originally “to make swim or float”. Cognate with Old English beswemman.

noun:Salsa.tx: From Spanish salsa. The (alternative) masculine gender for the dance is by analogy with Tanz and most German words for dances.

noun:Superkleber.tx: From super + Kleber, a calque of English superglue.

noun:Schlehdorn.tx: From Schlehe + Dorn. Compare Dutch sleedoorn, West Flemish sleedôorn.

noun:Speckstein.tx: From Speck (“fat, bacon”) + Stein (“stone”), a calque of Latin steatītis.

noun:Stellmacher.tx: From northern Middle High German stellemacher, reinforced by Middle Low German stellemāker. Equivalent to a prefixless byform of Gestell (“rack, frame”) + Macher (“maker”).

noun:Schmankerl.tx: Schmänkelein + -erl apparently, in 19th century cooking books also Schmankel, a culinary term for “was from Brey oder Muß ans Geschirr anbrät, Kruste” according to Schmeller’s Bavarian dictionary, then a kind of pastry from crusts, there explained as an expressive formation to Schmand.

noun:Straps.tx: From Low German Strapp (“strap, belt, strand”). Alternatively borrowed from or reinforced by English strap.

noun:Schmodder.tx: Blend of Schmadder + Modder, both with the same sense.

noun:Schanker.tx: Borrowed from French chancre (“cancer”), from Latin cancer (“tumor, cancer”).

noun:Synode.tx: 15th century, learned borrowing from Latin synodus. The form in -e (18th c.) was influenced by French synode. Displaced Send, from Middle High German sent, senet, itself partially from the same Latin source and partially from senatus.

noun:Spülküche.tx: From spülen (“to rinse or wash”) + Küche (“kitchen”).

verb:süffeln.tx: From obsolete süpfeln, an iterative formation of obsolete supfen, from Middle High German supfen (“to slurp”), from Old High German sūfan, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną. Doublet of saufen.

noun:Sofortnachricht.tx: Calque of English instant message. Analyzable as sofort + Nachricht.

verb:stochen.tx: Attested since the 16th century. In the 15th already the derivative Stogker (“stoker”). This gk-spelling as well the late attestations suggest an adapted borrowing from Middle Low German stōken, from Proto-West Germanic *stokōn, whence Dutch stoken, English stoke. However, Central Franconian dialects show descendants of this which appear to be native (compare Luxembourgish stachen), so it is also …

noun:Sprengbombe.tx: From sprengen (“to blow up, to blast”) + Bombe (“bomb”).

noun:Seereise.tx: From See + Reise. Compare Dutch zeereis.

noun:Schietwetter.tx: German Low German Schiet (“shit”) + Wetter (“weather”). Compare Dutch schijtweer.

noun:Syndikus.tx: 15th century, from Latin syndicus, from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos). At first in northern usage and thus chiefly through Middle Low German sindicus (13th c.). Compare English syndic.

noun:Strauchdieb.tx: From Strauch (“bush”) + Dieb (“thief”), indicating robbery from a hidden place

noun:Sexualwissenschaft.tx: From sexual + Wissenschaft. Appears for the first time in Sexuality in the Aetiology of the Neuroses by Sigmund Freud in 1898.

noun:Sechsfüßer.tx: From sechs (“six”) + Fuß (“foot”) + -er (“er”). Calque of translingual Hexapoda.

phrase:Schicht im Schacht.tx: Literally, “(end of) shift in the (mine)shaft”, from mining.

noun:Schächer.tx: From Middle High German schæchære, from Old High German scāhhāri, from Proto-West Germanic *skākārī (“robber”). Equivalent to obsolete schachen (“to plunder”) + -er.

noun:Schottenrock.tx: From Schotte (“Scotsman”) + -n- + Rock. The latter word probably in the sense of “skirt”, though it formerly also referred to various men’s garments (jacket, robe, uniform).

noun:Stößchen.tx: From Stoß + -chen. The interjectional use is a pun between the name of the beer glass and the verb anstoßen (“to clink glasses”).

intj:Stößchen.tx: From Stoß + -chen. The interjectional use is a pun between the name of the beer glass and the verb anstoßen (“to clink glasses”).

noun:Stilett.tx: Borrowed from Italian stiletto, diminutive of stilo, from Latin stilus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp; to sting”).

noun:Schmonzette.tx: 20th century, from now archaic Schmonzes (“idle talk”) + -ette (after Operette or the like). The first component is from Yiddish שמאָנצעס (shmontses), itself likely from Hebrew שְׁמוּעוֹת (šəmūʿōṯ, “rumours”). The alternative form with u probably through (etymologically unfounded) association with schmunzeln (“to smile slightly, smirk”).

noun:Spalier.tx: Borrowed from Italian spalliera, from Italian spalla (“shoulder”), from Late Latin spatula, from Latin spatha (“broad, flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “any broad blade, of wood or metal”).

noun:Spendenaktion.tx: From Spende + -n- + Aktion or spenden + Aktion.

noun:Stapfe.tx: Middle High German stapfe, Old High German stapho.

noun:Scheiblettenkäse.tx: From Scheiblette (“a slice of plastic cheese”) + -n- + Käse (“cheese”).

noun:Stadtindianer.tx: Stadt + Indianer (“Native American”), literally, “city Indian”, or more loosely translated as “urban Amerindian”.

adj:sexsüchtig.tx: From Sex + süchtig, equivalent to Sexsucht + -ig.

noun:Swag.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English swag. Popularised by rapper Money Boy in Dreh den Swag auf.

verb:schränken.tx: From Middle High German schrenken (“to place crosswise”), from Old High German screnken (“to spread out, throw down”), from Proto-Germanic *skrankijaną (“to cause to shrink or shrivel; to limit, restrict”).

noun:Sängerknabe.tx: From Middle High German sengerknabe. Equivalent to Sänger + Knabe.

noun:Supermond.tx: Calque of English supermoon, from super- + Mond (“moon”).

noun:Stepptanz.tx: Partial calque of English step dance. By surface analysis, steppen + Tanz.

noun:Schmiss.tx: 17th century, analogical ablaut derivation from schmeißen (“to throw, fling, hurl”).

noun:Secondhandladen.tx: From second-hand + Laden; adapted borrowing from English second-hand shop.

noun:Seichte.tx: From Middle High German sīhte (“shoal,shallow”). By surface analysis, seicht + -e.

verb:stänkern.tx: Frequentative of obsolete stänken (“to create bad smell”), which is a causative to stinken (“to smell badly”). Analysable as Stank + -ern.

noun:Strafanzeige.tx: From Strafe (“punishment; penalty; fine”) + Anzeige (“report to the authorities”).

noun:Silvesterrakete.tx: From Silvester (“New Year's Eve”) + Rakete (“rocket, missile”).

noun:Sommerfrische.tx: Sommer + Frische, with the concrete meaning of the latter from some Upper German dialect.

intj:Schalom.tx: Borrowed from Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (šālṓm), meaning “peace” (noun) and therefore capitalized in German.

verb:semmeln.tx: Sense “to dawdle” probably related to säumeln, from säumen.

noun:Splint.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German splinte.

phrase:so spielt man mit Studenten.tx: Literally, “that’s how you play with [university] students”. Probably alludes to the idea that students tend to overestimate themselves in comparison to players of lesser education but much greater experience, which commonly ends in embarrassing defeats.

verb:schniefen.tx: First attested in the 17th century as schnieben, a Central German variant of schnauben. The form with f is analogous to schnaufen, which compare. In spite of the late attestation, the form may be very old and continue the eu-variant of Proto-Germanic *sneufaną ~ *snūfaną (compare for this variation kriechen ~ krauchen). An alternative theory considers it a backformation from the strong past tense …

noun:Schröter.tx: Equivalent to modern Schröder, from German Low German schrōden (“to cut”). Cognate with English shredder.

intj:sodala.tx: so (“so”) + da (“there”) with an added rhyming syllable.

phrase:so sicher wie das Amen im Gebet.tx: Literally, “as certain as the Amen in a prayer”, that is, with the same certainty that a prayer is finished by saying “amen”.

phrase:so klein mit Hut.tx: Literally, “this little, hat included”, the latter part being added for hyperbole.

noun:Schuhputz.tx: From Schuh (“shoe”) + Putz (“cleaning, cleanliness, stately attire”).

noun:Sachbearbeiter.tx: From Sache (“matter, case”) + Bearbeiter (“person who edits, works on something”). First attested in the 20th c.

phrase:Stimmt's oder hab ich recht.tx: Literally, “Is it correct or am I right?”

noun:Sprech.tx: Generalized from Neusprech, from sprechen, probably influenced by similar usage of the noun sense of English speak.

noun:Schräge.tx: From Middle High German schrege, schreck. Equivalent to schräg + -e.

noun:Style.tx: Borrowed from English style. Doublet of Stiel and Stil.

noun:Schräger.tx: From schräg (“slanted”), either directly with -er or perhaps through a nominalization of the adjective (such as via schräger Strich) and a later shift away from adjectival inflection. While the exact origin is difficult to ascertain, multiple posts claim it as having been in use as jargon at Siemens, specifically. Attested by the 1990s.

verb:striegeln.tx: From Middle High German strigelen, derived from Old High German strigil, itself from Latin strigilis. By surface analysis, Striegel (“currycomb”) + -n.

noun:Sterlet.tx: From Russian сте́рлядь (stérljadʹ), itself from German Störling.

phrase:sieh mal einer an.tx: Literally, “may someone look on!”, or more loosely translated as “look at that!”. The form is actually incorrect from a strictly grammatical point of view, because it uses the imperative sieh (“see”) instead of the third-person singular subjunctive, which would be sehe (or apocopated seh). This is partly by confusion with the variant form sieh mal an, in which the imperative is correct, and …

phrase:sein wie.tx: Calque of English be like. Compare Spanish ser como.

noun:Stylist.tx: Borrowed from English stylist, equivalent to Style + -ist.

noun:Streicheleinheit.tx: From streicheln (“to carress, pet”) + Einheit (“unit”). Küpper dates it to 1970.

verb:strolchen.tx: According to DWDS, derived from German Strolch; see there for more. DWDS compares this verb also with Alemannic German strollen. English stroll stems from this set of words.

noun:Spasmus.tx: From Latin spasmus, Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”).
